country.name: United States
country.tagline: From mission vines and colonial vine laws to 280 AVAs and the most valuable Cabernet on earth.

stats.note: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026), preliminary: vineyard area includes table and raisin grapes; the US is the world's largest wine market (31.9 mhl consumed in 2025). 280 AVAs in 34 states as of October 2026 (TTB).

country.overview:
The United States is the world's fourth-largest wine producer and its largest wine market, and it makes wine in all 50 states. Yet American wine is overwhelmingly a California story: the state makes about four of every five American bottles and holds 154 of the country's 280 American Viticultural Areas. Washington, Oregon and New York form a second tier, and Virginia, Texas, Michigan, Pennsylvania and a dozen other states have serious and growing industries.

What makes American wine distinctive is not a single grape or style but a combination of freedom and science. There are no rules on what can be planted where, no yield limits and few winemaking restrictions, so growers have chosen varieties by trial, by market and by the heat-summation research of the University of California, Davis. Wines are labelled by grape variety rather than by place, a habit popularised after Prohibition by writers and importers such as Frank Schoonmaker and by Robert Mondavi, and adopted by much of the New World.

The country also has two vine worlds. East of the Rockies, native American grape species (Vitis labrusca, riparia, aestivalis, rotundifolia and others) evolved alongside phylloxera, powdery and downy mildew and Pierce's disease, which killed the European vines colonists planted for three centuries. That is why the East grew Concord, Catawba, Norton and Scuppernong, and why American native vines later saved Europe: when phylloxera crossed the Atlantic in the 1860s, rootstocks selected by Missouri and Texas scientists became the cure. Only in the 20th century, with grafting, fungicides and cold-climate pioneers like Konstantin Frank, did vinifera succeed widely in the East.

The West, with its dry Mediterranean summers, suited vinifera from the start. Franciscan missionaries brought the Mission grape north from Mexico; the Gold Rush, immigrant winemakers and the railroads built a 19th-century industry that won medals in Paris. Phylloxera and Prohibition (1920 to 1933) nearly destroyed it. The modern revival took off in the 1960s and 1970s, climaxing at the 1976 Judgment of Paris when Napa Cabernet and Chardonnay beat top Bordeaux and Burgundy in a blind tasting.

The modern map is a patchwork of distinct wine cultures. Napa and Sonoma built a luxury economy around Cabernet and estate tourism; the Central Coast and Oregon became the home of America's Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; Washington's irrigated deserts produce structured Bordeaux varieties and Syrah from own-rooted vines; the Finger Lakes made a name with Riesling; Virginia, Texas and the Midwest built regional industries on Cabernet Franc, Tempranillo, Norton and cold-hardy hybrids bred at the University of Minnesota. Much of the country's volume still comes from huge companies (E. & J. Gallo, The Wine Group, Constellation) blending California fruit, while thousands of small wineries sell directly to visitors and mailing-list customers. Direct-to-consumer shipping, legalised across most states after the Supreme Court's Granholm v. Heald ruling in 2005, transformed the economics of small producers.

Today the American wine industry faces a downturn. Consumption fell 4.3 percent in 2025 to 31.9 million hectolitres; production dropped to about 20 million hectolitres, 16 percent below the five-year average; and California growers have pulled tens of thousands of acres, with the 2025 crush the smallest in about two decades. Exports slumped in 2025, especially to Canada, where provinces pulled American wine from shelves in response to US tariffs. Wildfire and smoke (2017, 2020) and heat are the defining climate risks in the West, while new AVAs keep appearing across the country, from Tennessee to Massachusetts.

history.title: Virginia's Acte 12
history.text: The first General Assembly of the Virginia colony at Jamestown requires every householder to plant ten vines; French vignerons follow, but European vines die of disease the colonists cannot see.

history.title: First vines in New Mexico
history.text: Franciscan friars plant Mission grapes at the Piro pueblo mission of Senecú, near Socorro, to make sacramental wine: the first wine grapes in what is now the United States.

history.title: Mission San Diego and the Mission grape
history.text: Junípero Serra founds Mission San Diego de Alcalá; the Franciscans carry the Mission grape (Listán Prieto) up the chain of 21 California missions. Mission San Gabriel (1771) becomes the mother vineyard of the south.

history.title: Jefferson's failed vineyards
history.text: Thomas Jefferson plants European vines at Monticello and backs Philip Mazzei's Tuscan vineyard nearby; all fail. Jefferson concludes that native grapes may be the answer.

history.title: Longworth's sparkling Catawba
history.text: Nicholas Longworth plants Catawba near Cincinnati from 1825 and creates a celebrated sparkling wine; by 1860 Ohio leads the nation in wine production and Longfellow writes 'Catawba Wine'.

history.title: Haraszthy and Buena Vista
history.text: Agoston Haraszthy begins building California's first stone wine cellars at Buena Vista in Sonoma; in 1861 he brings back over 100,000 cuttings of more than 350 European varieties.

history.title: American rootstocks save Europe
history.text: As phylloxera ravages France, Missouri's George Husmann and Hermann Jaeger and Texas's T.V. Munson send resistant native vines and identify the rootstocks that allow Europe to replant. Jaeger receives the Légion d'honneur (1893), Munson the Mérite Agricole (1888).

history.title: Prohibition
history.text: The 18th Amendment closes most wineries. Sacramental wine (Beaulieu, Brotherhood, Concannon) and grapes shipped east for legal home winemaking keep some vineyards alive, but the industry emerges focused on sweet fortified wine.

history.title: Konstantin Frank in the Finger Lakes
history.text: Dr. Konstantin Frank releases his first vinifera wines from Keuka Lake, showing that Riesling and other European varieties can survive eastern winters when grafted.

history.title: Robert Mondavi Winery
history.text: Robert Mondavi opens the first major new winery in Napa since Prohibition, at Oakville, and campaigns for varietal labelling, French oak and cold fermentation.

history.title: Judgment of Paris
history.text: In Steven Spurrier's blind tasting in Paris, Stag's Leap Wine Cellars 1973 Cabernet and Chateau Montelena 1973 Chardonnay beat top Bordeaux and Burgundy; Time's George Taber reports it.

history.title: First AVA: Augusta
history.text: Under new rules issued in 1978, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms approves Augusta, Missouri as the first American Viticultural Area on 20 June 1980; Napa Valley follows in early 1981.

history.title: AXR1 and phylloxera biotype B
history.text: The AXR1 rootstock, widely recommended in California, fails to a new phylloxera biotype; growers replant tens of thousands of acres, often with better clones and denser spacing.

history.title: Wine-country wildfires
history.text: The October 2017 fires (Atlas, Tubbs, Nuns) and the 2020 Glass Fire and smoke burn wineries in Napa and Sonoma and cost many producers an entire vintage of reds.

history.title: Correction
history.text: Falling consumption and a grape glut lead to vine removals; California's 2025 crush is the smallest in about two decades. New AVAs still arrive: Tryon Foothills (2025), Nashoba Valley, Nine Lakes of East Tennessee and Columbia Hills (2026).

country.classification:
Wine origin in the US is regulated federally by the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB). American Viticultural Areas (AVAs) are delimited grape-growing regions defined by geography, climate and soils, proposed by petition and approved after public comment; there are 280 as of October 2026, from Ulupalakua on Maui (about 70 acres) to Ozark Mountain (about 33 million acres). Unlike European appellations, an AVA controls only origin: there are no rules on grape varieties, yields or winemaking.

Labelling rules: a wine naming an AVA must contain at least 85 percent grapes from that AVA; a state or county appellation needs 75 percent (California requires 100 percent for 'California', Oregon 95 percent for AVAs and 100 percent for the state, Washington 95 percent for AVAs). A varietal label requires at least 75 percent of the named grape (Oregon 90 percent for most varieties). A vintage date requires 95 percent from that year when an AVA is named (85 percent with a state or county). 'Estate bottled' requires the winery and vineyards to be in the same AVA. Some states require conjunctive labelling (e.g. Napa Valley must appear with any Napa sub-AVA, Sonoma County with Sonoma AVAs). Semi-generic names such as 'Champagne' and 'Chablis' can still appear on labels approved before 2006.
country.climate_soils: The US spans almost every wine climate. The Pacific coast has Mediterranean summers moderated by the cold California Current, fog and wind gaps; inland valleys are hot and dry. East of the Cascades, Washington and Idaho are semi-desert, irrigated and frozen in winter. The East and Midwest have humid continental or subtropical climates with summer rain, cold winters and disease pressure, moderated near the Great Lakes, Finger Lakes and Atlantic. The Southwest grows at altitude to escape heat. Soils range from volcanic (Napa, Lake County, Willamette's Jory) and ice-age flood gravels (Washington) to glacial till (New York), loess (Missouri, Iowa) and limestone (Paso Robles, Texas Hill Country).

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: The flagship of Napa, Sonoma, Paso Robles and Washington; the most valuable wine grape in America.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: The most planted white; from buttery California styles to taut Sonoma Coast, Santa Barbara and Willamette versions.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Oregon's signature and the star of California's coastal gaps (Russian River, Sonoma Coast, Santa Lucia Highlands, Sta. Rita Hills).

grapes.name: Zinfandel
grapes.note: Croatian Crljenak Kaštelanski (Tribidrag), but America's heritage grape; old vines in Sonoma, Lodi, Amador and Contra Costa.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.note: Important in Washington and Long Island; recovered from its 2004 'Sideways' slump.

grapes.name: Syrah
grapes.note: Washington, Paso Robles, Santa Barbara and the Rhône Rangers.

grapes.name: Concord
grapes.note: Native labrusca grape dominating the Lake Erie belt, mainly for juice.

grapes.name: Norton
grapes.note: Native American red, Missouri's state grape and a Virginia heritage variety.

grapes.name: Muscadine (Scuppernong)
grapes.note: Native southern grape resistant to Pierce's disease; sweet, musky wines.

grapes.name: Cold-hardy hybrids
grapes.note: Marquette, Frontenac, La Crescent from the University of Minnesota allow wine in the upper Midwest and New England.

regions.name: Napa Valley
regions.tagline: Fifty kilometres of valley floor and mountain that taught the world to take American Cabernet seriously.
regions.summary:
Napa Valley is small by California standards: about 45,000 acres (roughly 18,000 ha) of vines, around 4 percent of the state's wine grapes, yet it earns a share of the value and prestige out of all proportion to its size. The valley runs about 50 km from the tidal marshes of San Pablo Bay north to the volcanic bulk of Mount St. Helena, squeezed between the Mayacamas Mountains on the west and the Vaca Range on the east.

Cabernet Sauvignon is the crown, and the land under it is sliced into 17 nested AVAs inside the Napa Valley AVA. The logic of the map follows two gradients. North to south, the valley warms as you move away from the cool bay: Los Carneros and Coombsville get the fog and wind, Calistoga the heat. Valley floor to mountain, the alluvial benches of Rutherford and Oakville give generous, polished Cabernet while the mountain AVAs (Howell Mountain, Spring Mountain District, Mt. Veeder, Diamond Mountain District, Atlas Peak) sit above the fog in thin, rocky soils and give tighter, more tannic wines that age for decades.
regions.history:
George C. Yount, the first American settler in the valley, planted Mission vines around 1838. Charles Krug opened a commercial winery at St. Helena in 1861, and by the 1880s the valley had well over a hundred wineries, among them Gustave Niebaum's Inglenook and the Beringer brothers' Rhine House. Phylloxera in the 1890s and Prohibition (1920 to 1933) nearly erased that first golden age; Beaulieu survived on sacramental wine and, from 1938, the winemaking of André Tchelistcheff.

The modern era began in 1966, when Robert Mondavi built the first major new winery in the valley since Prohibition, at Oakville. Two years later Napa County created the Agricultural Preserve (1968), the first of its kind in the United States, which zoned the valley floor for farming and saved it from suburban sprawl. In 1976, at Steven Spurrier's blind tasting in Paris, Stag's Leap Wine Cellars 1973 Cabernet and Chateau Montelena 1973 Chardonnay beat top Bordeaux and Burgundy, and Napa became a global name. Napa Valley was approved as an AVA in 1981, the first in California. The 1990s brought a forced replanting when phylloxera biotype B overwhelmed the widely used AXR1 rootstock; growers used the moment to replant at higher density with better clones. Wildfires in 2017 (Atlas Fire) and 2020 (Glass Fire) burned wineries on Atlas Peak, Spring Mountain and Howell Mountain, and smoke cost many producers their 2020 reds.
regions.terroir: Napa is a geological jumble: volcanic ash and lava from the Sonoma Volcanics, uplifted marine sediments, and gravelly alluvial fans washed down from both ranges. Wine writers like to repeat the claim, popular with the vintners' association, that half of the world's soil orders occur here. Climate is Mediterranean, with dry summers and wet winters. Fog and wind from San Pablo Bay cool the south; the narrow north end around Calistoga is several degrees warmer by afternoon. On the mountains, vines above the fog line (roughly 300 to 450 m) get more hours of sun but cooler nights and less vigour, which is why mountain Cabernet has smaller berries, firmer tannin and higher natural acidity.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon dominates both plantings and prices, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot and Malbec for blending. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are concentrated in Los Carneros and Oak Knoll; Sauvignon Blanc is the main white. Old Zinfandel, Petite Sirah and Charbono survive in pockets, especially around Calistoga.
regions.styles: Full-bodied Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux blends are the headline: ripe cassis and dark plum, cedar and mocha from new French oak, and a velvety mouthfeel on the valley floor. Mountain wines are more structured. Chardonnay ranges from buttery to tense; Carneros makes serious traditional-method sparkling wine.
regions.classification: Labels carry the Napa Valley AVA or one of its 17 sub-AVAs. California law (the Napa conjunctive labeling rule) requires any wine labeled with a Napa sub-AVA to also state Napa Valley on the label. The federal 85 percent AVA rule applies; there is no official vineyard classification, though names like To Kalon, Martha's Vineyard and Stags Leap's S.L.V. work as unofficial grands crus.
appellations: Oak Knoll District of Napa Valley

regions.name: Sonoma County
regions.tagline: Coast, fog and redwoods on one side, Zinfandel benchland and Cabernet valleys on the other: California's most varied county.
regions.summary:
Sonoma County has roughly three times Napa's land area and close to 60,000 acres of vines, and it behaves less like one region than like a dozen. The Pacific is the organising force. Cold ocean air and fog push inland through gaps in the coastal hills (the Petaluma Gap, the Russian River corridor, the Estero Lowlands), so a 30-minute drive can take you from vineyards that struggle to ripen Pinot Noir to valleys where Zinfandel and Cabernet Sauvignon bake.

The cool west (Sonoma Coast, West Sonoma Coast, Fort Ross-Seaview, Russian River Valley, Green Valley, Petaluma Gap) is some of the best Pinot Noir and Chardonnay ground in the New World. The warm north and east (Dry Creek, Alexander, Knights valleys, Rockpile, Sonoma Valley's mountain sides) give old-vine Zinfandel, Cabernet and Rhône varieties. Northern Sonoma ties most of the northern AVAs together.
regions.history:
Russian colonists of the Russian-American Company founded Fort Ross on the coast in 1812 and are said to have planted vines there by 1817. Franciscans founded Mission San Francisco Solano at Sonoma in 1823, the last and northernmost of California's 21 missions, and General Mariano Vallejo took over its vineyards after secularisation. The Hungarian adventurer Agoston Haraszthy bought land near Sonoma in 1856, renamed it Buena Vista and in 1857 began building the first stone cellars in California; in 1861 he brought back more than 100,000 cuttings of over 350 European varieties. Italian Swiss Colony at Asti (1881) and families like the Simis, Foppianos, Pedroncellis and Seghesios made the north county a Zinfandel and jug-wine powerhouse.

After Prohibition the county lagged behind Napa until a wave of Burgundy-minded growers arrived. James Zellerbach planted Hanzell in 1953 and brought French oak barrels to California. In the 1970s and 1980s Joseph Swan, Rochioli, Williams Selyem, Dehlinger and Kistler built the Russian River Valley's reputation, and from 1980 David Hirsch and others pushed vines onto the ridges above the coastal fog. The October 2017 Tubbs Fire burned from Calistoga into Santa Rosa through the Fountaingrove District.
regions.terroir: Geology is a jumble along the San Andreas fault zone: Franciscan marine sediments, Sonoma Volcanics in the Mayacamas and Sonoma Mountain, and the fine, sandy Goldridge loam of the Russian River Valley and Green Valley, an ancient sea-bottom sandstone that drains well and is prized for Pinot Noir. Climate depends on fog and wind penetration: the coastal ridges above about 300 m sit in sun while fog fills the valleys below, the Russian River Valley gets fog on most summer mornings, and the northern valleys are warm and dry.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay dominate the cool south and west; Zinfandel (including some of California's oldest vines), Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc, Syrah and Petite Sirah dominate the north and east. Sonoma also grows Gewürztraminer, Grenache, Carignan and the field blends of old vineyards.
regions.styles: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with bright acidity from the coast; plush, spicy Zinfandel from Dry Creek and Rockpile; fleshy Alexander Valley Cabernet; traditional-method sparkling from Green Valley and Russian River.
regions.classification: The county name 'Sonoma County' is a legal appellation in its own right. There are 19 AVAs wholly or partly in the county, nested in layers: North Coast contains Northern Sonoma and Sonoma Coast, which contain many smaller AVAs. California law requires wines labeled with a Sonoma County AVA to also carry 'Sonoma County' (conjunctive labeling, in force since 2014).
appellations: Green Valley of Russian River Valley

regions.name: Mendocino County
regions.tagline: Redwoods, fog and old Italian vines: California's northernmost serious wine county, and a pioneer of organic farming.
regions.summary:
Mendocino County has around 16,000 to 17,000 acres of vines split between two different worlds. The cool Anderson Valley and the coastal ridges feel the Pacific and grow Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Gewürztraminer and sparkling wine. Inland, the warm Ukiah, Redwood and Potter valleys along the upper Russian River grow Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Carignan, Cabernet and Rhône varieties, much of it on old, dry-farmed vines planted by Italian families.

Mendocino has a higher share of certified organic and biodynamic vineyards than almost any US county, a legacy of Fetzer's organic commitment in the 1980s and of the county's back-to-the-land culture.
regions.history: Gold Rush-era farmers planted vines in the 1850s, and Italian immigrants built the inland industry around Ukiah and Redwood Valley before Prohibition. Parducci (1932) was the county's first post-Prohibition winery. Barney Fetzer founded Fetzer in Redwood Valley in 1968, and Roederer Estate brought Champagne investment to the Anderson Valley in 1982. In 2004 Mendocino became the first US county to ban the growing of genetically modified organisms.
regions.terroir: Coastal hills of Franciscan sandstone and redwood forest; the Anderson Valley channels fog inland from the Navarro River mouth. Inland valleys have deep alluvial soils and hot summers. Mendocino Ridge vineyards sit above the fog on isolated ridgetops.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Gewürztraminer and Riesling in the Anderson Valley; Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Carignan, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Sauvignon Blanc inland.
regions.styles: Traditional-method sparkling wine; lean, aromatic Pinot Noir; Alsace-style whites; old-vine Zinfandel and Carignan.
regions.classification: Mendocino AVA covers the main valleys; 'Mendocino County' is also a legal county appellation. Sub-AVAs are listed below.

regions.name: Lake County
regions.tagline: High-elevation volcanic country around California's largest natural lake.
regions.summary: Lake County sits over the Mayacamas from Napa and Sonoma, around Clear Lake, the largest natural freshwater lake wholly within California. Vineyards are high, mostly from 400 to more than 800 m, under bright sun with cold nights, and many grow in red, obsidian-studded volcanic soils from Mount Konocti and the Clear Lake volcanic field. Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet Sauvignon are the stars, and Napa wineries buy a great deal of Lake County fruit.
regions.history: Before Prohibition Lake County had more than 30 wineries. The English actress Lillie Langtry bought land in Guenoc Valley in 1888 and planned to make wine there. After Prohibition the vines were mostly pulled for walnuts and pears, and the replanting came from the 1960s onward.
regions.terroir: Volcanic soils, high elevation and clean air give intense UV and large day-night temperature swings. Clear Lake moderates temperatures near its shores.
regions.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah, Zinfandel, Merlot, Syrah.
regions.styles: Crisp, grassy Sauvignon Blanc and firm, dark Cabernet at good prices.
regions.classification: Clear Lake is the umbrella AVA around the lake; several smaller AVAs sit within it.

regions.name: Central Coast
regions.tagline: Four hundred kilometres of coast where east-west valleys pull the Pacific inland: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Rhône blends and mountain Cabernet.
regions.summary:
The Central Coast AVA stretches from the San Francisco Bay Area to Santa Barbara County, about 6.8 million acres with roughly 100,000 acres of vines. What unites it is the cold California Current. Where the Coast Ranges run north-south, they block the ocean and the inland valleys bake; where valleys open east-west (the Santa Ynez and Santa Maria valleys, the Salinas Valley funnel from Monterey Bay, the Templeton Gap), fog and wind pour inland and create some of the coolest vineyard climates in California.

The Central Coast contains Monterey's vast Salinas Valley plantings, the Santa Cruz Mountains' historic estates, Paso Robles with its 11 districts, and Santa Barbara County's cool-climate Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
regions.history: Franciscan missions planted vines from San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo (1770) to Santa Barbara (1786) and San Luis Obispo. In the 19th century Paul Masson and others built the Santa Cruz Mountains' reputation, and in Livermore Charles Wetmore, Carl Wente and James Concannon planted French cuttings in the 1880s. The modern era came in waves: Martin Ray and Dick Graff (Chalone) in the mountains, mass planting of the Salinas Valley in the 1970s, Santa Barbara's Pinot Noir pioneers (Sanford & Benedict, 1971) and the Rhône Rangers of Paso Robles in the 1980s and 1990s. The film Sideways (2004) made Santa Barbara Pinot Noir briefly the most fashionable wine in America.
regions.terroir: Geology is extremely varied: granite and limestone in the Gabilan and Santa Lucia ranges, calcareous soils on Paso Robles' west side and in Mt. Harlan, marine sediments and diatomaceous earth in Santa Barbara. Marine air governs everything.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Zinfandel, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling.
regions.styles: Bright, saline Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; Rhône blends; Paso Robles Cabernet and Zinfandel; mountain Cabernet from the Santa Cruz Mountains.
regions.classification: Central Coast is an umbrella AVA. California's 85 percent AVA rule applies; Paso Robles wines from its districts must also show 'Paso Robles' (state conjunctive labeling law).

regions.name: Santa Barbara County
regions.tagline: Where the mountains turn sideways and the Pacific pours in: California's coolest serious Pinot Noir country.
regions.summary:
Santa Barbara County's secret is geography. Here the Transverse Ranges run east-west, so the Santa Maria and Santa Ynez valleys open straight onto the Pacific and act as wind tunnels for cold ocean air. The result is a temperature gradient you can drive through: Sta. Rita Hills at the western end, near Lompoc, is as cool as anywhere in California; Ballard Canyon and Los Olivos are moderate; Happy Canyon in the east is warm enough for Cabernet Sauvignon.

The county has about 15,000 acres of vines and seven AVAs nested inside the Central Coast.
regions.history: Mission Santa Barbara (1786) and Mission Santa Inés (1804) grew Mission grapes. Modern planting began around 1964 to 1971: Uriel Nielsen planted in the Santa Maria Valley in 1964, and Richard Sanford and Michael Benedict planted Pinot Noir and Chardonnay west of Buellton in 1971, a vineyard that became the founding block of Sta. Rita Hills. Bien Nacido (1973), Au Bon Climat (Jim Clendenen, 1982) and Qupé (Bob Lindquist) followed. Sideways (2004) was filmed here.
regions.terroir: Marine sediments, sandy loams and diatomaceous earth in the west; serpentine soils in Happy Canyon; calcareous soils in Ballard Canyon and Los Olivos. Strong afternoon winds and morning fog.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay in the west; Syrah, Grenache, Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon toward the east.
regions.styles: Taut, saline Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; peppery Syrah; Bordeaux varieties from Happy Canyon.
regions.classification: Seven AVAs inside the Central Coast AVA; Santa Ynez Valley contains Sta. Rita Hills, Ballard Canyon, Los Olivos District and Happy Canyon of Santa Barbara.

regions.name: Paso Robles
regions.tagline: A big, hot, limestone-laced district split in two by Highway 101 and subdivided into 11 AVAs.
regions.summary:
Paso Robles is a big AVA, about 610,000 acres with some 40,000 acres of vines and more than 200 wineries. Highway 101 is the cultural divide. The west side, in the Santa Lucia foothills, has calcareous soils, more rainfall and cool air from the Templeton Gap; it grows Rhône varieties, Zinfandel and structured Cabernet. The east side is flatter, hotter and higher-yielding, with alluvial soils and Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot for larger brands.

In 2014 TTB split the AVA into 11 districts based on soils, rainfall and temperature. Paso Robles has one of the largest daily temperature swings in California, often 20 degrees Celsius or more between afternoon and night.
regions.history: Franciscans at Mission San Miguel planted vines in the late 18th century. Zinfandel arrived with Andrew York at York Mountain in 1882 and with Italian families such as the Pesentis and Dusis in the Templeton area. The Polish pianist Ignacy Paderewski planted Zinfandel on his Rancho San Ignacio in the 1910s. The Rhône revival started when Gary Eberle (1970s) and especially Tablas Creek (the Perrins of Château de Beaucastel and Robert Haas, from 1989) imported French clones.
regions.terroir: Calcareous shale and limestone on the west side, alluvial and sandy soils on the east, granitic soils in parts of Creston; summer heat moderated by marine air through the Templeton Gap.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Petite Sirah, Merlot, Roussanne, Viognier.
regions.styles: Ripe Cabernet; powerful Zinfandel; Rhône blends ('GSM') and Châteauneuf-style whites.
regions.classification: Paso Robles AVA plus 11 district AVAs (2014). Wines labeled with a district must also carry 'Paso Robles'.

regions.name: California
regions.tagline: Four of every five bottles of American wine, from Mission-grape beginnings to the most expensive Cabernet on earth.
regions.summary:
California makes roughly 80 percent of all US wine and would rank among the world's largest producers if it were a country. It has 154 of the 280 American AVAs. Its wine geography is a contest between the cold Pacific and the hot interior. Along the coast, the cold California Current and the Coast Ranges create fog belts and wind gaps; where valleys open to the sea (Carneros, the Petaluma Gap, the Salinas Valley, the Santa Ynez Valley) Pinot Noir and Chardonnay thrive. Behind the coastal mountains, Napa, Sonoma's inland valleys and Paso Robles give Cabernet, Zinfandel and Rhône varieties. The vast Central Valley, irrigated and hot, grows most of the state's tonnage for everyday wine, while Lodi and the Sierra Foothills keep some of the world's oldest Zinfandel vines.

The industry is in a correction. After years of falling US consumption and a glut of grapes, growers pulled tens of thousands of acres from 2023 onward. The preliminary 2025 crush was 2.76 million tons, down 6.2 percent from 2024 and the smallest in about two decades, with an average price of 979 dollars a ton. OIV puts US vineyard area at 415,000 ha in 2025, the seventh straight year of decline, mainly because of uprooting in California.
regions.history:
Franciscan friars brought the Mission grape (Listán Prieto) north from Mexico; Junípero Serra is traditionally credited with the first planting at Mission San Diego de Alcalá in 1769, and Mission San Gabriel became the mother vineyard of the south. Jean-Louis Vignes, a Bordelais, imported French vines to Los Angeles in the 1830s. The Gold Rush (1848) created a market, Agoston Haraszthy's Buena Vista (1857) and 1861 vine-collecting trip widened the range of varieties, and by the 1880s California wines were winning medals in Paris. Phylloxera, then Prohibition (1920 to 1933), wrecked the industry; growers survived by shipping grapes east for legal home winemaking, which favoured thick-skinned Alicante Bouschet over fine varieties.

Recovery was slow until the 1960s. UC Davis (Maynard Amerine and Albert Winkler's heat-summation regions, 1944) supplied science; Robert Mondavi (1966) supplied ambition; the 1976 Judgment of Paris supplied fame. The 1980s and 1990s brought the AXR1 phylloxera disaster and replanting, the rise of cult Cabernets and a Rhône movement. Since 2017 wildfire and smoke, drought and heat have become the defining risks.
regions.terroir: Mediterranean climate: dry summers, wet winters. Heat summation runs from Region I (cool coast) to Region V (Central Valley). Soils range from volcanic to marine sedimentary, granitic and alluvial. Most quality vineyards are drip-irrigated.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay are the most planted wine grapes, followed by Pinot Noir, Zinfandel, Merlot, French Colombard, Rubired, Sauvignon Blanc, Syrah and Pinot Gris.
regions.styles: Everything from bulk wine and fortified wine to world-famous Cabernet, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and sparkling wine.
regions.classification: AVAs under federal law (85 percent of grapes from the AVA); a wine labeled 'California' must be 100 percent California grapes. County names are also legal appellations (75 percent). State law requires conjunctive labeling for Napa, Sonoma, Paso Robles and Lodi sub-AVAs.

regions.name: Lodi
regions.tagline: Old, own-rooted Zinfandel on sandy river soils: the grower capital of California.
regions.summary: Lodi, in the northern San Joaquin Valley between Sacramento and Stockton, grows a large share of California's premium wine grapes, much of it sold to wineries elsewhere. Afternoon breezes from San Francisco Bay through the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta cool it more than the Central Valley to the south. Its glory is old-vine Zinfandel, head-trained and often own-rooted in deep, sandy soils where phylloxera struggles to survive. Lodi also grows Cinsault, Carignan and a growing list of Iberian and German varieties.
regions.history: German farmers who moved from the Dakotas settled Lodi in the late 19th century and planted Zinfandel and Flame Tokay table grapes. Many families still farm the same land. The Bechthold Vineyard's Cinsault was planted in 1886. The Lodi AVA was approved in 1986 and expanded in 2002, and in 2006 TTB created seven sub-AVAs. Lodi Rules, launched in 2005, was California's first third-party certified sustainable winegrowing programme.
regions.terroir: Deep sandy loam on the Mokelumne River fan in the west; clay and cobbly soils in the eastern foothills (Clements Hills, Borden Ranch). Delta breezes.
regions.grapes: Zinfandel, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Merlot, Cinsault, Carignan, Petite Sirah, Albariño, Tempranillo.
regions.styles: Ripe, spicy Zinfandel; light, perfumed old-vine Cinsault; everyday varietals.
regions.classification: Lodi AVA with seven sub-AVAs (2006); sub-AVA labels must also carry 'Lodi'.

regions.name: Sierra Foothills
regions.tagline: Gold Rush country, where miners planted Zinfandel and some of the vines are still alive.
regions.summary: The Sierra Foothills AVA follows the western slopes of the Sierra Nevada through eight counties from Yuba south to Mariposa, mostly between 300 and 900 m. Summers are hot and dry, nights cool, and soils are decomposed granite and volcanic loam. Amador County's Shenandoah Valley is the heart of old-vine Zinfandel; El Dorado and Fair Play climb higher for Rhône, Barbera and cooler-climate varieties.
regions.history: Miners and the merchants who fed them planted vines during the Gold Rush of the 1850s; by the 1890s there were more than a hundred wineries. Prohibition and the end of mining emptied the hills, but some old Zinfandel survived, including the Original Grandpère vineyard in Amador, claimed to have been planted before 1869. Sutter Home's Amador Zinfandel from Deaver Vineyard (1968) brought the region back to attention, and a stuck fermentation of Zinfandel at Sutter Home in 1975 gave the world White Zinfandel.
regions.terroir: Decomposed granite and volcanic soils, elevations of 300 to 1,000 m, hot days and cool nights.
regions.grapes: Zinfandel, Barbera, Syrah, Petite Sirah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Sangiovese, Cabernet Sauvignon.
regions.styles: Full, spicy Zinfandel and juicy Barbera; Rhône blends from higher elevations.
regions.classification: Sierra Foothills umbrella AVA with five sub-AVAs.

regions.name: Southern California
regions.tagline: Where California wine began, then vanished under freeways: missions, Cucamonga's old vines, Temecula's wineries and Malibu's hillsides.
regions.summary:
Southern California was the first wine region of the state. Mission San Gabriel (founded 1771) became the mother vineyard; Los Angeles was the wine capital of California in the 1840s and 1850s; and the Cucamonga Valley east of LA had more than 20,000 acres of vines in the early 20th century. Urban growth and Pierce's disease erased most of it.

Today the main centre is Temecula Valley, with dozens of tourist-oriented wineries, plus small AVAs from the Malibu hills to the high desert and San Diego County, where two new AVAs were approved in 2024 and two more (Rancho Guejito, Rancho Santa Fe) were proposed in 2024 and 2026.
regions.history: Jean-Louis Vignes planted French vines in Los Angeles in the 1830s. Anaheim was founded in 1857 by German winegrowers; its vineyards were wiped out in the 1880s by a mysterious vine disease, later identified as Pierce's disease. Secondo Guasti's Italian Vineyard Company at Cucamonga (from 1900) claimed to be the largest vineyard in the world. In 1999 to 2000 the glassy-winged sharpshooter spread Pierce's disease through Temecula.
regions.terroir: Warm Mediterranean to semi-arid climate, tempered by marine air through coastal gaps; sandy and decomposed granite soils.
regions.grapes: Zinfandel, Mission, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Grenache, Viognier, Sangiovese.
regions.styles: Rhône and Mediterranean reds; old-vine Zinfandel; rosé.
regions.classification: South Coast umbrella AVA plus independent AVAs in Los Angeles, San Bernardino and Kern counties.
appellations: Antelope Valley of the California High Desert

regions.name: Central Valley
regions.tagline: The irrigated heartland where most California wine by volume is grown.
regions.summary: The Central Valley (the Sacramento and San Joaquin valleys) is one of the world's most productive farm regions, and its hot, irrigated vineyards supply most of California's wine by volume, along with table grapes and raisins. Big producers such as E. & J. Gallo (Modesto) are based here. A handful of AVAs cover the cooler foothill margins and the Delta.
regions.history: Large-scale planting followed irrigation projects in the late 19th and 20th centuries. After Prohibition the valley made fortified 'port' and 'sherry' and later jug wine. Madera became known for fortified Muscat and port-style wines (Ficklin, Quady).
regions.terroir: Deep alluvial soils, very hot summers, irrigation from Sierra snowmelt.
regions.grapes: French Colombard, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Rubired, Muscat, Merlot.
regions.styles: Everyday wine, fortified and sweet Muscats.
regions.classification: Few AVAs; most wine is labeled California.

regions.name: Oregon
regions.tagline: America's Pinot Noir state, built by small growers who ignored the experts.
regions.summary:
Oregon has more than 1,100 wineries and roughly 44,000 acres of vines (2022 census), fourth in the US by production after California, Washington and New York, and more than half the acreage is Pinot Noir. Almost everything important happens west of the Cascades in the Willamette Valley, a cool, rainy valley that the University of California's professors told the first growers was too cold for wine. Southern Oregon is warmer and more varied; the Columbia Gorge, Walla Walla and Snake River Valley AVAs reach into the dry interior.

Oregon's identity is small, family-owned, sustainability-minded and Burgundian. The state's labeling law is stricter than federal rules: most varietal wines must be at least 90 percent of the named grape (federal minimum 75 percent), and vintage-dated AVA wines need 95 percent from the AVA.
regions.history:
Henderson Luelling brought grapevines to Oregon Territory over the Oregon Trail in 1847, and Peter Britt opened Valley View winery at Jacksonville in 1852. Prohibition and its aftermath left the industry dormant for decades. In 1961 Richard Sommer planted Riesling at HillCrest in the Umpqua Valley, Oregon's oldest continuously operating estate winery. Then a group of mostly Californian dropouts arrived: David Lett (The Eyrie Vineyards, first Pinot Noir in the Willamette Valley in 1965 and 1966), Charles Coury, Dick Erath, David Adelsheim, Dick Ponzi and the Sokol Blossers.

In 1979 Eyrie's 1975 South Block Reserve Pinot Noir placed among the top Pinots at the Gault-Millau 'Wine Olympics' in Paris; at Robert Drouhin's 1980 rematch in Beaune it finished a close second to his 1959 Chambolle-Musigny. Drouhin bought land in the Dundee Hills and opened Domaine Drouhin Oregon in 1988. Since then Burgundian families (Lafon, Louis Jadot, Bouchard via Henriot, Lingua Franca with Dominique Lafon) and Californian and Champagne companies have invested heavily.
regions.terroir: Marine-influenced, cool and wet in winter, dry and warm in summer; the Coast Range shelters the Willamette Valley from Pacific storms, while the Van Duzer Corridor lets cooling winds in. The Willamette's three key soil families are volcanic Jory (from Columbia River basalt flows about 15 million years ago), marine sedimentary soils (Willakenzie and relatives) and wind-blown Laurelwood loess. Southern Oregon is warmer and drier with very old, varied geology.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir dominates, then Pinot Gris, Chardonnay, Riesling, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Merlot and Gamay.
regions.styles: Pinot Noir of perfume and acidity; increasingly serious Chardonnay; Pinot Gris; sparkling wine; Tempranillo and Syrah from the south.
regions.classification: Federal AVAs plus stricter state rules: most varietals need 90 percent of the stated grape; AVA wines need 95 percent of grapes from that AVA. Oregon has 23 AVAs wholly or partly in the state.

regions.name: Willamette Valley
regions.tagline: A cool, green valley between the Coast Range and the Cascades where Oregon proved it could grow great Pinot Noir.
regions.summary: The Willamette Valley AVA (1983) runs about 240 km from the Columbia River near Portland south to Eugene and holds roughly two-thirds of Oregon's vineyards and most of its wineries. Vineyards sit on the foothills and isolated hill groups on the valley's west side, mostly between 60 and 300 m, above the frost-prone valley floor and the old flood sediments. It is subdivided into 11 nested AVAs, each defined largely by soil and exposure to Pacific wind.
regions.history: See Oregon: Eyrie (1965 to 1966), Erath, Adelsheim, Ponzi, Sokol Blosser and the Drouhins set the pattern. The valley floor's sediments came from the Missoula Floods, ice-age deluges that backed up the Willamette and dropped erratic boulders from Montana; vineyards prefer the older hillside soils above them.
regions.terroir: Three soil families shape style: volcanic Jory (red, iron-rich, from Columbia River basalt) in the Dundee Hills, Eola-Amity Hills and parts of the Chehalem Mountains; marine sedimentary soils (Willakenzie) in Yamhill-Carlton and Ribbon Ridge; and wind-blown loess (Laurelwood) in the Chehalem Mountains and Tualatin Hills. Ocean wind through the Van Duzer Corridor cools the western side every afternoon.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir (the majority), Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc, Riesling, Gamay.
regions.styles: Pinot Noir of red-fruit perfume and silky texture; Chardonnay of tension; traditional-method sparkling wine.
regions.classification: Willamette Valley AVA plus 11 sub-AVAs (2004 to 2022).

regions.name: Southern Oregon
regions.tagline: Warm valleys under old mountains: Tempranillo, Syrah and Bordeaux varieties alongside Pinot Noir.
regions.summary: Southern Oregon (2004) joins the Umpqua and Rogue valleys, both warmer and drier than the Willamette. The Klamath Mountains and Coast Range here contain some of the oldest and most varied rocks in Oregon, and the climate ranges from cool, Pacific-influenced Elkton to the hot, dry Rogue Valley near Medford. Abacela's Earl and Hilda Jones planted Tempranillo in the Umpqua in 1995, and Syrah, Grenache, Albariño, Viognier, Cabernet and Merlot all grow well.
regions.history: Peter Britt founded Valley View winery at Jacksonville in 1852, and Richard Sommer's HillCrest (1961) near Roseburg restarted Oregon wine after Prohibition.
regions.terroir: Complex geology: marine sediments, volcanic and metamorphic rocks; warm, dry summers with big day-night swings.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir, Syrah, Tempranillo, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Viognier, Albariño, Grenache.
regions.styles: Warm-climate reds and aromatic whites; cool-climate Pinot Noir from Elkton.
regions.classification: Southern Oregon contains Umpqua Valley (with Elkton Oregon and Red Hill Douglas County, Oregon) and Rogue Valley (with Applegate Valley).

regions.name: Washington
regions.tagline: Desert vineyards on ice-age flood soils, irrigated by the Columbia: America's second-largest wine state.
regions.summary:
Washington is the second-largest wine producer in the United States, with more than 1,000 wineries and about 60,000 acres of vines, nearly all east of the Cascade Mountains. The Cascades block Pacific storms, leaving the Columbia Basin a semi-desert with 150 to 250 mm of rain a year, hot summer days, cold nights and, at 46 degrees north, around 17 hours of summer daylight. Irrigation from the Columbia, Yakima and Snake rivers makes viticulture possible.

With the Columbia Hills AVA (2026), Washington has 22 AVAs, almost all inside the vast Columbia Valley. The big, consistent style (deep colour, ripe fruit and fresh acidity) suits Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah, and Riesling made the state's name in the 1970s and 1980s.
regions.history: Vines arrived with the Hudson's Bay Company at Fort Vancouver around 1825, and Italian and German immigrants planted in the Walla Walla and Yakima valleys in the late 19th century. After Prohibition, the industry made sweet fortified wine from Concord and other grapes. The modern era began with Associated Vintners, founded by a group of University of Washington professors led by Lloyd Woodburne (first commercial vintage 1967), and with the American Wine Growers company that became Chateau Ste. Michelle, which hired André Tchelistcheff as a consultant in 1967. Leonetti (1977), Woodward Canyon (1981) and L'Ecole No 41 (1983) put Walla Walla on the map; Quilceda Creek's Cabernets earned perfect scores in the 2000s.
regions.terroir: Between about 15,000 and 13,000 years ago the Missoula Floods repeatedly burst from glacial Lake Missoula in Montana and scoured eastern Washington, depositing sand, silt and gravel over Columbia River basalt. Wind then piled up fine loess. These sandy, low-organic soils are hostile to phylloxera, so most Washington vines are planted on their own roots, unusual among major wine regions. The trade-off is winter freezes: severe cold events (1996, 2004, 2024) can kill vines to the ground, and growers bury graft unions or rely on own-rooted vines that can regrow from below the soil.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Chardonnay, Riesling, Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Sauvignon Blanc, Grenache.
regions.styles: Structured Cabernet and Bordeaux blends; plush Merlot; savoury Syrah; off-dry and dry Riesling.
regions.classification: Federal AVA rules (85 percent), but Washington requires 95 percent from the AVA for wines labeled with one. Washington has 22 AVAs, including those shared with Oregon and Idaho.

regions.summary: Columbia Valley (1984, realigned 2001 and 2016) covers about a quarter of Washington plus a slice of Oregon. regions.name: Idaho
regions.tagline: High-desert vineyards along the Snake River, at some of the highest elevations in the Northwest.
regions.summary: Idaho has around 70 wineries and a few thousand acres of vines, mostly in the Snake River Valley west of Boise, at elevations of roughly 600 to 900 m. Hot days, cold nights and volcanic and lake-bed soils give fresh Riesling, Syrah, Tempranillo and Cabernet. Cold winters are the main risk. The Lewis-Clark Valley on the Idaho-Washington border, at a much lower elevation, was a thriving wine region before Prohibition.
regions.history: French and German settlers planted vines around Lewiston from the 1860s, and the Lewis-Clark area was the centre of a small pre-Prohibition industry. Statewide prohibition, which Idaho adopted in 1916, ended it. Ste. Chapelle (1975) led the revival.
regions.terroir: Lake Idaho sediments and volcanic soils in the Snake River Plain; wide temperature swings.
regions.grapes: Riesling, Syrah, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Tempranillo, Malbec.
regions.styles: Aromatic whites and fresh, high-elevation reds.
regions.classification: Three AVAs: Snake River Valley (shared with Oregon), Eagle Foothills, Lewis-Clark Valley (shared with Washington).

regions.name: New York
regions.tagline: Riesling on glacial lakes, Merlot by the sea, and America's oldest winery in the Hudson Valley.
regions.summary: New York is the third- or fourth-largest US wine state by volume, depending on the year, and second only to California in grapes grown, because the Lake Erie shore is a huge Concord juice-grape belt. Wine grapes cover about 11,000 acres, with roughly 470 wineries across 11 AVAs. The Finger Lakes, with Riesling as its flagship, is the quality heart; Long Island's maritime vineyards grow Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Chardonnay; the Hudson Valley has the longest history; and the Niagara Escarpment and Lake Erie hug the Great Lakes.
regions.history:
Grapes were planted on Manhattan by the Dutch in the 1640s and by Huguenots in Ulster County in the 1670s. The Hudson Valley had commercial vineyards by 1827 (Croton Point), and Brotherhood Winery at Washingtonville made its first commercial vintage in 1839. In the Finger Lakes, Rev. William Bostwick planted vines at Hammondsport in 1829, and the Pleasant Valley Wine Company (1860) made 'Great Western' sparkling wine that won in Paris in 1867.

After Prohibition, labrusca and hybrid grapes ruled until Dr. Konstantin Frank, a Ukrainian-born viticulturist who arrived at Cornell's Geneva station in 1953, persuaded Charles Fournier of Gold Seal that vinifera could survive the winters if grafted onto the right rootstocks. Frank released his first vinifera vintage in 1962. Hermann J. Wiemer (1979) followed. The Farm Winery Act of 1976 let small grape growers open wineries, and their number grew from 19 in 1976 to hundreds today. Alex and Louisa Hargrave planted Long Island's first commercial vineyard in 1973.
regions.terroir: Great Lakes and the deep Finger Lakes moderate winter cold and delay spring budbreak; glacial soils (shale, limestone, gravel) dominate upstate. Long Island has sandy, well-drained glacial outwash and a maritime climate with a long growing season.
regions.grapes: Concord and Niagara for juice; Riesling, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Gewürztraminer, Lemberger (Blaufränkisch), Saperavi; hybrids such as Seyval Blanc, Vidal and Baco Noir.
regions.styles: Dry and off-dry Riesling; ice wine; Cabernet Franc; Long Island Merlot and rosé; sparkling wine.
regions.classification: 11 AVAs; New York's Finger Lakes Riesling uses the International Riesling Foundation sweetness scale on many labels.

regions.name: Virginia
regions.tagline: Where English colonists were ordered to plant vines in 1619, and where Jefferson failed so the state could succeed.
regions.summary: Virginia has more than 300 wineries and roughly 4,000 to 5,000 acres of vines, concentrated in the Piedmont along the Blue Ridge, where elevation and hillside air drainage reduce the humidity, frost and disease that plague the eastern lowlands. The state has 9 AVAs. Its best wines are Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Bordeaux blends, Viognier (promoted as the state grape) and Petit Manseng, plus the native Norton.
regions.history:
In 1619 the first General Assembly of the Virginia colony, meeting at Jamestown, passed Acte 12, requiring every householder to plant and tend at least ten vines, and the Virginia Company sent French vignerons from Languedoc. Vinifera died of phylloxera, mildews and Pierce's disease, though the colonists did not know why. Thomas Jefferson planted European vines at Monticello from 1770 and backed Philip Mazzei's Tuscan vineyard nearby (1774); none succeeded. Around 1820 to 1830 Dr. Daniel Norton of Richmond introduced the Norton grape, a native American variety, and Norton from Virginia and Missouri won medals in Europe in the 1870s.

The modern era began in the 1970s; the Zonin family of Italy founded Barboursville Vineyards in 1976 on the ruins of Governor James Barbour's estate, whose mansion Jefferson designed. Virginia now draws wine tourism to Charlottesville, Loudoun County and the Shenandoah Valley.
regions.terroir: Humid continental to subtropical climate with summer rain; the Blue Ridge foothills give elevation and air drainage. Clay-rich, granitic and greenstone soils in the Piedmont; limestone in the Shenandoah Valley.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Viognier, Petit Manseng, Chardonnay, Norton, Tannat.
regions.styles: Bordeaux-style blends; Viognier and Petit Manseng; sparkling wine; Norton.
regions.classification: Federal AVA rules; Virginia sets no stricter standards but has a Governor's Cup competition and Virginia Wine Board programmes.

regions.name: Mid-Atlantic
regions.tagline: Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Maryland: colonial wine dreams and a modern coastal-plain revival.
regions.summary: The Mid-Atlantic states have long winemaking histories and growing modern industries. New Jersey's sandy Outer Coastal Plain and Cape May Peninsula, Pennsylvania's Lehigh and Lancaster valleys and Lake Erie shore, and Maryland's Piedmont AVAs grow vinifera, hybrids and natives. Pennsylvania is one of the larger grape-growing states thanks to Concord on Lake Erie.
regions.history: William Penn tried to plant French vines near Philadelphia in 1683. James Alexander, gardener to the Penn family, found the Alexander grape near Philadelphia in the 1740s, a chance cross of a native vine with a European one and the first hybrid grape in America. New Jersey's Renault Winery (1864) at Egg Harbor City is one of the oldest continuously operating wineries in the country.
regions.terroir: Varied: sandy coastal plain, Piedmont clays, limestone valleys; humid summers.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Albariño, Chambourcin, Vidal, Concord.
regions.styles: Bordeaux-style reds, aromatic whites, sparkling.
regions.classification: Federal AVAs.

regions.name: Southeast
regions.tagline: Muscadine country, mountain vinifera and the oldest cultivated vine in America.
regions.summary: The humid Southeast is the home of the muscadine (Vitis rotundifolia), the native grape that resists Pierce's disease and produces sweet, musky wines from Scuppernong and other varieties. In the cooler Blue Ridge and Appalachian highlands, growers plant vinifera and hybrids. North Carolina has seven AVAs, Georgia two, Tennessee four (including shared ones).
regions.history: Giovanni da Verrazzano recorded abundant grapes on the North Carolina coast in 1524, and Sir Walter Raleigh's captains Amadas and Barlowe wrote in 1584 that the coast was 'so full of grapes'. The Mother Vine on Roanoke Island, a Scuppernong, is reputed to be about 400 years old. Garrett & Company's 'Virginia Dare' wine, first made from Scuppernong in North Carolina, was one of America's best-selling wines before Prohibition. In Georgia, the 1880 census ranked it among the leading wine states.
regions.terroir: Humid subtropical lowlands; Appalachian highlands with thermal belts on slopes.
regions.grapes: Scuppernong and other muscadines, Chambourcin, Cabernet Franc, Viognier, Petit Manseng, Chardonnay, Merlot, Vidal.
regions.styles: Sweet muscadine wines; mountain reds and whites.
regions.classification: Federal AVAs.
appellations: Crest of the Blue Ridge Henderson County

regions.name: Midwest
regions.tagline: Missouri's German wine country, the first AVA, and the rootstocks that saved Europe.
regions.summary:
Before Prohibition, the Midwest was a serious wine region. German immigrants in the Missouri River valley built Hermann into one of the largest wine towns in the country; Cincinnati's sparkling Catawba was famous on two continents; and Missouri and Texas scientists sent phylloxera-resistant American rootstocks that rescued French vineyards in the 1870s and 1880s. Today the region grows mostly hybrids and natives (Norton, Chambourcin, Vidal, Vignoles, Traminette and the University of Minnesota's cold-hardy Marquette, Frontenac and La Crescent) with vinifera on the Lake Michigan shore and Ohio's Lake Erie islands.

Augusta, Missouri became the first American Viticultural Area on 20 June 1980, eight months before Napa Valley.
regions.history: German settlers founded Hermann in 1837; by the 1880s Stone Hill Winery was said to be the second-largest winery in the US. George Husmann, Hermann's horticulturist and later state entomologist Charles V. Riley's collaborator, promoted native grapes; Hermann Jaeger of Neosho bred phylloxera-resistant varieties and, with Husmann, shipped carloads of resistant cuttings to France, for which he was made a Chevalier of the Légion d'honneur in 1893. Nicholas Longworth planted Catawba at Cincinnati from 1825 and produced America's first celebrated sparkling wine; Longfellow wrote 'Catawba Wine' in his honour. By 1860 Ohio was the leading wine state. Black rot, the Civil War and Prohibition ended the era; Stone Hill grew mushrooms in its cellars.
regions.terroir: Continental climate with cold winters, hot humid summers and spring frosts. Loess bluffs along the Missouri; Ozark limestone and chert; glacial soils farther north.
regions.grapes: Norton (Cynthiana), Chambourcin, Vidal Blanc, Vignoles, Traminette, Catawba, Concord, Marquette, Frontenac, La Crescent, Seyval Blanc, Riesling.
regions.styles: Norton reds, off-dry hybrid whites, port-style wines, ice wine in the north.
regions.classification: Federal AVAs. Missouri's state grape is Norton.

regions.name: Great Lakes
regions.tagline: Lake-effect vineyards in Michigan and Ohio: Riesling on cherry-orchard peninsulas and island wineries in Lake Erie.
regions.summary: The Great Lakes act as giant heat sinks: they delay spring budbreak, protect vines from the worst winter cold and extend autumn. Michigan has five AVAs, most famous for Riesling, Pinot Noir and sparkling wine on the Old Mission and Leelanau peninsulas near Traverse City. Ohio's Lake Erie islands (Isle St. George) and Grand River Valley grow vinifera and hybrids; the Lake Erie AVA spans three states.
regions.history: Lake Erie's Bass Islands had commercial vineyards by the 1850s; Golden Eagle Winery on Middle Bass Island (later Lonz) was billed as the largest in the US in the 1870s. In Michigan, Edward O'Keefe planted vinifera at Chateau Grand Traverse in 1974.
regions.terroir: Glacial sands and gravels; lake moderation within a few kilometres of the shore.
regions.grapes: Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer, Vidal, Catawba.
regions.styles: Dry and off-dry Riesling, sparkling wine, ice wine, light reds.
regions.classification: Federal AVAs.

regions.name: Texas
regions.tagline: Mission vines by 1650s El Paso, Munson's rootstocks, and a modern boom split between the High Plains and the Hill Country.
regions.summary:
Texas has well over 400 wineries and ranks among the top five US wine-producing states. The geography is split. About 80 to 85 percent of the grapes grow on the Texas High Plains around Lubbock, at 900 to 1,200 m, where hot days, cool nights, wind and sandy loam over caliche suit Tempranillo, Mourvèdre, Tannat, Viognier and Roussanne. Most wineries and tourists, though, are 600 km away in the Texas Hill Country west of Austin, around Fredericksburg, which crushes much of the High Plains fruit. Hail, spring frost and Pierce's disease are constant risks.

Two new Hill Country AVAs, Llano Uplift (2,096 square miles) and Hickory Sands District (193 square miles), were proposed in August 2026.
regions.history: Franciscan missionaries planted Mission grapes around El Paso del Norte in the 1650s or 1660s, more than a century before California. German immigrants in the Hill Country made wine in the 19th century, and Val Verde Winery at Del Rio (1883) is the state's oldest continuously operating winery. T.V. Munson of Denison bred hundreds of grape varieties and identified Texas native species whose rootstocks helped save French vineyards from phylloxera; France made him a Chevalier du Mérite Agricole in 1888, and Cognac became Denison's sister city. Prohibition ended the industry; Llano Estacado (1976) and Pheasant Ridge near Lubbock started the revival.
regions.terroir: High Plains: caliche, sandy loam, high elevation, wide diurnal swings. Hill Country: limestone, granite (Llano Uplift) and sandy soils, hotter and more humid.
regions.grapes: Tempranillo, Cabernet Sauvignon, Mourvèdre, Tannat, Merlot, Sangiovese, Viognier, Roussanne, Blanc du Bois, Black Spanish (Lenoir).
regions.styles: Mediterranean-style reds and whites; rosé.
regions.classification: Federal AVAs; 'Texas' on a label requires 75 percent Texas fruit, and there is pressure from producers to raise it.
appellations: Fredericksburg in the Texas Hill Country

regions.name: Southwest and Mountain West
regions.tagline: High-desert vineyards in Arizona, New Mexico and Colorado, and the oldest wine tradition in the United States.
regions.summary: The Southwest grows grapes at altitude to escape the heat: Arizona's Sonoita, Willcox and Verde Valley AVAs sit at 1,000 to 1,500 m, Colorado's Grand Valley and West Elks at 1,300 to 2,000 m, and New Mexico's vineyards along the Rio Grande at 1,100 to 1,700 m. Rhône, Spanish and Italian varieties thrive; frost, hail and monsoon rains are the main hazards.
regions.history: Franciscan friars planted the first vines in what is now the United States in New Mexico around 1629, at the Piro pueblo mission of Senecú south of Socorro, to make sacramental wine; New Mexico wine thus predates California by more than a century. Floods and Prohibition ended its 19th-century industry. Arizona's modern wine began with Dr. Gordon Dutt's experimental vineyard at Sonoita in the 1970s; Sonoita became Arizona's first AVA in 1984. Colorado's Palisade growers planted vinifera in the 1890s, before Prohibition, and again from the 1970s.
regions.terroir: Volcanic, granitic and alluvial soils; intense sun, low humidity, big day-night swings; late spring frosts.
regions.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Tempranillo, Malbec, Cabernet Franc, Riesling, Malvasia Bianca, Chardonnay; Mission in New Mexico.
regions.styles: Rhône and Spanish-style reds; New Mexico sparkling wine.
regions.classification: Federal AVAs.

us-adelaida-district.name: Adelaida District
us-adelaida-district.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Roussanne, Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel
us-adelaida-district.summary: The northwestern hills of Paso Robles (2014), at 275 to 670 m in the Santa Lucia foothills, with calcareous shale and limestone soils, more rain than the east and cool nights. It is home to Tablas Creek, where the Perrin family of Château de Beaucastel and importer Robert Haas planted French Rhône clones from 1989, and to Justin's Isosceles and Halter Ranch.

us-alexander-valley.name: Alexander Valley
us-alexander-valley.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Zinfandel, Sauvignon Blanc
us-alexander-valley.summary:
The upper Russian River valley (1984, expanded 1990s to 2008) from Healdsburg north to Cloverdale, named for Cyrus Alexander, who settled here in the 1840s. It is one of Sonoma's warmest areas, with less fog than the lower river, and it is the county's Cabernet Sauvignon heartland: round, plush and approachable, with soft tannin and notes of black cherry and cocoa.

Hillside vineyards on the Mayacamas side give darker, firmer wines. Jordan (1972) and Silver Oak's Alexander Valley Cabernet made the style famous; Simi has made wine at Healdsburg since 1876.
us-alexander-valley.terroir: Deep alluvial loams on the valley floor, gravelly benches and volcanic hillsides on the east.

us-alexandria-lakes.name: Alexandria Lakes
us-alexandria-lakes.summary: A small AVA (2005) of about 9,000 acres among the glacial lakes near Alexandria, Minnesota, created around Carlos Creek Winery and among the most northerly AVAs in the US. Cold-hardy hybrids.

us-alisos-canyon.name: Alisos Canyon
us-alisos-canyon.summary: A small AVA (2020) of about 5,800 acres in the hills between the Santa Maria and Santa Ynez valleys, near Los Alamos. A cool, foggy marine climate and sandy, calcareous soils suit Syrah and Rhône varieties.

us-alta-mesa.name: Alta Mesa
us-alta-mesa.summary: A high, flat terrace (2006) in the northeastern part of Lodi, in Sacramento County, with shallow sandy loam over hardpan that limits vine vigour. It is warmer than western Lodi because it lies farther from the Delta breezes, and it grows Zinfandel and Rhône varieties.

us-altus.name: Altus
us-altus.summary: A small AVA (1984) around the town of Altus in western Arkansas, settled by Swiss and German immigrants in the 1880s. Wiederkehr Wine Cellars (1880) and Post Winery (1880) are among the oldest in the South; Mount Bethel and Chateau aux Arc also operate here.

us-ancient-lakes-of-columbia-valley.name: Ancient Lakes of Columbia Valley
us-ancient-lakes-of-columbia-valley.grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Sauvignon Blanc
us-ancient-lakes-of-columbia-valley.summary: A cool northern AVA (2012) of about 162,800 acres near Quincy, named for lakes left in coulees carved by the Missoula Floods. Caliche-rich soils and a cooler climate make it Washington's best area for crisp Riesling, Chardonnay and Pinot Gris. At approval it had 1,399 acres in six vineyards.

us-anderson-valley.name: Anderson Valley
us-anderson-valley.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Gewürztraminer, Riesling, Pinot Gris
us-anderson-valley.summary:
A narrow, 25 km valley (1983) along the Navarro River that opens toward the Pacific, so fog and cool air pour in every evening. It is one of California's coolest wine valleys and its most Alsatian: Gewürztraminer, Riesling and Pinot Gris grow beside Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and the valley hosts an annual Alsace festival.

Roederer Estate arrived from Champagne in 1982 and showed that the valley could make world-class sparkling wine; its L'Ermitage is a benchmark. Pinot Noir from the 'deep end' near Philo and Navarro is tense, floral and savoury.
us-anderson-valley.terroir: Marine sedimentary soils on benches and slopes; fog and large daily temperature swings.
us-anderson-valley.nerd_note: The valley had its own jargon, Boontling, invented by Boonville residents around 1900; a 'horn of Bahl' is a glass of good wine.

us-antelope-valley-of-the-california-hig.name: Antelope Valley of the California High Desert
us-antelope-valley-of-the-california-hig.summary: A large AVA (2011) in the western Mojave Desert in Los Angeles and Kern counties, at around 700 to 900 m. Hot days, cold nights, strong winds and very low rainfall; vineyards are small and irrigated.

us-appalachian-high-country.name: Appalachian High Country
us-appalachian-high-country.summary: A high, mountainous AVA (2016) of about 2,400 square miles straddling North Carolina, Tennessee and Virginia around Boone, with vineyards from about 900 to 1,200 m, among the highest in the East. Short seasons and cold winters favour cold-hardy hybrids such as Marquette and Frontenac. At approval it had 21 vineyards (71 acres) and 10 wineries.

us-applegate-valley.name: Applegate Valley
us-applegate-valley.grapes: Syrah, Zinfandel, Viognier, Cabernet Sauvignon, Vermentino
us-applegate-valley.summary: A sub-AVA (2000) of the Rogue Valley along the Applegate River, warm and dry with decomposed granite and alluvial soils. Small family wineries grow Syrah, Zinfandel, Viognier and Rhône and Bordeaux varieties; Troon converted to biodynamic farming.

us-arkansas-mountain.name: Arkansas Mountain
us-arkansas-mountain.summary: An AVA (1986) of about 2.9 million acres in the Arkansas River valley and the Boston Mountains of northwestern Arkansas, petitioned by Al Wiederkehr. Swiss and German immigrants planted here in the 1880s.

us-arroyo-grande-valley.name: Arroyo Grande Valley
us-arroyo-grande-valley.summary: A valley (1990) southeast of Edna Valley that grades from cool and foggy near the coast to warmer at its inland end. Talley Vineyards' Rincon and Rosemary's vineyards give fine Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; at the warmer top end, Saucelito Canyon farms Zinfandel planted in 1880.

us-arroyo-seco.name: Arroyo Seco
us-arroyo-seco.grapes: Chardonnay, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon
us-arroyo-seco.summary: An AVA (1983, boundaries adjusted 2006, 2018 and 2021) around the Arroyo Seco river where it emerges from the Santa Lucia Range near Greenfield. The cool eastern section is known for Riesling and Chardonnay grown on 'Greenfield potatoes', rounded river cobbles that store heat. The warmer canyon to the west grows Cabernet and Zinfandel.

us-atlas-peak.name: Atlas Peak
us-atlas-peak.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Sangiovese, Chardonnay
us-atlas-peak.summary:
High mountain AVA (1992) in the Vaca Range northeast of Napa city, with vineyards from about 230 to 800 m. The elevation keeps summer afternoons cooler than on the valley floor, nights are cold, and the red volcanic soils are thin and rocky. Cabernet Sauvignon is fresh, dark-fruited and firmly built.

Atlas Peak Vineyards was founded in the 1980s by a partnership that included Piero Antinori, who planted Sangiovese here before it was fashionable; Antinori's Antica estate continues the link. On 8 October 2017 the Atlas Fire started on these slopes and burned through vineyards and homes across the district.
us-atlas-peak.terroir: Shallow volcanic soils, red and rocky, on a high plateau and slopes; above the fog with cool nights.
us-atlas-peak.nerd_note: Atlas Peak was one of the early AVAs defined largely by elevation and is a source of Sangiovese that pre-dates the 1990s 'Cal-Ital' boom.

us-augusta.name: Augusta
us-augusta.summary:
The first American Viticultural Area, approved on 20 June 1980, eight months before Napa Valley. It covers about 15,000 acres around the town of Augusta on the Missouri River west of St. Louis, founded by German settlers in the 1830s; before Prohibition it had a dozen wineries. Loess-capped bluffs and a valley moderated by the river grow Norton, Chambourcin, Vignoles and Chardonel. Mount Pleasant Estates (1859) is the anchor winery.

Augusta's 19th-century winemakers were mostly German immigrants, many of them liberal refugees of the failed revolutions of 1848. The Missouri River Valley was dubbed the 'Missouri Rhineland'. After Prohibition the industry vanished until Lucian Dressel bought Mount Pleasant in 1966 and replanted. Norton, a native grape that thrives in humid summers, makes deep, inky, high-acid reds that are the region's calling card.
us-augusta.nerd_note: Augusta won the race to be first partly because the 1978 rules were brand new and its petition was simple: a small, well-defined valley with a clear historical name.

us-ballard-canyon.name: Ballard Canyon
us-ballard-canyon.summary: A small, north-south canyon AVA (2013) between Buellton and Los Olivos, with about 7,800 acres. Its growers decided to focus on Syrah, which shows dark fruit and savoury, peppery depth on the canyon's calcareous and sandy soils. Grenache and Sauvignon Blanc also grow well.

us-bell-mountain.name: Bell Mountain
us-bell-mountain.summary: Texas's first AVA (1986), a single granite-and-sand hill north of Fredericksburg owned by the Oberhelman family. It would be enclosed by the proposed Llano Uplift AVA.

us-ben-lomond-mountain.name: Ben Lomond Mountain
us-ben-lomond-mountain.summary: A small mountain AVA (1987) inside the Santa Cruz Mountains, on a ridge northwest of Santa Cruz above the fog line, at 120 to 800 m. Sandy soils from granite and limestone; cool Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Cabernet.

us-benmore-valley.name: Benmore Valley
us-benmore-valley.summary: A small, high valley (1991) in the Mayacamas on the western edge of Lake County, at about 730 m. Once planted mainly to Chardonnay for large brands, it now has few vines.

us-bennett-valley.name: Bennett Valley
us-bennett-valley.grapes: Merlot, Syrah, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay
us-bennett-valley.summary: A small AVA (2003) in the hills southeast of Santa Rosa, cooled by marine air that flows through the Crane Canyon gap from the Petaluma side. That coolness suits Merlot, Syrah, Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir. Matanzas Creek (1977), known for Merlot and Sauvignon Blanc and its lavender fields, is the best-known winery.

us-beverly-washington.name: Beverly, Washington
us-beverly-washington.summary: A small AVA (2024) of about 2,415 acres on terraces above the Columbia River at the hamlet of Beverly, just north of Sentinel Gap. It was proposed as 'Wanapum Village', but the petitioner asked for a new name after members of the Wanapum tribe objected to the use of their name, and TTB approved it as 'Beverly, Washington'.

us-big-valley-district-lake-county.name: Big Valley District-Lake County
us-big-valley-district-lake-county.summary: A flat basin (2013) on the southwest shore of Clear Lake around Kelseyville, with about 1,800 acres of vines at approval. High water tables and cold-air pooling give a cooler, frostier site than the surrounding hills; Sauvignon Blanc is the signature.

us-borden-ranch.name: Borden Ranch
us-borden-ranch.summary: Hilly eastern Lodi AVA (2006) of cobbled, gravelly old river terraces at the foot of the Sierra, on the old Borden ranch. Bordeaux varieties and Zinfandel.

us-california-shenandoah-valley.name: California Shenandoah Valley
us-california-shenandoah-valley.summary:
The core of Amador County wine (1983), a valley of rolling hills around Plymouth at 300 to 600 m, with decomposed granite and volcanic soils. It holds some of the oldest Zinfandel vines in California, including the Original Grandpère vineyard claimed to date from before 1869, and Deaver Vineyard, whose fruit made Sutter Home's 1968 Amador Zinfandel. Barbera and Rhône varieties also do well.

The name includes 'California' to separate it from the older Shenandoah Valley AVA of Virginia and West Virginia.

us-calistoga.name: Calistoga
us-calistoga.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Charbono, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
us-calistoga.summary:
Napa's northernmost and warmest valley-floor AVA, approved in late 2009 after a long fight over the use of the name by a brand that sourced grapes elsewhere. It sits at the head of the valley under Mount St. Helena, where the valley floor narrows and is ringed by the Mayacamas and Vaca ranges.

Days are hot, but cool air spills in at night through the Knights Valley gap from the Russian River side, so the daily temperature swing is among the largest in Napa. The wines are bold and dark: Cabernet Sauvignon with real tannic grip, plus Zinfandel, Petite Sirah and Charbono from old vineyards that never got replanted to Cabernet. Chateau Montelena, whose 1973 Chardonnay won the white half of the 1976 Paris tasting, is the most famous estate; Araujo's former Eisele Vineyard, now Eisele Vineyard estate, is its cult Cabernet.
us-calistoga.terroir: Volcanic soils derived from Mount St. Helena and the Sonoma Volcanics, plus alluvial fans; hot afternoons and cold nights.
us-calistoga.nerd_note: The town's name is a slip of the tongue: founder Sam Brannan meant to promise 'the Saratoga of California' and is said to have blurted 'the Calistoga of Sarafornia'. In 2024 TTB adjusted Calistoga's boundary when it created the neighbouring Crystal Springs of Napa Valley AVA.

us-candy-mountain.name: Candy Mountain
us-candy-mountain.summary: One of Washington's smallest AVAs (2020), about 815 acres on the southwest-facing slope of Candy Mountain near Richland, close to Red Mountain. Steep slopes, shallow loess and wind give dense Cabernet. TTB modified the Yakima Valley boundary to include it.

us-capay-valley.name: Capay Valley
us-capay-valley.summary: A long valley (2002) in western Yolo County along Cache Creek, between the Blue Ridge and the Capay Hills. Warm and dry, it grows Rhône and Mediterranean varieties on a small scale, and the area is known more widely for organic farms.

us-cape-may-peninsula.name: Cape May Peninsula
us-cape-may-peninsula.summary: A peninsula AVA (2018) at New Jersey's southern tip, surrounded by the Atlantic and Delaware Bay. The petition stressed its warmth: water keeps autumns mild and the frost-free season long. Sandy soils; at approval six vineyards on about 115 acres. Albariño, Merlot and Chardonnay.

us-carmel-valley.name: Carmel Valley
us-carmel-valley.summary: A narrow valley (1983) running inland from Carmel-by-the-Sea, sheltered from fog at its upper end by the Santa Lucia Range, where vineyards sit at 200 to 600 m. It is warm enough for Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot; Durney Vineyards (later Heller Estate) planted the first commercial vineyard in 1968.

us-catoctin.name: Catoctin
us-catoctin.summary: A Piedmont AVA (1983) in Frederick and Washington counties, Maryland, at the foot of the Catoctin Mountains. Black Ankle and Sugarloaf Mountain are leading wineries nearby.

us-cayuga-lake.name: Cayuga Lake
us-cayuga-lake.grapes: Riesling, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Cayuga White
us-cayuga-lake.summary: The first Finger Lakes sub-AVA (1988), on the slopes of the longest Finger Lake. Cayuga is deep enough to moderate the climate, though slightly cooler than Seneca; the Cayuga Wine Trail (1983) was the first organised wine trail in America. Riesling and sparkling wines lead.
us-cayuga-lake.nerd_note: Cayuga White, a hybrid bred at Cornell's Geneva station and released in 1972, is named for the lake.

us-central-coast.name: Central Coast
us-central-coast.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Zinfandel
us-central-coast.summary: Umbrella AVA (1985, adjusted 1999, 2006 and 2024) of about 6.8 million acres covering the coastal counties from Contra Costa and Alameda south to Santa Barbara. It is used for multi-county blends and contains famous AVAs from the Santa Cruz Mountains to Sta. Rita Hills.

us-central-delaware-valley.name: Central Delaware Valley
us-central-delaware-valley.summary: An AVA (1984) along both banks of the Delaware River in Pennsylvania (Bucks County) and New Jersey (Hunterdon and Mercer), sheltered by the valley; Unionville Vineyards and others make Chardonnay and Bordeaux varieties.

us-chalk-hill.name: Chalk Hill
us-chalk-hill.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon
us-chalk-hill.summary: A warm corner of the Russian River Valley (1983) east of Windsor, in hills above the fog. The 'chalk' is a misnomer: the pale soils are volcanic ash from Mount St. Helena's eruptions, mixed with river sediments. It is warmer than the rest of the Russian River Valley and better suited to Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Bordeaux varieties than to Pinot Noir.

us-chalone.name: Chalone
us-chalone.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Chenin Blanc, Pinot Blanc
us-chalone.summary: A remote, high bench (1982) at about 500 m in the Gavilan (Gabilan) Mountains, under the volcanic spires of Pinnacles National Park. Its limestone and granite soils are rare in California, and vines were first planted here around 1919. Dick Graff bought the property in 1965 and made Chalone's Burgundian Chardonnay and Pinot Noir; its 1974 Chardonnay was third among the whites in Paris in 1976.
us-chalone.nerd_note: Chalone's water had to be trucked up the mountain for years; the Chenin Blanc vines planted in 1919 are among the oldest in California.

us-champlain-valley-of-new-york.name: Champlain Valley of New York
us-champlain-valley-of-new-york.summary: A cold AVA (2016) of about 500 square miles in Clinton and Essex counties on the western shore of Lake Champlain.
