TTB accepted that its short season suits cold-hardy hybrids (Frontenac, La Crescent, Marquette) rather than vinifera. At approval it had six wineries. A Champlain Valley of Vermont AVA across the lake was proposed in 2026.

us-chehalem-mountains.name: Chehalem Mountains
us-chehalem-mountains.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc
us-chehalem-mountains.summary: The highest landform in the northern Willamette Valley (2006), a 30 km ridge southwest of Portland rising to about 500 m at Bald Peak. It has all three Willamette soil types: volcanic Jory, marine sediments and wind-blown Laurelwood loess. Adelsheim (1971) and Ponzi were early settlers; the AVA contains Ribbon Ridge and the Laurelwood District.

us-chiles-valley.name: Chiles Valley
us-chiles-valley.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc
us-chiles-valley.summary:
A small, high side valley (1999) tucked into the Vaca Range east of the main Napa Valley, at about 250 to 370 m. Cold air drains into it at night, so it is cooler than the valley floor, with a long season and a later harvest. Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel are firm and fresh.

The valley takes its name from Joseph Ballinger Chiles, an early overland pioneer who received the Catacula land grant in 1844. Volker Eisele, who farmed here organically from the 1970s, was one of the leaders who defended Napa's Agricultural Preserve.
us-chiles-valley.terroir: Alluvial valley floor and surrounding slopes, cooler nights from cold-air pooling.
us-chiles-valley.nerd_note: Brown Estate, known for Zinfandel, is widely cited as the first Black-owned estate winery in Napa Valley.

us-cienega-valley.name: Cienega Valley
us-cienega-valley.grapes: Zinfandel, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Pfeffer, Négrette
us-cienega-valley.summary: Historic valley (1982) in San Benito County along the San Andreas fault, where vines were planted in the 1850s. William Palmtag and later Almaden made wine here; DeRose Vineyards farms old, own-rooted Zinfandel and Négrette. Limestone and granite soils.
us-cienega-valley.nerd_note: The vineyard sits directly on the San Andreas fault; the creep of the fault slowly bends rows and has cracked the old winery walls.

us-clarksburg.name: Clarksburg
us-clarksburg.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Petite Sirah, Chardonnay, Albariño
us-clarksburg.summary: Delta country (1984, expanded 2022) south of Sacramento, where vineyards grow on reclaimed river islands behind levees. Cool afternoon breezes through the Carquinez Strait make it cooler than Lodi. Chenin Blanc is the historic speciality, plus Petite Sirah and Albariño; much fruit is sold to wineries elsewhere.

us-clear-lake.name: Clear Lake
us-clear-lake.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah, Zinfandel, Merlot
us-clear-lake.summary: The large umbrella AVA (1984) around Clear Lake, covering most of Lake County's vineyards. The lake moderates temperatures, while altitudes of 400 m and more give cool nights. Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet Sauvignon lead, with Petite Sirah and Zinfandel from older plantings.

us-clements-hills.name: Clements Hills
us-clements-hills.summary: Rolling hills (2006) in the eastern part of Lodi, with red, cobbly clay-loam soils on old river terraces; slightly warmer than the west. Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel and Iberian varieties.

us-cole-ranch.name: Cole Ranch
us-cole-ranch.summary: Once the smallest AVA in the United States (1983) at about 150 to 190 acres, a single ranch in a narrow valley in the hills between Ukiah and Boonville, owned by the Cole family. It grows Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot. Hawaii's Ulupalakua (2021) has since taken the 'smallest AVA' title.
us-cole-ranch.nerd_note: Cole Ranch is essentially a one-owner AVA, which is legal as long as the petition proves the area is geographically distinct.

us-columbia-gorge.name: Columbia Gorge
us-columbia-gorge.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Gewürztraminer, Riesling, Syrah, Zinfandel
us-columbia-gorge.summary: A dramatic AVA (2004) straddling the Columbia River where it cuts through the Cascade Range, on both the Oregon (Hood River, Wasco) and Washington (Klickitat, Skamania) sides. In about 65 km, rainfall falls from more than 90 cm a year in the west to under 25 cm in the east, so the gorge grows everything from cool-climate Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Gewürztraminer near Hood River to Zinfandel, Syrah and Cabernet near The Dalles. Old Zinfandel planted by Italian immigrants survives at The Pines 1852 vineyard.

us-columbia-hills.name: Columbia Hills
us-columbia-hills.summary:
Washington's 22nd AVA (effective September 2026), about 29,387 acres in Klickitat County along the north bank of the Columbia River opposite The Dalles and around Maryhill. Eighty percent of the land lies within a mile of the river, which acts as a heat reservoir; soils are coarse basalt colluvium and wind-blown sand and gravel bars left by the ice-age floods, much coarser than the loess common elsewhere. At approval there were about 338 acres of vines owned by 19 landowners and four wineries.

The name comes from the Columbia Hills Natural Area Preserve and Columbia Hills Historical State Park, home to the petroglyph 'She Who Watches'.

us-columbia-valley.name: Columbia Valley
us-columbia-valley.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Chardonnay, Riesling, Cabernet Franc
us-columbia-valley.summary:
Washington's giant umbrella AVA (1984) of about 11.5 million acres covering most of eastern Washington and a strip of northern Oregon. Low rainfall, long sunny days, cold nights and Missoula flood soils give wines of ripe fruit and fresh acidity. Most Washington wine, including the biggest brands, carries this name. Inside it are 19 sub-AVAs.

The scale is hard to grasp: Columbia Valley covers about a quarter of Washington State, yet vines occupy only a small fraction, clustered on south-facing slopes and benches near the rivers where cold air drains away in winter. Growing degree days range from cool (Ancient Lakes) to very warm (Wahluke Slope, Red Mountain). Most vineyards are own-rooted on sandy, phylloxera-hostile soils, which lets growers replant quickly after freezes. The AVA also crosses into Oregon around Milton-Freewater and the Columbia Gorge, so some Oregon wineries use the name.

us-comptche.name: Comptche
us-comptche.summary: A small AVA (2024) of about 1,422 acres around the hamlet of Comptche, a few kilometres inland from Mendocino town. Unusually, TTB excluded it from the North Coast AVA because its foggy, cold, coastal climate and soils differ so sharply from the larger area. It grows Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling-wine grapes on a handful of small vineyards.
us-comptche.nerd_note: Comptche is one of very few AVAs that is surrounded by, but not part of, a larger AVA.

us-contra-costa.name: Contra Costa
us-contra-costa.summary:
A new AVA (2024) of about 167,100 acres in eastern Contra Costa County, around Oakley, Brentwood and Antioch, with at least 60 vineyards on about 1,700 acres. Its treasure is ungrafted, century-old Zinfandel, Mourvèdre (Mataro), Carignan and Petite Sirah on deep, sandy soils where phylloxera never took hold, much of it bought by producers such as Bedrock, Cline, Turley and Ridge.

Creating it required TTB to enlarge both San Francisco Bay and Central Coast so that Contra Costa sits fully inside them.
us-contra-costa.nerd_note: The Evangelho Vineyard in Antioch, planted in the 1890s, grows own-rooted vines in deep sand dunes left by an ancient river delta.

us-coombsville.name: Coombsville
us-coombsville.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir
us-coombsville.summary:
Coombsville (2011) is a horseshoe of hills east of the city of Napa, often described as the eroded rim of an ancient volcanic caldera. Close to the bay, it is one of Napa's coolest Cabernet areas, with fog and afternoon wind; harvest comes later and the wines show fresh acidity, red and black fruit and less overt alcohol.

Growers such as Tom Farella planted here in the 1970s, but the area was a secret source for valley wineries until the AVA gave it its own name. Syrah, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir also grow well.
us-coombsville.terroir: Volcanic tuff and ash on the slopes, alluvial fans below; cool marine influence from San Pablo Bay.
us-coombsville.nerd_note: The name honours Nathan Coombs, who laid out the town of Napa in 1847.

us-cosumnes-river.name: Cosumnes River
us-cosumnes-river.summary: The northwestern Lodi sub-AVA (2006) on the Cosumnes River, close to the Delta and among the coolest, with heavy clay and alluvial soils; Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay and Zinfandel.

us-covelo.name: Covelo
us-covelo.summary: A remote, high valley (2006) of about 38,000 acres in northeastern Mendocino County, at about 425 m, surrounded by mountains and the Round Valley Indian Reservation. Cold winters and warm summers; plantings are very small.

us-crest-of-the-blue-ridge-henderson-cou.name: Crest of the Blue Ridge Henderson County
us-crest-of-the-blue-ridge-henderson-cou.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Petit Manseng, Riesling
us-crest-of-the-blue-ridge-henderson-cou.summary: A mountain AVA (2019) of about 215 square miles in Henderson County near Hendersonville, defined by elevation (most land at 640 to 960 m) and a cooler climate. At approval it had 14 vineyards on about 70 acres and two bonded wineries.

us-creston-district.name: Creston District
us-creston-district.summary: A district (2014) in the southeast of Paso Robles around the hamlet of Creston, in foothills of the La Panza Range at 300 to 600 m. Mixed alluvial and granitic soils, low rainfall and a warm, dry climate grow Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel and Syrah.

us-crystal-springs-of-napa-valley.name: Crystal Springs of Napa Valley
us-crystal-springs-of-napa-valley.summary:
Napa's newest sub-AVA (effective November 2024) covers about 4,000 acres of the western face of the Vaca Range between St. Helena and Calistoga. TTB describes it as an all-hillside region: every slope is between 15 and 40 percent, mostly facing west to southwest, and the boundary runs from the 400-foot contour (where the foothills meet the frost-prone valley floor) up to the 1,400-foot contour where Howell Mountain begins.

About 30 vineyards cover some 230 acres. Afternoon sun and warm air draining off the slopes make it a warm Cabernet Sauvignon site with less frost risk than the floor below. The name comes from Crystal Springs Road and the springs that gave the road its name.
us-crystal-springs-of-napa-valley.terroir: All hillside, 120 to 430 m, volcanic soils on west and southwest slopes; less frost than the valley floor and less elevation cooling than Howell Mountain above.
us-crystal-springs-of-napa-valley.nerd_note: Creating it also moved Calistoga's boundary, after a grower showed that one 17-acre vineyard on North Fork Crystal Springs Road would otherwise have been split between two AVAs.

us-cucamonga-valley.name: Cucamonga Valley
us-cucamonga-valley.summary: A historic AVA (1995) in San Bernardino and Riverside counties, east of Los Angeles. In 1900 Secondo Guasti founded the Italian Vineyard Company here and planted about 5,000 acres, then billed as the largest vineyard in the world; by the 1920s the valley had more than 20,000 acres of vines. Warehouses, freeways and Ontario airport have replaced most of them, but scattered old, dry-farmed Zinfandel and Mission vines survive, some more than a century old, and Galleano Winery (1927) still makes wine from them.

us-cumberland-valley.name: Cumberland Valley
us-cumberland-valley.summary: An AVA (1985) in the limestone Cumberland Valley of south-central Pennsylvania and western Maryland, part of the Great Appalachian Valley that runs from New York to Alabama. The valley's sheltered floor and well-drained soils grow hybrids and vinifera for a handful of small wineries.

us-dahlonega-plateau.name: Dahlonega Plateau
us-dahlonega-plateau.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Petit Manseng, Chardonnay
us-dahlonega-plateau.summary: Georgia's first wholly in-state AVA (2018), about 133 square miles on a plateau in Lumpkin and White counties, the site of the 1829 Georgia gold rush. Elevation and slope give better air drainage than the surrounding land. At approval it had seven wineries and about 110 acres; Wolf Mountain, Frogtown and Three Sisters grow Cabernet, Petit Manseng and sparkling-wine grapes.

us-diablo-grande.name: Diablo Grande
us-diablo-grande.summary: A single-development AVA (1998) in the Diablo Range foothills west of Patterson, Stanislaus County, created alongside a planned resort and golf community. It is cooler than the San Joaquin Valley floor below, but its vineyards are small and few wines use the name.

us-diamond-mountain-district.name: Diamond Mountain District
us-diamond-mountain-district.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Petit Verdot
us-diamond-mountain-district.summary:
A steep, small mountain AVA (2001) on the Mayacamas slopes just southwest of Calistoga, rising from about 120 to 670 m. The soils are volcanic ash and weathered lava, light and fast-draining, and the vines sit above much of the valley's heat. Cabernet Sauvignon here is dense, mineral and tannic in youth, and it is among the longest-lived in Napa.

Diamond Creek defined the place. Al Brounstein planted it in 1968 and from 1972 bottled separate Cabernets from neighbouring blocks with different soils (Volcanic Hill, Red Rock Terrace, Gravelly Meadow), an early and very Burgundian statement that site matters in California. Schramsberg's caves are dug into the same mountainside.
us-diamond-mountain-district.terroir: Volcanic ash, tuff and red lava soils on steep, mostly northeast-facing slopes; cooler and less foggy than the valley floor.
us-diamond-mountain-district.nerd_note: Brounstein reportedly brought his first Bordeaux cuttings in by way of Mexico, and Diamond Creek's block-by-block bottlings were among the first vineyard-parcel Cabernets in the United States.

us-dos-rios.name: Dos Rios
us-dos-rios.summary: A tiny, remote AVA (2005) of about 15,500 acres where the Middle Fork and main stem of the Eel River meet ('two rivers'), in rugged northern Mendocino County. It has only a few acres of vines.

us-dry-creek-valley.name: Dry Creek Valley
us-dry-creek-valley.grapes: Zinfandel, Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah, Syrah, Grenache
us-dry-creek-valley.summary:
A narrow valley (1983) running 25 km northwest of Healdsburg, now dammed at its head by Lake Sonoma. Italian immigrant families planted Zinfandel and field blends here in the late 19th century, and many of those head-trained, dry-farmed vines survive on the gravelly benches. Dry Creek Zinfandel is the archetype: brambly blackberry, black pepper and spice, ripe but rarely jammy.

The valley floor's deep alluvial loam suits Sauvignon Blanc; David Stare's Dry Creek Vineyard (1972) was the first new winery here after Prohibition and championed the grape. Rhône varieties and Cabernet are increasingly important.
us-dry-creek-valley.terroir: Gravelly, iron-rich red benchland on both sides of a deep alluvial valley floor; warm days, with fog reaching the southern end.
us-dry-creek-valley.nerd_note: Ridge labels its Lytton Springs Zinfandel blend as Dry Creek Valley; the old vines there were planted around 1900 and include Petite Sirah, Carignan and Mataro.

us-dundee-hills.name: Dundee Hills
us-dundee-hills.summary:
The birthplace of Oregon Pinot Noir and still its most famous address (2004). The Dundee Hills are a compact block of hills above the town of Dundee, and the AVA boundary follows the 200-foot contour, roughly where red volcanic Jory soil begins. Jory is deep, iron-rich, red clay loam weathered from Columbia River basalt that flowed here about 15 million years ago; it drains well and holds enough water for dry farming.

David and Diana Lett planted the first Pinot Noir in the Willamette Valley at their Eyrie Vineyards site in the Dundee Hills in 1965 to 1966, and Erath, Sokol Blosser, Domaine Drouhin Oregon (1988), Archery Summit, Domaine Serene and Lingua Franca followed. Dundee Hills Pinot Noir is classically red-fruited and perfumed, with silky tannin and a hint of earth and spice.
us-dundee-hills.terroir: Volcanic Jory soils on southeast-facing slopes above 200 feet; protected from the worst Pacific winds by the Coast Range.
us-dundee-hills.nerd_note: Jory soil is Oregon's official state soil, named after Jory Hill near Salem.

us-dunnigan-hills.name: Dunnigan Hills
us-dunnigan-hills.summary: Rolling hills (1993) in northern Yolo County beside Interstate 5, created at the request of R.H. Phillips, which planted large vineyards here in the 1980s. Warm days and Delta breezes; Syrah, Viognier and Chardonnay.

us-eagle-foothills.name: Eagle Foothills
us-eagle-foothills.grapes: Syrah, Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Gris
us-eagle-foothills.summary: A sub-AVA (2015) of about 49,800 acres in the foothills north of Eagle, west of Boise, slightly higher and cooler than the surrounding Snake River Valley, with nine vineyards (67 acres) at approval. Bitner Vineyards and 3 Horse Ranch are known producers.

us-eagle-peak-mendocino-county.name: Eagle Peak Mendocino County
us-eagle-peak-mendocino-county.summary: A mountainous AVA (2014) of about 26,260 acres northwest of Redwood Valley, with about 120 acres in 16 vineyards at the time of approval. The petition cited a marine-influenced climate, strong breezes, steep slopes and shallow soils with little water-holding capacity, which keep yields low for Pinot Noir and Rhône varieties.

us-eastern-connecticut-highlands.name: Eastern Connecticut Highlands
us-eastern-connecticut-highlands.grapes: Seyval Blanc, Cayuga White, Chardonnay, St. Croix
us-eastern-connecticut-highlands.summary: An AVA (2019) of about 1,250 square miles in the hills of eastern Connecticut, with 16 vineyards (about 115 acres) and six wineries at approval.

us-edna-valley.name: Edna Valley
us-edna-valley.summary:
A cool, east-west valley (1982) just south of San Luis Obispo city, open to the Pacific through Morro Bay so that fog and wind flow straight in. It has one of the longest growing seasons in California, ideal for Chardonnay with crisp acidity and Pinot Noir. Soils include volcanic plugs (the Nine Sisters) and marine sediments.

Paragon Vineyard, planted by the Niven family from 1973, was the valley's pioneer and still supplies many wineries; the Nivens later founded Baileyana and Tangent, and Edna Valley Vineyard was a joint venture with Chalone. Because the valley points straight at the Pacific through Morro Bay, the afternoon breeze arrives early and the growing season can stretch from February budbreak to November harvest, giving Chardonnay its hallmark combination of ripeness and acidity. Since 2022 Edna Valley has sat inside the San Luis Obispo Coast AVA.
us-edna-valley.nerd_note: John Alban planted Viognier, Roussanne and Grenache here around 1990; Alban Vineyards bills itself as the first American winery founded exclusively for Rhône varieties.

us-el-dorado.name: El Dorado
us-el-dorado.grapes: Zinfandel, Syrah, Barbera, Grenache, Cabernet Franc
us-el-dorado.summary: A high AVA (1983) in El Dorado County, near where gold was found at Coloma in 1848, with vineyards from about 365 to 1,070 m, among the highest in California. Volcanic and granitic soils and cool nights suit Rhône varieties, Barbera, Zinfandel and even Riesling.

us-el-pomar-district.name: El Pomar District
us-el-pomar-district.summary: A district (2014) southeast of Templeton on high, old alluvial terraces with calcareous patches, where some marine air from the Templeton Gap still reaches. Moderate temperatures suit Zinfandel, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot; the name recalls the El Pomar ('the orchard') land grant.

us-elkton-oregon.name: Elkton Oregon
us-elkton-oregon.summary: The coolest and wettest part of the Umpqua (2013), about 74,900 acres along the Umpqua River near Elkton, only about 50 km from the Pacific, so marine air flows straight up the river. It is cool-climate Pinot Noir, Riesling and Gewürztraminer country, cooler than much of the Willamette.

us-eola-amity-hills.name: Eola-Amity Hills
us-eola-amity-hills.summary: A north-south ridge (2006) northwest of Salem, directly in line with the Van Duzer Corridor, so cold ocean wind blows across it most summer afternoons. The wind keeps acidity high and skins thick; the soils are thin volcanic basalt with some marine sediment. Eola-Amity Pinot Noir is dark-fruited, firm and taut, and Chardonnay is among Oregon's best. Bethel Heights (1977) and Cristom were pioneers; Evening Land's Seven Springs Vineyard is famous.

us-escondido-valley.name: Escondido Valley
us-escondido-valley.summary: A small AVA (1992) in Pecos County, West Texas, where large vineyards were planted on University of Texas land near Fort Stockton in the 1980s, at about 900 m. The desert setting means intense heat and irrigation; the vineyards have long supplied grapes to Texas wineries.

us-fair-play.name: Fair Play
us-fair-play.summary: A high sub-AVA (2001, expanded 2015) around the hamlet of Fair Play in southern El Dorado County, at about 600 to 900 m on decomposed granite. Small family wineries make Rhône and Spanish varieties and Zinfandel.

us-fennville.name: Fennville
us-fennville.summary: One of the first AVAs (1981), a small area near Lake Michigan in Allegan County around Fenn Valley Vineyards, which petitioned for it. Sandy soils and lake moderation.

us-fiddletown.name: Fiddletown
us-fiddletown.summary: A small AVA (1983) in Amador County above the Shenandoah Valley, at about 450 to 760 m, with old Zinfandel vineyards such as Eschen, planted around 1910.

us-finger-lakes.name: Finger Lakes
us-finger-lakes.grapes: Riesling, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Gewürztraminer, Lemberger, Saperavi, Seyval Blanc, Vidal
us-finger-lakes.summary:
One of the great Riesling regions outside Europe (AVA 1982), an area of more than 2 million acres around eleven long, narrow glacial lakes in upstate New York. The deepest lakes (Seneca reaches about 190 m, Cayuga about 130 m) store summer heat and release it in winter, protecting vines on the slopes from the worst cold and delaying spring budbreak until frost danger has passed. Soils are shale, limestone and glacial gravels.

Dr. Konstantin Frank proved at Keuka Lake in the late 1950s that vinifera could survive here, and his winery's first vintage came in 1962. Today Riesling is the signature, from bone-dry to ice wine, with tense acidity and slate-and-citrus flavours, followed by Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir, Lemberger, Gewürztraminer, Grüner Veltliner and Saperavi. The region has more than 100 wineries.
us-finger-lakes.terroir: Glacial lakes moderate temperatures; slopes of shale, limestone and gravel; cold winters with snow cover.

us-fort-ross-seaview.name: Fort Ross-Seaview
us-fort-ross-seaview.summary:
A ridgetop AVA (2011) of about 27,500 acres just inland from the ruins of the Russian colony at Fort Ross. The vineyards mostly sit above about 280 m (920 feet), above the marine layer, so they get sun while the valleys below are blanketed in fog, and cold air drains away at night. Yields are low and berries small.

David Hirsch planted here in 1980, Walt and Joan Flowers in 1989, and Helen Turley and John Wetlaufer's Marcassin estate followed. The Pinot Noirs combine coastal brightness with surprising concentration.
us-fort-ross-seaview.terroir: Steep ridges of Franciscan sandstone and shale along the San Andreas fault zone; above the fog line with large diurnal swings.
us-fort-ross-seaview.nerd_note: The San Andreas fault runs right along the base of the ridges here, and Hirsch Vineyards straddles terrain on both tectonic plates.

us-fountaingrove-district.name: Fountaingrove District
us-fountaingrove-district.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Zinfandel, Chardonnay
us-fountaingrove-district.summary:
A hilly AVA (2015) of about 38,000 acres in the Mayacamas foothills northeast of Santa Rosa, with around 500 acres of vines. It is named for Fountaingrove, the utopian Brotherhood of the New Life founded by Thomas Lake Harris in 1875. Kanaye Nagasawa, a young Japanese samurai who came with Harris, ran its winery and became one of California's leading winemakers before Prohibition.

Volcanic soils and elevation suit Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah. The October 2017 Tubbs Fire swept through the district, destroying Fountaingrove's famous 1899 Round Barn and hundreds of homes.
us-fountaingrove-district.nerd_note: Nagasawa (1852 to 1934) is often called California's 'Wine King'; land laws against Japanese ownership meant his estate was lost after his death.

us-fredericksburg-in-the-texas-hill-coun.name: Fredericksburg in the Texas Hill Country
us-fredericksburg-in-the-texas-hill-coun.summary: A small AVA (1988) of about 66,000 acres (roughly 100 square miles) around the German-founded town of Fredericksburg (1846). Sandy, granite-derived soils and the town's tourist trade have made it the epicentre of Hill Country wine; Pedernales Cellars petitioned for it.

us-gabilan-mountains.name: Gabilan Mountains
us-gabilan-mountains.summary: A large mountain AVA (2022) of about 98,000 acres along the Gabilan (Gavilan) Range between the Salinas Valley and San Benito County, defined by elevation, a cooler climate and granitic and limestone soils. It encloses Chalone and Mt. Harlan, but TTB kept those older AVAs as they are.

us-goose-gap.name: Goose Gap
us-goose-gap.summary: A small AVA (2021) of about 8,129 acres in the hills south of Red Mountain near Richland. At approval it had two vineyards covering more than 1,800 acres and one winery; the petition stressed geology and soils on the hill's folded basalt.

us-grand-river-valley.name: Grand River Valley
us-grand-river-valley.grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Cabernet Franc, Vidal
us-grand-river-valley.summary: An AVA (1983) in northeast Ohio along the Grand River near Lake Erie, where lake moderation and gravelly soils allow vinifera. Debonné Vineyards and Ferrante are leading producers of Riesling and ice wine.

us-grand-valley.name: Grand Valley
us-grand-valley.grapes: Riesling, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon
us-grand-valley.summary: Colorado's main wine area (1991), along the Colorado River around Palisade and Grand Junction at about 1,400 m. Cold air drains down the river canyon at night and warm air off the Book Cliffs reduces frost, making it fruit country (Palisade peaches) as well as wine country. Riesling, Cabernet Franc, Syrah and Merlot.

us-green-valley-of-russian-river-valley.name: Green Valley of Russian River Valley
us-green-valley-of-russian-river-valley.summary:
A small, foggy AVA (1983) in the southwestern corner of the Russian River Valley around Forestville, Graton and Occidental, one of the coolest parts of the larger valley. The soil is almost all Goldridge sandy loam. It is classic ground for sparkling wine and taut Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

Iron Horse, founded by Barry and Audrey Sterling in 1976, made sparkling wines that were poured at the Reagan-Gorbachev summits from 1985 and at many White House dinners since.
us-green-valley-of-russian-river-valley.nerd_note: Until 2007 the AVA was called 'Sonoma County Green Valley'; TTB renamed it to avoid confusion with Solano County Green Valley.

us-guenoc-valley.name: Guenoc Valley
us-guenoc-valley.grapes: Petite Sirah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc
us-guenoc-valley.summary: An early single-proprietor AVA (1981) in southern Lake County, on the old Guenoc Ranch. The English actress Lillie Langtry, a friend of the future Edward VII, bought the ranch in 1888 and hired a Bordeaux winemaker; her portrait was later used on the labels of Langtry Estate. Warm and dry, it grows Petite Sirah, Cabernet Sauvignon and Sauvignon Blanc.

us-hames-valley.name: Hames Valley
us-hames-valley.summary: The southernmost Monterey AVA (1994), a warm inland valley near the San Luis Obispo County line with wide day-night temperature swings. Shallow, rocky soils grow Bordeaux and Rhône varieties, mostly sold to wineries elsewhere in the Central Coast.

us-happy-canyon-of-santa-barbara.name: Happy Canyon of Santa Barbara
us-happy-canyon-of-santa-barbara.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot
us-happy-canyon-of-santa-barbara.summary: The eastern and warmest part of the Santa Ynez Valley (2009), a 23,900-acre canyon area with serpentine and rocky soils. Bordeaux varieties ripen here, and Star Lane, Grassini and Happy Canyon Vineyard make Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc. The name supposedly dates from Prohibition, when moonshine was made in the canyon.

us-haw-river-valley.name: Haw River Valley
us-haw-river-valley.summary: A Piedmont AVA (2009) of about 868 square miles along the Haw River in central North Carolina, named for the Sissipahaw people. At approval it had about 60 acres and six wineries.

us-hermann.name: Hermann
us-hermann.summary: An AVA (1983) of about 51,000 acres (80 square miles) along the Missouri River around the German-founded town of Hermann (1837). By the 1880s Stone Hill Winery was one of the largest in the country, winning medals at world fairs, and the town's Norton, known locally as Cynthiana, became famous; Missouri adopted Norton as its official state grape. Stone Hill and Hermannhof restored the 19th-century cellars after Prohibition.
us-hermann.nerd_note: Adam Puchta Winery (1855) claims to be the oldest continuously family-owned winery in the US.

us-high-valley.name: High Valley
us-high-valley.summary: A narrow, east-west valley (2005) in northeastern Lake County above Clear Lake, at about 500 to 920 m. Cool air drains down from the surrounding ridges, giving a long season for Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet and Syrah. Its boundary was trimmed in 2023 when the neighbouring Long Valley-Lake County AVA was created.

us-horse-heaven-hills.name: Horse Heaven Hills
us-horse-heaven-hills.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Chardonnay, Riesling
us-horse-heaven-hills.summary: A big AVA (2005) of about 570,000 acres on the south-facing slopes above the Columbia River, south of the Yakima Valley. Steady wind from the river reduces frost and disease. Champoux Vineyard (planted 1972 as Mercer Ranch) has given perfect-score Cabernets to Quilceda Creek and Andrew Will; Columbia Crest is based here. At approval there were 6,040 acres of vines.

us-howell-mountain.name: Howell Mountain
us-howell-mountain.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Viognier
us-howell-mountain.summary:
The first sub-AVA lying wholly inside Napa Valley, approved in late 1983 and effective in January 1984, and still one of the most distinctive. It is a high plateau in the Vaca Range above St. Helena, and the boundary follows the 1,400-foot (about 430 m) contour, roughly the top of the summer fog layer. Vines above the fog get longer sun and cooler nights, in thin red volcanic soils and white volcanic ash (tufa).

The result is mountain Cabernet at its most monumental: deep colour, blue and black fruit, iron and graphite, and tannin that can take a decade to unwind. Randy Dunn's Howell Mountain Cabernet set the style from 1979. The stone wineries of Ladera (built 1886 for Brun and Chaix) and La Jota recall a 19th-century reputation for Zinfandel.
us-howell-mountain.terroir: Above 430 m: red volcanic soils and white tufa ash, low fertility, sunny days above the fog and cool nights.
us-howell-mountain.nerd_note: Howell Mountain was one of the first AVAs anywhere defined by elevation; the 2024 Crystal Springs of Napa Valley AVA was drawn to stop exactly at Howell Mountain's 1,400-foot line.

us-hudson-river-region.name: Hudson River Region
us-hudson-river-region.grapes: Seyval Blanc, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Baco Noir, Riesling
us-hudson-river-region.summary: The oldest wine region in the United States still making wine (AVA 1982), along the Hudson valley north of New York City. French Huguenots planted vines in Ulster County in the 1670s, Croton Point had a commercial vineyard by 1827, and Brotherhood Winery has operated at Washingtonville since its first commercial vintage in 1839. The region pioneered hybrids after Prohibition; Benmarl, Millbrook and Whitecliff grow Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc and Seyval Blanc.
us-hudson-river-region.nerd_note: Benmarl's vineyard at Marlboro is often cited as one of the oldest continuously planted vineyards in the US, dating to the 1770s.

us-indiana-uplands.name: Indiana Uplands
us-indiana-uplands.summary: An AVA (2013) of about 4,600 square miles in the hills of southern Indiana, carved out of the Ohio River Valley AVA. At approval it had 19 vineyards (about 200 acres) and 17 wineries, including Oliver Winery, the state's largest, and Huber's Orchard. Limestone karst geology; Traminette, Chambourcin and Vidal.

us-inwood-valley.name: Inwood Valley
us-inwood-valley.summary: A small valley (2012) of about 28,400 acres in eastern Shasta County, in the foothills of the southern Cascades east of Redding. At approval it had about 60 acres of vines; volcanic soils and cool nights from the Cascades suit Bordeaux and Rhône varieties.

us-isle-st-george.name: Isle St. George
us-isle-st-george.summary: An island AVA (1982) of about 700 acres covering North Bass Island in Lake Erie, close to the Canadian border. The lake keeps winters mild and autumns long, and vines have grown here since the 1850s. Meier's Wine Cellars, which petitioned for the AVA, farmed much of the island's land in Catawba, Riesling and Chardonnay.

us-jahant.name: Jahant
us-jahant.summary: A small Lodi sub-AVA (2006) between the Mokelumne and Cosumnes rivers, close to the Delta, with clay-loam soils and cool afternoon winds. Zinfandel, Cabernet and Petite Sirah.

us-kanawha-river-valley.name: Kanawha River Valley
us-kanawha-river-valley.summary: An AVA (1986) in the Kanawha River valley of West Virginia, around Charleston, within the Ohio River Valley AVA. A small number of wineries grow hybrids.

us-kelsey-bench-lake-county.name: Kelsey Bench-Lake County
us-kelsey-bench-lake-county.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah, Sauvignon Blanc
us-kelsey-bench-lake-county.summary: A gently sloping bench (2013) between Big Valley and the Red Hills, at about 410 to 610 m, with about 900 acres of vines at approval. Better air drainage than Big Valley and deep, well-drained alluvial soils suit Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah and Sauvignon Blanc.

us-knights-valley.name: Knights Valley
us-knights-valley.summary: A small, elevated valley (1983) between Alexander Valley and Calistoga, at the southeast corner of northern Sonoma. Volcanic soils from Mount St. Helena and warm, sunny days give Cabernet Sauvignon of structure and depth, and Sauvignon Blanc. Beringer owns a large share of the vineyards; Peter Michael Winery, founded by British electronics entrepreneur Sir Peter Michael in 1982, is the star estate.

us-lake-chelan.name: Lake Chelan
us-lake-chelan.grapes: Riesling, Pinot Gris, Syrah, Malbec, Pinot Noir
us-lake-chelan.summary: A glacial-lake AVA (2009) of about 24,000 acres around the southern end of Lake Chelan, about 80 km long and one of the deepest lakes in the United States. The lake moderates temperatures and extends the season. At approval it had 13 bonded wineries and 140 acres; Riesling, Pinot Noir, Syrah and Malbec now grow among apple orchards.

us-lake-erie.name: Lake Erie
us-lake-erie.grapes: Concord, Niagara, Riesling, Vidal, Chardonnay, Catawba
us-lake-erie.summary: A three-state AVA (1983) along the south shore of Lake Erie in New York, Pennsylvania and Ohio, about 2.2 million acres. The lake keeps autumn mild, and the narrow strip between lake and escarpment is the largest Concord grape-growing area in the world, supplying Welch's juice; Welch's founder Charles Welch moved his operations to Westfield, New York in 1897. Wineries also grow Riesling, Vidal and hybrids. TTB proposed a Conneaut Creek sub-AVA in Ohio in 2024.

us-lake-michigan-shore.name: Lake Michigan Shore
us-lake-michigan-shore.grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Vidal, Concord
us-lake-michigan-shore.summary: An AVA (1983) in southwestern Michigan near Lake Michigan, where lake winds protect vines from cold. It is Michigan's most productive area, with St. Julian (1921) and Tabor Hill (1968) among its wineries.

us-lake-wisconsin.name: Lake Wisconsin
us-lake-wisconsin.grapes: Marquette, Maréchal Foch, St. Pepin, La Crescent
us-lake-wisconsin.summary: A small AVA (1994) of about 32,000 acres in Columbia and Dane counties, Wisconsin, on the Wisconsin River near Prairie du Sac. Wollersheim Winery occupies the site where the Hungarian Agoston Haraszthy planted vines in the 1840s before he left for California; its hillside caves were dug in 1858.

us-lamorinda.name: Lamorinda
us-lamorinda.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay
us-lamorinda.summary: A small, hilly AVA (2016) in western Contra Costa County named for the towns of Lafayette, Moraga and Orinda. Many tiny vineyards (46 covering 139 acres at approval) on the slopes of the Berkeley Hills grow Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, cooled by bay fog.

us-lancaster-valley.name: Lancaster Valley
us-lancaster-valley.summary: An AVA (1982) in Pennsylvania's Lancaster and Chester counties, in Pennsylvania Dutch farm country with deep, fertile limestone soils. Conestoga Vineyards petitioned for it; today wineries such as Waltz Vineyards grow Chardonnay and Bordeaux varieties alongside hybrids.

us-laurelwood-district.name: Laurelwood District
us-laurelwood-district.summary: A sub-AVA (2020) of about 33,600 acres on the northern and eastern slopes of the Chehalem Mountains, defined by Laurelwood soil: wind-blown loess deposited after the Missoula Floods over basalt. At approval it had about 70 vineyards (975 acres) and 25 wineries. Laurelwood Pinot Noir tends to be lifted and spicy.

us-leelanau-peninsula.name: Leelanau Peninsula
us-leelanau-peninsula.grapes: Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Blanc, Gewürztraminer
us-leelanau-peninsula.summary: A peninsula AVA (1982) between Lake Michigan and Grand Traverse Bay, home to dozens of wineries. Larry Mawby, who petitioned for the AVA, is known for sparkling wine; Riesling, Pinot Noir and Gewürztraminer are the main grapes.

us-lehigh-valley.name: Lehigh Valley
us-lehigh-valley.grapes: Riesling, Grüner Veltliner, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Chambourcin
us-lehigh-valley.summary: An AVA (2008) of about a million acres in eastern Pennsylvania along the Lehigh River, named from a Lenape word for river forks. Rolling hills; at approval nine wineries and 220 acres. Galen Glen and Fox & Hound are known for Grüner Veltliner and Riesling.

us-leona-valley.name: Leona Valley
us-leona-valley.summary: A narrow valley (2008) in northern Los Angeles County that follows the San Andreas fault, at about 900 m, with cold winters and hot summers. About 20 acres of vines at approval.

us-lewis-clark-valley.name: Lewis-Clark Valley
us-lewis-clark-valley.summary: A low, deep river canyon (2016) of about 307,000 acres where the Snake and Clearwater rivers meet at Lewiston, Idaho and Clarkston, Washington, far lower and warmer than the Snake River Valley to the south. Before Prohibition it was a thriving wine region. At approval it had 16 vineyards (81 acres) and three wineries. TTB realigned the Columbia Valley to avoid overlap.

us-lime-kiln-valley.name: Lime Kiln Valley
us-lime-kiln-valley.summary: A tiny valley (1982) within Cienega Valley, named for lime kilns that once burned local limestone. Old vineyards grow Zinfandel and Mourvèdre on limestone-rich soils.

us-linganore.name: Linganore
us-linganore.summary: An AVA (1983) in Frederick and Carroll counties, Maryland, around Linganore Creek in the Piedmont. Linganore Winecellars (Berrywine Plantations), founded in 1976, petitioned for it and makes grape and fruit wines; the area grows hybrids and vinifera.

us-livermore-valley.name: Livermore Valley
us-livermore-valley.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah
us-livermore-valley.summary:
One of California's oldest wine districts (AVA 1982, expanded 2006), an east-west valley in Alameda County where cool air from San Francisco Bay flows in each afternoon. Gravelly soils reminded early growers of Graves; Charles Wetmore planted Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc from Château d'Yquem cuttings in the 1880s, and his Cresta Blanca white won a gold medal at the 1889 Paris Exposition.

Carl Wente (1883) and James Concannon (1883) founded wineries that are still family-run. The Wente clone of Chardonnay, propagated from cuttings Ernest Wente obtained in 1912, is the ancestor of most Chardonnay planted in California. Concannon's Petite Sirah was the first varietal bottling of that grape (1961).
us-livermore-valley.nerd_note: Most Chardonnay in California descends from the 'Wente clone', making Livermore the grandmother of the state's most planted white.

us-lodi.name: Lodi
us-lodi.grapes: Zinfandel, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cinsault, Carignan, Petite Sirah, Chardonnay
us-lodi.summary:
Lodi (1986, expanded 2002) is a grower's appellation of about 540,000 acres and roughly 100,000 acres of vines in San Joaquin and Sacramento counties. It is California's Zinfandel capital, with hundreds of acres of vines more than 50 and some more than 100 years old, often own-rooted in sand. Cooling Delta breezes keep it fresher than the rest of the Central Valley.

The 'Lodi Native' project has bottled single-vineyard old-vine Zinfandels with minimal intervention to show site differences, and producers from Turley to Bedrock and Michael David buy Lodi old vines.

Lodi's sandy soils matter for more than texture: phylloxera cannot move easily through sand, so many old vineyards were never grafted, and some own-rooted Zinfandel and Cinsault vines are more than 130 years old. Growers here developed the Lodi Rules sustainability standard in 2005, now used outside the region. The style ranges from big, ripe, oaky Zinfandel to lighter, fresher bottlings from young producers who pick earlier.

us-loess-hills-district.name: Loess Hills District
us-loess-hills-district.summary: An AVA (2016) of about 4.6 million acres (some 7,200 square miles) along the Missouri River in western Iowa and northwestern Missouri, defined by its extraordinarily deep wind-blown loess soils, which form steep bluffs. At approval it had 66 vineyards on 112 acres and 13 wineries.

us-long-island.name: Long Island
us-long-island.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon
us-long-island.summary: The AVA (2001) covering Nassau and Suffolk counties, surrounding the North Fork and Hamptons AVAs. Long Island's maritime climate gives a growing season of about 220 days, longer than upstate, and sandy glacial soils. Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay and rosé are its strengths.

us-long-valley-lake-county.name: Long Valley-Lake County
us-long-valley-lake-county.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Petite Sirah
us-long-valley-lake-county.summary: A small, high valley (2023) of about 7,605 acres in northeastern Lake County, northeast of Clear Lake, with five vineyards (about 149 acres) and three wineries at approval. Elevation and cold winters distinguish it from High Valley, part of which it took over. Unusually, it lies outside the Clear Lake AVA; TTB adjusted the North Coast boundary to include it.

us-loramie-creek.name: Loramie Creek
us-loramie-creek.summary: A tiny AVA (1982) in Shelby County, western Ohio, created for a single farm winery; no longer commercially active, but still on the TTB list.

us-los-carneros.name: Los Carneros
us-los-carneros.summary:
Los Carneros (1983) straddles the southern ends of Napa and Sonoma counties along San Pablo Bay, and it was one of the first AVAs drawn by climate rather than county lines. Its name means 'the rams', for the sheep that once grazed its low, rolling hills. Fog and a near-daily wind off the bay keep it cool, and the shallow, dense clay soils restrain vigour.

That made it the natural home for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, first planted seriously by Louis M. Martini and Beaulieu (with Tchelistcheff) in the 1930s and 1940s, and later by Saintsbury (1981). Champagne and Cava houses followed: Domaine Carneros (Taittinger), Gloria Ferrer (Freixenet) and Artesa (Codorníu). Hyde and Hudson are its most famous grower vineyards; Larry Hyde's partnership with Aubert de Villaine of Domaine de la Romanée-Conti produces HdV.
us-los-carneros.terroir: Shallow, heavy clay loams over hardpan; persistent wind and fog from San Pablo Bay; one of the coolest parts of the North Coast.
us-los-carneros.nerd_note: Carneros wines can be labeled with Napa Valley or Sonoma Valley as well as Los Carneros, depending on which side of the county line the grapes grew.

us-los-olivos-district.name: Los Olivos District
us-los-olivos-district.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Syrah, Grenache, Cabernet Franc
us-los-olivos-district.summary: An alluvial plain (2016) of about 22,800 acres around the town of Los Olivos, between Ballard Canyon and Happy Canyon, with 47 vineyards (about 1,120 acres) at approval. Moderate temperatures and well-drained soils suit Sauvignon Blanc, Rhône and Bordeaux varieties.

us-lower-long-tom.name: Lower Long Tom
us-lower-long-tom.summary: The southernmost Willamette sub-AVA (2021), about 25,000 acres in the hills west of the Long Tom River near Monroe, between Eugene and Corvallis. Thin, uplifted marine sedimentary soils (Bellpine and Bellpine/Jory) and a slightly warmer climate. At approval it had 22 vineyards (492 acres) and 10 wineries.

us-madera.name: Madera
us-madera.grapes: Touriga Nacional, Tinta Cão, Orange Muscat, Black Muscat, French Colombard
us-madera.summary: A warm Central Valley AVA (1985) in Madera and Fresno counties, known for fortified and sweet wines: Ficklin pioneered port-style wines from Portuguese varieties in 1946, and Andrew Quady's Essensia (orange Muscat) and Elysium (black Muscat) are dessert-wine classics.

us-malibu-coast.name: Malibu Coast
us-malibu-coast.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir
us-malibu-coast.summary: An AVA (2014) of about 44,590 acres in the Santa Monica Mountains of Los Angeles and Ventura counties, with about 52 small vineyards on 198 acres at approval. Ocean views and marine air, but also the constant threat of wildfire: the 2018 Woolsey Fire burned through many vineyards. Los Angeles County has since restricted new vineyard planting in the Santa Monica Mountains.

us-malibu-newton-canyon.name: Malibu-Newton Canyon
us-malibu-newton-canyon.summary: A bowl-shaped AVA (1996) of about 850 acres high in the Santa Monica Mountains, created around Rosenthal's vineyard, which was planted in 1987. Above the marine layer, it grows Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay.

us-manton-valley.name: Manton Valley
us-manton-valley.summary: A small valley (2014) of about 11,200 acres on the western slope of Mount Lassen in Shasta and Tehama counties. Volcanic soils from Lassen and elevations around 600 m give cool nights; a few small wineries.

us-marthas-vineyard.name: Martha's Vineyard
us-marthas-vineyard.summary: An island AVA (1985) covering Martha's Vineyard, petitioned by Chicama Vineyards, which planted the island's first vinifera in 1971. Not to be confused with Heitz's famous Martha's Vineyard Cabernet in Napa. Little commercial production remains.

us-mcdowell-valley.name: McDowell Valley
us-mcdowell-valley.summary: A tiny bench valley (1982) east of Hopland at around 300 m. It is best known for old Syrah and Grenache, among California's oldest Rhône plantings (some vines date from 1919), which McDowell Valley Vineyards bottled in the early days of the Rhône Rangers movement.

us-mcminnville.name: McMinnville
us-mcminnville.summary: A sub-AVA (2005) in the Coast Range foothills west and southwest of McMinnville, limited to elevations of 200 to 1,000 feet, with uplifted marine sediments and basalt. Close to the Van Duzer Corridor, it is cool and windy, and the Pinot Noirs are dark and firmly structured. Eyrie's winery is in town, though its vineyards are in the Dundee Hills.

us-mendocino.name: Mendocino
us-mendocino.grapes: Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Carignan, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
us-mendocino.summary: The main AVA (1984) for the southern and central valleys of Mendocino County, including Anderson, Ukiah, Redwood and Potter valleys and McDowell Valley. It is used for blends from across those valleys; inland it means warm-climate Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Carignan and Cabernet.

us-mendocino-ridge.name: Mendocino Ridge
us-mendocino-ridge.summary:
The only non-contiguous AVA in the United States (1997): it consists of every piece of land above 1,200 feet (366 m) in a coastal strip of southwestern Mendocino County, so its map looks like an archipelago of 'islands in the sky' poking above the marine layer. Old Zinfandel vineyards such as Zeni and Ciapusci, planted by Italian families, grow on these ridges alongside newer Pinot Noir.

In January 2024 TTB proposed renaming it 'Mendocino Coast Ridge' to stress its coastal identity; as of late 2026 that proposal had not been finalised.
us-mendocino-ridge.nerd_note: Because only land above 1,200 feet counts, the AVA covers about 87,000 acres on paper but has only a few hundred acres of vines.

us-merritt-island.name: Merritt Island
us-merritt-island.summary: A Delta island (1983) of about 5,000 acres inside Clarksburg, bounded by the Sacramento River and Elk Slough. Sandy loam over peat and cool Delta breezes; the Bogle family petitioned for it.

us-mesilla-valley.name: Mesilla Valley
us-mesilla-valley.summary: An AVA (1985) along the Rio Grande from Las Cruces, New Mexico into far West Texas near El Paso, where Spanish friars planted Mission vines in the 17th century. Hot desert summers; St. Clair and La Viña are among its wineries.

us-middle-rio-grande-valley.name: Middle Rio Grande Valley
us-middle-rio-grande-valley.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Mission, Cabernet Sauvignon
us-middle-rio-grande-valley.summary: An AVA (1988) along the Rio Grande from Santa Fe's southern edge through Albuquerque to Socorro. Spanish friars planted Mission vines near Socorro around 1629, the first in what became the United States. Gruet, founded by a Champagne family from Bethon in 1984, makes traditional-method sparkling wine here.

us-middleburg-virginia.name: Middleburg Virginia
us-middleburg-virginia.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Merlot, Chardonnay, Viognier
us-middleburg-virginia.summary: An AVA (2012) of about 190 square miles in Loudoun and Fauquier counties, horse country an hour from Washington, D.C. At approval it had 10 vineyards and 14 wineries. Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot and Chardonnay; Boxwood and RdV (founded by Rutger de Vink) make some of Virginia's most serious Bordeaux blends nearby.

us-mimbres-valley.name: Mimbres Valley
us-mimbres-valley.summary: An AVA (1985) in the Mimbres River valley of southwestern New Mexico around Deming. Large vineyards here, many owned by European investors in the 1980s, supply much of New Mexico's wine grapes.

us-mississippi-delta.name: Mississippi Delta
us-mississippi-delta.summary: A large alluvial AVA (1984) of about 4.1 million acres covering the Mississippi Delta in Mississippi, Louisiana and Tennessee. The Rushing Winery petitioned for it; muscadines dominate the little wine made here.

us-mokelumne-river.name: Mokelumne River
us-mokelumne-river.summary: The largest and most important Lodi sub-AVA (2006), on the deep, sandy alluvial fan of the Mokelumne River west of the foothills. It holds most of Lodi's oldest Zinfandel and Cinsault, own-rooted because phylloxera cannot thrive in such sand. Bechthold, Soucie and Royal Tee are famous old-vine sites.

us-monterey.name: Monterey
us-monterey.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot
us-monterey.summary: Large AVA (1984) covering the Salinas Valley and its side valleys. Cold wind blows up the valley from Monterey Bay every afternoon, so the north is among the coolest places in California and yields are high on the flat valley floor; the south around King City is warmer. Monterey is a major source of Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Riesling for big brands, with a small number of exceptional sites on the benches.

us-monticello.name: Monticello
us-monticello.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Merlot, Viognier, Petit Manseng, Chardonnay
us-monticello.summary:
Virginia's most important AVA (1984, expanded 2018), around Charlottesville in the Piedmont foothills of the Blue Ridge, named for Thomas Jefferson's home. Jefferson's vinifera failed, but modern growers on well-drained, clay-rich slopes make Virginia's best Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Viognier and Bordeaux blends. Barboursville, Early Mountain, King Family, Jefferson Vineyards and Michael Shaps are leading producers.

Charlottesville's wine scene grew from Gabriele Rausse's 1976 plantings at Barboursville and Horton Vineyards' bet on Viognier (from 1991), which led Virginia to adopt Viognier as its signature white. Petit Manseng, whose thick skins resist humidity, has become another local success. Summer rain and hurricanes remain the main threats, so growers favour well-drained slopes in the foothills (around 150 to 450 m), open canopies and early-ripening clones.
us-monticello.nerd_note: Jefferson Vineyards grows on land that Jefferson gave to Philip Mazzei for his 1774 vineyard experiment.

us-moon-mountain-district-sonoma-county.name: Moon Mountain District Sonoma County
us-moon-mountain-district-sonoma-county.summary:
A steep mountain AVA (2013) of about 17,600 acres on the western face of the Mayacamas above the Sonoma Valley, with 40 commercial vineyards at the time of the petition. Volcanic rock and red soils on west-facing slopes give dense Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel.

Monte Rosso, planted in the 1880s by Emmanuel Goldstein and bought by Louis M. Martini in 1938, is its most famous vineyard, with Zinfandel and Cabernet vines more than a century old.
us-moon-mountain-district-sonoma-county.nerd_note: 'Sonoma County' is part of the official AVA name to keep it from being confused with other Moon Mountains.

us-mount-pisgah-polk-county-oregon.name: Mount Pisgah, Polk County, Oregon
us-mount-pisgah-polk-county-oregon.summary: A small AVA (2022) of about 5,850 acres around Mount Pisgah, a hill west of Salem near the town of Dallas. Its soils come from Siletz River volcanics, basalt about 40 to 60 million years old and much older than the Jory of the Dundee Hills. At approval it had 10 vineyards (531 acres) and two wineries, including Freedom Hill Vineyard, a famous source of Pinot Noir.

us-mt-harlan.name: Mt. Harlan
us-mt-harlan.summary:
A one-producer mountain AVA (1990) high in the Gabilan Range, about 670 to 790 m, created for Josh Jensen's Calera. After studying in Burgundy, Jensen searched California for limestone and found it on an old lime kiln site here; he planted Pinot Noir from 1975 in named parcels (Selleck, Reed, Jensen, Mills, de Villiers, Ryan).

The Pinots are lean, mineral and long-lived, and Calera's Viognier was one of the first in America.

Jensen planted his first three Pinot Noir parcels in 1975 at about 670 m, far from any town and with scarce water. Yields are very low because of the thin soils and drought. Calera's Pinots are known for long ageing: they start firm and savoury and open into mushroom, rose and red-fruit perfume after a decade. Jensen sold the winery to Duckhorn in 2017, and the estate continues to bottle each named parcel separately.
us-mt-harlan.nerd_note: Calera means lime kiln in Spanish; the old kiln Jensen found on the mountain told him the limestone he wanted was there.

us-mt-veeder.name: Mt. Veeder
us-mt-veeder.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec, Merlot, Syrah, Zinfandel, Chardonnay
us-mt-veeder.summary:
Mountain AVA (1990) in the southern Mayacamas, west of the city of Napa, with vineyards from about 150 to 750 m on steep, forested slopes. Unlike the volcanic north, much of Mt. Veeder is uplifted ancient seabed: shallow, acidic sandstone and shale soils that keep yields tiny. The wines are taut and powerful, Cabernet Sauvignon and Malbec with firm acid and dusty tannin that need years in bottle.

Mayacamas Vineyards, built around an 1889 stone winery, is the reference. Its 1971 Cabernet was in the 1976 Paris red flight and tied for third place at the 30th-anniversary rematch in 2006. The Hess Collection pairs mountain Cabernet with a museum of contemporary art.
us-mt-veeder.terroir: Shallow, sedimentary marine soils (sandstone, shale) with some volcanic intrusions; steep slopes, cooler marine-influenced climate.
us-mt-veeder.nerd_note: Mayacamas's 1970s Cabernets were famously hard in youth; bottles from the Travers era (1968 to 2013) are now prized for how slowly they evolved.

us-naches-heights.name: Naches Heights
us-naches-heights.summary: A volcanic plateau (2011) of about 13,250 acres northwest of Yakima, at 365 to 640 m, formed by the Tieton andesite lava flow; its soils are wind-blown loess over that volcanic rock. At approval it had 105 acres of vines.

us-napa-valley.name: Napa Valley
us-napa-valley.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Zinfandel
us-napa-valley.summary:
The most famous wine address in the Americas, approved in 1981 as California's first AVA and the second in the country after Augusta, Missouri. The AVA covers almost all of Napa County apart from the area around Lake Berryessa, so it includes the valley floor, both mountain ranges and the side valleys, and it contains 17 smaller AVAs.

Napa's reputation rests on Cabernet Sauvignon. The style that made it famous is ripe and dense, with blackcurrant, plum, cocoa and sweet tannin, often lifted by new French oak. Thoughtful producers have moved toward earlier picking and less oak since the 2010s, but generosity of fruit is the house signature. A Napa Valley label alone usually means a blend of sites, while the sub-AVAs and named vineyards tell you where on the map the wine comes from.

The valley is also a lesson in land politics. The Agricultural Preserve of 1968 forbade subdivision of the valley floor into lots smaller than 20 acres (later 40), which is why the valley still looks like farmland rather than the Silicon Valley sprawl a few miles south. Land values are now among the highest for any vineyard outside Burgundy and Champagne, and a ton of Napa Cabernet costs several times the California average.
us-napa-valley.terroir: Mediterranean climate with a strong north-south temperature gradient: cool and foggy near San Pablo Bay, warm toward Calistoga. Soils mix volcanic material from the Sonoma Volcanics, uplifted marine sediments and gravelly alluvial fans. Mountain vineyards above the fog line give smaller berries and firmer tannin.
us-napa-valley.nerd_note: Napa Valley was the first AVA approved in California (1981). Wines from any of its 17 sub-AVAs must also show 'Napa Valley' on the label under California's conjunctive labeling law.
contains: Oak Knoll District of Napa Valley

us-nashoba-valley.name: Nashoba Valley
us-nashoba-valley.grapes: Albariño, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Riesling, St. Croix
us-nashoba-valley.summary: A new AVA (effective April 2026) of about 18,367 acres in Worcester County, Massachusetts, around Bolton, Harvard and Stow, an old apple-orchard area west of Boston. The soils formed in glacial till and outwash; the most common series, Paxton, is a well-drained, deep loam. TTB accepted about 1,697 growing degree days (Celsius base), placing it in Winkler Region III. At approval it had three commercial vineyards on about 16 acres, growing Albariño, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Riesling and St. Croix. Nashoba Valley Winery (1978), known for fruit wines, is the best-known producer.

us-niagara-escarpment.name: Niagara Escarpment
us-niagara-escarpment.summary: An AVA (2005) on the bench below the Niagara Escarpment in Niagara County, the US counterpart of Ontario's Niagara benchlands across the river. Lake Ontario's moderating effect and limestone-rich soils suit Riesling, Cabernet Franc and ice wine. At approval it had about 400 acres of vineyards.

us-nine-lakes-of-east-tennessee.name: Nine Lakes of East Tennessee
us-nine-lakes-of-east-tennessee.grapes: Chambourcin, Cabernet Franc, Muscadine, Vidal, Traminette
us-nine-lakes-of-east-tennessee.summary: A large AVA (effective April 2026) of about 4,064 square miles in the Valley and Ridge Province of East Tennessee, named for the nine reservoirs created by Tennessee Valley Authority dams in the 14 counties around Knoxville. Parallel ridges (about 330 to 460 m) and valleys let growers choose slopes where morning sun dries the dew. At approval it had about 232 acres of vines and 29 wineries, many of them busy tourist wineries around the Great Smoky Mountains gateway towns.

us-north-coast.name: North Coast
us-north-coast.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Zinfandel, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot
us-north-coast.summary: A vast umbrella AVA (1983) of about 3.3 million acres covering the wine country north of San Francisco: most of Napa, Sonoma, Mendocino and Lake counties plus parts of Solano and Marin. It contains dozens of smaller AVAs and is mostly used for blends that draw on several counties, much as 'Central Coast' is used farther south.
us-north-coast.nerd_note: TTB modified the North Coast boundary when it created the Petaluma Gap AVA (2017) and again for Long Valley-Lake County (2023); the 2024 Comptche AVA was deliberately left outside it.

us-north-fork-of-long-island.name: North Fork of Long Island
us-north-fork-of-long-island.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
us-north-fork-of-long-island.summary: The northern prong (1986) of eastern Long Island, between Long Island Sound and Peconic Bay, with most of the island's vineyards and about 40 wineries. Water on three sides moderates temperatures; well-drained sandy loam suits Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Chardonnay in a fresh, Bordeaux-like style. Alex and Louisa Hargrave planted the first vineyard at Cutchogue in 1973.

us-north-fork-of-roanoke.name: North Fork of Roanoke
us-north-fork-of-roanoke.summary: A small AVA (1983) in the valley of the North Fork of the Roanoke River in Montgomery and Roanoke counties, in the Ridge and Valley region of southwestern Virginia. Very few vineyards today.

us-north-yuba.name: North Yuba
us-north-yuba.summary: A small, high foothill AVA (1985) in Yuba County, created around Renaissance Vineyard, a winery founded by a spiritual community in the 1970s and known for long-aged Cabernet and late-harvest whites.

us-northern-neck-george-washington-birth.name: Northern Neck George Washington Birthplace
us-northern-neck-george-washington-birth.summary: An AVA (1987) on the Northern Neck peninsula between the Potomac and Rappahannock rivers, where George Washington was born in 1732. Rivers and the Chesapeake moderate the climate; Ingleside Vineyards, which petitioned for the AVA, is the leading winery.

us-northern-sonoma.name: Northern Sonoma
us-northern-sonoma.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Zinfandel
us-northern-sonoma.summary: An umbrella AVA (1985) covering most of northern Sonoma County, including the Russian River, Dry Creek, Alexander and Knights valleys, Chalk Hill and Rockpile. It was petitioned by E. & J. Gallo, whose estate vineyards span several of those valleys, and it is used mainly by producers blending across them.

us-oak-knoll-district-of-napa-valley.name: Oak Knoll District of Napa Valley
us-oak-knoll-district-of-napa-valley.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc
us-oak-knoll-district-of-napa-valley.summary:
The southernmost valley-floor AVA (2004) apart from Carneros, between the city of Napa and Yountville. Cool, foggy mornings and a long, even season suit Chardonnay, Riesling and Merlot as well as a more restrained, savoury style of Cabernet Sauvignon.

Trefethen is the anchor. Its 1886 Eshcol winery, one of Napa's surviving 19th-century wooden 'ghost wineries', was badly damaged in the magnitude 6.0 South Napa earthquake of 2014 and rebuilt. Trefethen's 1976 Chardonnay was judged best Chardonnay at the 1979 Gault-Millau 'Wine Olympics' in Paris.
us-oak-knoll-district-of-napa-valley.terroir: Alluvial fans from the Mayacamas and Dry Creek, deep gravelly and clay loams; marine-cooled.
producers: Robert Biale (Black Chicken Zinfandel sourced nearby)
us-oak-knoll-district-of-napa-valley.nerd_note: Oak Knoll is one of the few Napa sub-AVAs whose official name includes 'of Napa Valley', a compromise to avoid clashing with other Oak Knolls.

us-oakville.name: Oakville
us-oakville.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Petit Verdot, Sauvignon Blanc
us-oakville.summary:
Oakville (1993) is the richest square mile in American wine. The western bench below the Mayacamas holds To Kalon, the vineyard H.W. Crabb planted in the 1860s and named from the Greek for 'the highest beauty'; Robert Mondavi built his winery on it in 1966, the first major new winery in Napa since Prohibition. Opus One stands across Highway 29, Harlan Estate is on the western hills above, and Screaming Eagle, Dalla Valle and the old Heitz Martha's Vineyard are minutes away.

Oakville Cabernet combines the depth of Rutherford with a little more freshness and polish: cassis, violets, graphite and long, fine-grained tannin. Vineyards on the western alluvial fans give the most perfumed wines; the eastern side toward the Silverado Trail has heavier soils and more muscular reds.
us-oakville.terroir: Gravelly alluvial fans from the Mayacamas on the west; volcanic-derived soils from the Vaca Range on the east; moderately warm, with fog burning off by late morning.
us-oakville.nerd_note: To Kalon today is divided among several owners (Mondavi/Constellation, Beckstoffer, Opus One, the Detert and MacDonald families), and Constellation's trademark on the name has been the subject of lawsuits.

us-ohio-river-valley.name: Ohio River Valley
us-ohio-river-valley.grapes: Chambourcin, Vidal, Catawba, Traminette, Cabernet Franc
us-ohio-river-valley.summary: A huge AVA (1983) of about 16 million acres along the Ohio River in Indiana, Kentucky, Ohio and West Virginia. This was the scene of America's first commercial wine boom: Swiss settlers at Vevay, Indiana planted vines in the early 1800s, and Nicholas Longworth's Catawba at Cincinnati made 'sparkling Catawba' famous in the 1840s and 1850s. Today it is a broad umbrella for scattered wineries.

us-old-mission-peninsula.name: Old Mission Peninsula
us-old-mission-peninsula.grapes: Riesling, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Gewürztraminer
us-old-mission-peninsula.summary: A narrow, 30 km peninsula (1987) jutting into Grand Traverse Bay north of Traverse City. Lake Michigan surrounds it on three sides, delaying spring and extending autumn; cherry orchards share the slopes with Riesling, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Edward O'Keefe planted vinifera at Chateau Grand Traverse in 1974, Michigan's first commercial vinifera vineyard.

us-outer-coastal-plain.name: Outer Coastal Plain
us-outer-coastal-plain.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Chardonnay, Albariño, Chambourcin
us-outer-coastal-plain.summary: New Jersey's largest AVA (2007, expanded 2017), about 2.25 million acres of sandy coastal plain in the southern half of the state. The Atlantic and Delaware Bay moderate the climate and give a long season; sandy, well-drained soils suit Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Chardonnay, Albariño and Chambourcin. Renault Winery at Egg Harbor City has operated since 1864.

us-ozark-highlands.name: Ozark Highlands
us-ozark-highlands.summary: A large AVA (1987) of about 1.85 million acres on the Ozark Plateau of south-central Missouri, around St. James, with chert and limestone soils. Italian immigrants at Rosati and St. James grew Concord and Catawba; St. James Winery is one of Missouri's largest.

us-ozark-mountain.name: Ozark Mountain
us-ozark-mountain.summary: By area the largest AVA in the United States: about 33 million acres (around 52,000 square miles) of the Ozark Plateau in Missouri, Arkansas and Oklahoma, approved in 1986. It contains the Hermann, Ozark Highlands, Altus and Arkansas Mountain AVAs and is used mostly as a catch-all for wines from the Ozarks.

us-pacheco-pass.name: Pacheco Pass
us-pacheco-pass.summary: A small AVA (1984) at the pass through the Diablo Range between Santa Clara and San Benito counties. Strong marine winds; a few vineyards on the historic route to the San Joaquin Valley.

us-paicines.name: Paicines
us-paicines.summary: A small AVA (1982) in San Benito County south of Hollister, petitioned by Almaden, which once planted large vineyards here. Cool breezes; mostly grape-growing for other wineries.

us-palos-verdes-peninsula.name: Palos Verdes Peninsula
us-palos-verdes-peninsula.summary: A small coastal AVA (2021) of about 15,900 acres on the hilly peninsula south of Los Angeles, with only about 7 acres of vines at approval. Uplifted marine terraces and constant ocean breezes.

us-paso-robles.name: Paso Robles
us-paso-robles.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Petite Sirah, Merlot
us-paso-robles.summary:
The large Paso Robles AVA (1983, expanded 2009) covers about 610,000 acres and more than 40,000 acres of vines in northern San Luis Obispo County. Hot days, very cold nights and limestone-rich hills on the west side give powerful Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel and Rhône blends. Since 2014 it has been divided into 11 district AVAs.

The 2014 division into 11 districts came after a decade of debate and studies by the Paso Robles AVA Committee showing large differences in rainfall (from under 250 mm in the east to over 760 mm in the west), soils and temperature. Paso is also one of California's most ambitious Rhône regions: the Rhône Rangers movement of the 1980s and 1990s found its home here, and Saxum's James Berry Vineyard bottlings have been among the most highly scored American Rhône blends. Water is the key political issue, since the Paso Robles groundwater basin is overdrawn and the county has limited new plantings.

us-paso-robles-estrella-district.name: Paso Robles Estrella District
us-paso-robles-estrella-district.summary: Rolling plains (2014) northeast of Paso Robles along the Estrella River, warm and dry with alluvial terraces. Gary Eberle planted Syrah here in the 1970s, among California's first.

us-paso-robles-geneseo-district.name: Paso Robles Geneseo District
us-paso-robles-geneseo-district.summary: An area of low hills (2014) east of Paso Robles city, with old alluvial terraces, some calcareous soils and moderate warmth, rainfall slightly higher than further east. Bordeaux and Rhône varieties do well, and Cass and Tobin James are among its wineries.

us-paso-robles-highlands-district.name: Paso Robles Highlands District
us-paso-robles-highlands-district.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Syrah, Petite Sirah
us-paso-robles-highlands-district.summary: The high, remote southeastern district (2014), at 365 to 610 m, with the largest day-night temperature swings in Paso Robles, low rainfall and sandy alluvial soils. Large vineyards grow Cabernet, Zinfandel and Rhône varieties.

us-paso-robles-willow-creek-district.name: Paso Robles Willow Creek District
us-paso-robles-willow-creek-district.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Zinfandel, Cabernet Sauvignon
us-paso-robles-willow-creek-district.summary: Rolling hills (2014) west of Paso Robles town, with calcareous soils, cool marine air from the Templeton Gap and some of the region's most famous estates. Saxum's James Berry Vineyard, Linne Calodo and L'Aventure make dense, ripe Rhône and Cabernet blends here.

us-paulsell-valley.name: Paulsell Valley
us-paulsell-valley.summary: A foothill AVA (2022) of about 34,155 acres in eastern Stanislaus County, in rolling grazing land at the edge of the Sierra foothills east of Modesto. The petition stressed its rolling topography and soils, distinct from the flat, irrigated valley floor to the west.

us-petaluma-gap.name: Petaluma Gap
us-petaluma-gap.summary:
One of the only AVAs defined by wind. Petaluma Gap (approved December 2017, effective 2018) covers about 202,500 acres in southern Sonoma and northern Marin, where a break in the coastal hills between Bodega Bay and San Pablo Bay funnels cold ocean air inland every afternoon. The petition cited afternoon wind speeds well above those of the surrounding areas.

Wind makes grape skins thicker and slows ripening while keeping acidity high, so the 4,000-odd acres of vines give Pinot Noir with deep colour and firm structure, and peppery cool-climate Syrah.
us-petaluma-gap.nerd_note: Wind was the main distinguishing feature in the petition, which made Petaluma Gap a test case for TTB's idea of what counts as terroir.

us-pine-mountain-cloverdale-peak.name: Pine Mountain-Cloverdale Peak
us-pine-mountain-cloverdale-peak.summary: A small mountain AVA (2011) of about 4,570 acres around Pine Mountain, a 900 m peak on the western flank of the Mayacamas above Cloverdale, straddling the Sonoma-Mendocino line. Vineyards sit roughly from 490 to 900 m, above the Alexander Valley heat and fog, in thin, rocky volcanic and sedimentary soils. Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc are dark, firm and mineral.
us-pine-mountain-cloverdale-peak.nerd_note: The petitioners first asked for 'Pine Mountain-Mayacmas'; the name was changed after objections that it could be confused with Mayacamas Vineyards on Mt. Veeder.

us-potter-valley.name: Potter Valley
us-potter-valley.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay
us-potter-valley.summary: A high, cool valley (1983) northeast of Ukiah, ringed by mountains and fed by water diverted from the Eel River into the Russian River. Cold nights and a long season favour aromatic whites (Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc) and botrytised dessert wines, as well as Pinot Noir.

us-puget-sound.name: Puget Sound
us-puget-sound.grapes: Madeleine Angevine, Siegerrebe, Müller-Thurgau, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris
us-puget-sound.summary: A large AVA (1995) of about 4.5 million acres west of the Cascades, around Seattle and the islands of Puget Sound. Cool, cloudy and wet, it suits early-ripening grapes such as Madeleine Angevine, Siegerrebe, Müller-Thurgau and Pinot Noir. It is home to many wineries that buy grapes from eastern Washington, so the AVA name is used on only a small share of their wines.

us-ramona-valley.name: Ramona Valley
us-ramona-valley.summary: An upland AVA (2006) of about 89,000 acres in San Diego County, at 300 to 900 m around the town of Ramona. At approval it had 17 vineyards on about 45 acres; many small wineries now grow Rhône and Bordeaux varieties.

us-rattlesnake-hills.name: Rattlesnake Hills
us-rattlesnake-hills.summary: A sub-AVA (2006) of about 68,500 acres on the south-facing slopes of the Rattlesnake Hills north of the Yakima River, at 260 to 900 m, with many small wineries. Higher elevation and good air drainage reduce frost risk.

us-red-hill-douglas-county-oregon.name: Red Hill Douglas County, Oregon
us-red-hill-douglas-county-oregon.summary: One of Oregon's smallest AVAs (2005), about 5,500 acres around a single hill near Yoncalla in the northern Umpqua, with red, Jory-type volcanic soil similar to the Dundee Hills. Essentially one large vineyard; Pinot Noir.

us-red-hills-lake-county.name: Red Hills Lake County
us-red-hills-lake-county.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Petite Sirah
us-red-hills-lake-county.summary: Volcanic hills (2004, expanded 2024) on the flanks of Mount Konocti south of Clear Lake, at about 430 to 900 m. The red soils are full of obsidian and the light is intense, so Cabernet Sauvignon develops thick skins, dark colour and firm tannin, often with surprising freshness. Andy Beckstoffer's Amber Knolls and Obsidian Ridge are among its best-known vineyards.
us-red-hills-lake-county.nerd_note: The 2004 petition reported about 3,100 acres of vineyards; obsidian chips glitter in the soil after rain.

us-red-mountain.name: Red Mountain
us-red-mountain.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot
us-red-mountain.summary:
Washington's smallest AVA from 2001 until Candy Mountain arrived in 2020, about 4,000 acres on the southwest-facing slope of a low ridge near Benton City, at the east end of the Yakima Valley. It is one of the warmest spots in the state, with constant wind and very low rainfall; sandy, calcareous, rocky soils and wind stress produce small berries with thick skins.

The result is Washington's most tannic, concentrated Cabernet Sauvignon. Jim Holmes and John Williams planted Kiona and Ciel du Cheval in 1975; Hedges, Col Solare (Ste. Michelle and Antinori), Klipsun and Tapteil followed.

The sandy, calcareous soils over basalt are low in organic matter and very free-draining, so growers control vigour tightly with drip irrigation; vines are often own-rooted. Afternoon wind keeps the canopy dry and stresses the berries, shrinking them and thickening their skins, which is why the wines carry Washington's firmest tannins. The 2001 AVA was one of the first Washington appellations defined on such a small scale. Col Solare (founded by Antinori and Ste. Michelle), Duckhorn's Canvasback and Quilceda Creek's Galitzine Vineyard show how outside investment followed the reputation.
us-red-mountain.nerd_note: Despite the name, the mountain is not red; it is named for the cheatgrass (downy brome) that turns the slopes reddish in spring.

us-redwood-valley.name: Redwood Valley
us-redwood-valley.grapes: Zinfandel, Carignan, Petite Sirah, Cabernet Sauvignon
us-redwood-valley.summary: A warm valley (1997) north of Ukiah, at the head of the Russian River watershed, with red, iron-rich soils. Italian families planted Zinfandel, Carignan and Petite Sirah here early in the 20th century, and Fetzer was founded here in 1968. Old vines still give some of Mendocino's best Zinfandel and Carignan.

us-ribbon-ridge.name: Ribbon Ridge
us-ribbon-ridge.summary: A tiny ridge (2005) about 5.6 km long within the Chehalem Mountains, made of uplifted ocean sediments (Willakenzie soils) and sheltered by the larger mountains. At approval it had 14 vineyards on 286 acres. Beaux Frères (founded in 1986 by Mike Etzel with his brother-in-law Robert Parker) and Patricia Green made it famous for dark, dense Pinot Noir.

us-river-junction.name: River Junction
us-river-junction.summary: A small AVA (2001) at the confluence of the Stanislaus and San Joaquin rivers in San Joaquin County, defined by river-borne alluvial soils and Delta breezes. It was created around a single large vineyard, and the name is rarely seen on labels.

us-rockpile.name: Rockpile
us-rockpile.grapes: Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah
us-rockpile.summary: A rugged, remote AVA (2002) of ridges above the west arm of Lake Sonoma, limited to land above about 240 m (800 feet). Thin, rocky soils, wind and sun above the fog give concentrated, spicy Zinfandel and Petite Sirah with firm structure. The name comes from Rockpile Ranch, homesteaded in the 1850s by an ancestor of the Mauritson family.

us-rocky-knob.name: Rocky Knob
