us-rocky-knob.summary: A small, high AVA (1983) on the Blue Ridge plateau in Floyd and Patrick counties along the Blue Ridge Parkway, near Rocky Knob. Cool, elevated and wind-swept; Villa Appalaccia makes Italian varieties here.

us-rocky-reach.name: Rocky Reach
us-rocky-reach.summary: A small AVA (2022) of about 32,000 acres on terraces along the Columbia River north of Wenatchee, near the Rocky Reach Dam. Its gravelly, rocky soils were deposited when the Missoula Floods and glacial outburst floods reshaped the canyon.

us-rogue-valley.name: Rogue Valley
us-rogue-valley.grapes: Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Tempranillo, Viognier, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir
us-rogue-valley.summary: A large, warm valley system (1991) around Medford and Grants Pass along the Rogue River and its tributaries (Applegate, Illinois, Bear Creek). The eastern part around Ashland is high and continental; the west is wetter. Syrah, Tempranillo, Cabernet, Merlot and Viognier thrive; Peter Britt's Valley View (1852) at Jacksonville was Oregon's first recorded winery.

us-royal-slope.name: Royal Slope
us-royal-slope.summary: A large AVA (2020) of 156,389 acres on the gentle, south-facing slopes of the Frenchman Hills, north of the Wahluke Slope. At approval 13 vineyards covered about 14,100 acres, many of them very large; the elevation and slope keep cold air draining away.

us-russian-river-valley.name: Russian River Valley
us-russian-river-valley.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Zinfandel, Syrah, Sauvignon Blanc
us-russian-river-valley.summary:
California's most celebrated cool-climate Pinot Noir appellation (1983, expanded in 2005 and 2011), about 171,000 acres around the lower Russian River from Healdsburg south to Sebastopol. Fog rolls up the river and through the Petaluma Gap most summer nights and mornings, so days start cold, warm by mid-afternoon and cool again by evening. That pattern gives ripe red-berry and cola Pinot Noir with bright acidity, and rich, citrusy Chardonnay.

The Burgundian pioneers were Joseph Swan (first vintage 1969), the Rochioli family (Pinot from the late 1960s), Williams Selyem (first vintage 1981), Dehlinger and Kistler. Westside Road, along the river south of Healdsburg, is the Pinot Noir 'Golden Mile'. Old-vine Zinfandel and sparkling wine also thrive.
us-russian-river-valley.terroir: Goldridge sandy loam (ancient marine sandstone), alluvial river terraces and some clay; fog-driven daily temperature swings.
us-russian-river-valley.nerd_note: Burt Williams and Ed Selyem started as weekend garagistes; their 1987 Rochioli Vineyard Pinot Noir won the California State Fair's top prize and made the label a mailing-list sensation.
contains: Green Valley of Russian River Valley

us-rutherford.name: Rutherford
us-rutherford.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Sauvignon Blanc
us-rutherford.summary:
Rutherford (1993) is classic Napa Cabernet country, a band across the valley floor between Oakville and St. Helena. Its fame rests on the Rutherford Bench, gravelly alluvial fans on the west side where Beaulieu and Inglenook built the reputation of California Cabernet before and after Prohibition. André Tchelistcheff, Beaulieu's winemaker from 1938, summed up the place in a line every Napa guide quotes: it takes Rutherford dust to grow great Cabernet.

The 'dust' is a texture as much as a taste: a fine, cocoa-powder tannin and a savoury, dusty, dried-herb note over ripe blackcurrant. Inglenook's 1941 Cabernet and Beaulieu's Georges de Latour Private Reserve (from the 1936 vintage) are touchstones of American wine history.
us-rutherford.terroir: Deep, well-drained gravelly loam on the western bench; heavier, more volcanic soils toward the Silverado Trail. Moderately warm with morning fog.
us-rutherford.nerd_note: Gustave Niebaum, a Finnish sea captain who made his fortune in the Alaska fur trade, founded Inglenook around 1880. Francis Ford Coppola bought the estate in 1975 and, in 2011, bought back the Inglenook name and restored it.

us-saddle-rock-malibu.name: Saddle Rock-Malibu
us-saddle-rock-malibu.summary: A tiny AVA (2006) of about 2,090 acres in the Santa Monica Mountains above Malibu, at 520 to 680 m, essentially the Semler family's Malibu Family Wines vineyard (planted 1997). Its hilltop vines produce Bordeaux and Rhône reds.

us-salado-creek.name: Salado Creek
us-salado-creek.summary: A small AVA (2004) of about 2,940 acres at the foot of the Diablo Range in western Stanislaus County, with 44 acres of vines at approval. Spanish explorer Gabriel Moraga named Salado ('salty') Creek.

us-san-antonio-valley.name: San Antonio Valley
us-san-antonio-valley.summary: A remote valley (2006) west of the Salinas Valley in southern Monterey County, near Mission San Antonio de Padua (1771) and the Fort Hunter Liggett army base. Warm days and cold nights; Rhône and Bordeaux varieties and Zinfandel.

us-san-benito.name: San Benito
us-san-benito.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Zinfandel, Cabernet Sauvignon
us-san-benito.summary: Umbrella AVA (1987) for the winegrowing valleys of San Benito County, east of Monterey across the Gabilan Range, including Cienega Valley, Paicines and Lime Kiln Valley. Almaden once farmed thousands of acres here.

us-san-bernabe.name: San Bernabe
us-san-bernabe.summary: An AVA (2004) defined by one enormous vineyard south of King City in the Salinas Valley, at one time described as the largest contiguous vineyard in the world (more than 5,000 acres, owned by Delicato). Sandy, wind-deposited soils grow a range of varieties for large brands.

us-san-francisco-bay.name: San Francisco Bay
us-san-francisco-bay.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Zinfandel, Petite Sirah
us-san-francisco-bay.summary: An umbrella AVA (1999) covering the counties around San Francisco Bay, roughly 2,450 square miles at creation, expanded in 2006, 2008 and 2024 (to take in all of the new Contra Costa AVA). It contains Livermore Valley, Santa Clara Valley, Lamorinda, Contra Costa and others and is used for blends from around the Bay.

us-san-juan-creek.name: San Juan Creek
us-san-juan-creek.summary: The eastern, hottest and driest of the Paso Robles districts (2014), in the upper Cholame and San Juan Creek valleys, with low rainfall and big vineyards.

us-san-lucas.name: San Lucas
us-san-lucas.summary: A warm AVA (1987) in the southern Salinas Valley around San Lucas, beyond the reach of most of Monterey Bay's cold afternoon wind. Large vineyards on alluvial benches, some owned by Delicato, which petitioned for it, supply Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Chardonnay to big producers.

us-san-luis-obispo-coast.name: San Luis Obispo Coast
us-san-luis-obispo-coast.summary: A coastal AVA (2022) of about 408,500 acres stretching the length of San Luis Obispo County west of the Santa Lucia Range, from the Monterey line to the Santa Maria River. It is cooled directly by the Pacific and encloses the Edna Valley and Arroyo Grande Valley AVAs. Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Syrah are the focus.

us-san-luis-rey.name: San Luis Rey
us-san-luis-rey.summary: A new AVA (2024) of about 97,700 acres in northern San Diego County around Fallbrook, Bonsall, Pala and Pauma Valley, named for the San Luis Rey River and Mission San Luis Rey de Francia (1798). At approval it had 44 vineyards on about 256 acres and 23 wineries. Marine air reaches the valleys through the river corridor.

us-san-miguel-district.name: San Miguel District
us-san-miguel-district.summary: The northern district (2014) around the town and mission of San Miguel Arcángel (1797), warm with alluvial soils along the Salinas and Estrella rivers. Large vineyards for Cabernet and Merlot.

us-san-pasqual-valley.name: San Pasqual Valley
us-san-pasqual-valley.summary: One of the earliest AVAs (1981), a small valley near Escondido in San Diego County. Its vineyards have mostly disappeared, but it remains on the TTB list. The proposed Rancho Guejito AVA would partly overlap it.

us-san-ysidro-district.name: San Ysidro District
us-san-ysidro-district.summary: A small district (1990) on the eastern side of the Santa Clara Valley near Gilroy, cooled by marine air through the Pajaro Gap. It mostly supplies Chardonnay and Pinot Noir to wineries elsewhere.

us-santa-clara-valley.name: Santa Clara Valley
us-santa-clara-valley.summary: The historic valley (1989) south of San Francisco Bay, now Silicon Valley. In the 19th century it had dozens of wineries, including Paul Masson's and Almaden (founded 1852 by Charles Lefranc), but urban growth erased most vineyards. Vines remain in the south around Gilroy, Morgan Hill and the Hecker Pass.

us-santa-cruz-mountains.name: Santa Cruz Mountains
us-santa-cruz-mountains.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Merlot, Zinfandel
us-santa-cruz-mountains.summary:
One of the first AVAs defined by its mountains (1982): the boundary follows elevation lines on both sides of the range, roughly above 400 feet on the ocean side and 800 feet on the bay side, to take in the slopes rather than the valleys. The range between Silicon Valley and the Pacific has vineyards scattered through redwood and oak forest, many above the fog.

Its history is outsized. Paul Masson made sparkling wine at Saratoga from the 1890s; Martin Ray founded Mount Eden in the 1940s and preached 100 percent varietal wines; Ridge's Monte Bello Cabernet (made under Paul Draper from 1969) placed fifth in the red flight at the 1976 Paris tasting and won the 30th-anniversary rematch outright in 2006. Rhys, Mount Eden and others make thrilling Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
us-santa-cruz-mountains.terroir: Steep slopes of fractured Franciscan shale, sandstone and some limestone (Monte Bello); marine influence, fog in the valleys, and the San Andreas fault running through the range.
us-santa-cruz-mountains.nerd_note: Ridge has printed full ingredient lists on its labels since 2011, a direct challenge to secretive winemaking.

us-santa-lucia-highlands.name: Santa Lucia Highlands
us-santa-lucia-highlands.summary:
Terraced benches (1992) on the eastern flank of the Santa Lucia Range, facing east across the Salinas Valley, from about 30 to 370 m. Morning fog and fierce afternoon winds from Monterey Bay give a long, cool season, while the southeast-facing slopes catch the morning sun. The result is dense, dark-fruited, deeply coloured Pinot Noir and rich Chardonnay and Syrah.

The Pisoni family (Gary Pisoni planted from 1982) and Garys' Vineyard (with Gary Franscioni), Rosella's and Sleepy Hollow are the famous names.
us-santa-lucia-highlands.terroir: Gravelly, well-drained alluvial terraces of granitic origin; strong afternoon winds.

us-santa-margarita-ranch.name: Santa Margarita Ranch
us-santa-margarita-ranch.summary: The southernmost Paso Robles district (2014), a single historic ranch near Santa Margarita that was part of the mission lands of San Luis Obispo. Cooler and wetter than most of Paso Robles; large vineyards of Cabernet and Chardonnay.

us-santa-maria-valley.name: Santa Maria Valley
us-santa-maria-valley.summary:
A wide, funnel-shaped valley (1981, expanded 2010) that opens west to the Pacific, among the first AVAs in California. Morning fog, afternoon wind and a long, cool season (harvests can run into November) give Pinot Noir and Chardonnay with bright acidity and spice.

Bien Nacido Vineyard, planted by the Miller family from 1973 on benches above the Santa Maria River, has supplied scores of producers with vineyard-designated fruit; Au Bon Climat and Qupé share a winery on the property.

us-santa-ynez-valley.name: Santa Ynez Valley
us-santa-ynez-valley.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Syrah, Sauvignon Blanc, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon
us-santa-ynez-valley.summary:
The broad valley AVA (1983) along the Santa Ynez River, running from Lompoc east toward Lake Cachuma, with a strong west-to-east warming gradient. It contains Sta. Rita Hills, Ballard Canyon, Los Olivos District and Happy Canyon, and is used for blends across them.

The valley is a textbook of how distance from the ocean controls style. At the western end, Sta. Rita Hills grows taut Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; in the middle, Ballard Canyon and Los Olivos ripen Syrah and Grenache; at the eastern end, Happy Canyon is much warmer on summer afternoons and grows Cabernet. The town of Los Olivos and Solvang, a Danish-themed village, are the tourist hubs, and the 2004 film Sideways was largely shot along this valley's roads.

us-seiad-valley.name: Seiad Valley
us-seiad-valley.summary: One of California's northernmost AVAs (1994), a tiny valley on the Klamath River in Siskiyou County near the Oregon border. It was established for a single grower and has almost no commercial vineyards today.

us-seneca-lake.name: Seneca Lake
us-seneca-lake.grapes: Riesling, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir, Gewürztraminer, Lemberger
us-seneca-lake.summary: The largest and deepest Finger Lake gives its name to a sub-AVA (2003) with more than 50 wineries on its slopes. The lake rarely freezes, so the 'banana belt' on its southeastern shore is the warmest part of the Finger Lakes, good for Riesling, Cabernet Franc and even Merlot. Hermann J. Wiemer, Red Newt, Ravines and Fox Run are here.

us-shawnee-hills.name: Shawnee Hills
us-shawnee-hills.summary: An AVA (2006) in the unglaciated hills of southern Illinois, between the Ohio and Mississippi rivers. The region had about 1,250 acres of vineyards in 1890; today about a dozen wineries grow Chambourcin, Norton and Traminette.

us-shenandoah-valley.name: Shenandoah Valley
us-shenandoah-valley.grapes: Chardonnay, Riesling, Cabernet Franc, Vidal, Chambourcin
us-shenandoah-valley.summary: A long limestone valley AVA (1982) between the Blue Ridge and the Allegheny Mountains in Virginia and West Virginia, drier than the Piedmont thanks to the rain shadow of the mountains. Riesling, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc and hybrids; Bluestone and Barren Ridge are among its wineries. Not to be confused with California Shenandoah Valley.

us-sierra-foothills.name: Sierra Foothills
us-sierra-foothills.grapes: Zinfandel, Barbera, Syrah, Petite Sirah, Sangiovese
us-sierra-foothills.summary: A long umbrella AVA (1987) of about 2.6 million acres following the Sierra Nevada foothills through eight counties. Gold Rush vineyards of Zinfandel survive here, and the higher reaches grow Rhône varieties and Barbera.

us-sierra-pelona-valley.name: Sierra Pelona Valley
us-sierra-pelona-valley.summary: A small valley (2010) in northern Los Angeles County near Agua Dulce, at about 760 to 1,000 m, with about 96 acres of vines at approval. A high-desert-edge climate with big temperature swings.

us-sloughhouse.name: Sloughhouse
us-sloughhouse.summary: The northeastern and warmest Lodi sub-AVA (2006), in Sacramento County in the Sierra foothills along the Cosumnes River, with red, cobbly soils. Zinfandel and Rhône varieties.

us-snake-river-valley.name: Snake River Valley
us-snake-river-valley.grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Malbec
us-snake-river-valley.summary: A huge AVA (2007) of about 5.2 million acres along the Snake River across southwestern Idaho and two Oregon counties. Vineyards mostly sit at 600 to 900 m on volcanic and old lake-bed soils (from Pliocene Lake Idaho), with hot days, cold nights and frequent winter freeze risk. At approval it had 15 wineries and 1,107 acres of vines.

us-snipes-mountain.name: Snipes Mountain
us-snipes-mountain.summary: A small AVA (2009) of 4,145 acres on a single uplift rising from the floor of the Yakima Valley near Sunnyside. Its rocky soils include rounded cobbles carried by the ancestral Columbia River. William B. Bridgman planted vinifera on its slopes around 1917 and founded Upland Winery in 1934, and Harrison Hill Vineyard has Cabernet Sauvignon planted in 1963, among the oldest in the state. Named for cattle baron Ben Snipes, who settled at its base in the 1850s.

us-solano-county-green-valley.name: Solano County Green Valley
us-solano-county-green-valley.summary: A small valley (1983) in the hills of western Solano County, next door to Napa's Wild Horse Valley and east of Coombsville, cooled by air from San Pablo Bay through the Carquinez Strait. Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay grow on gentle slopes. It was renamed in its current form to distinguish it from Sonoma's Green Valley.

us-sonoita.name: Sonoita
us-sonoita.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Tempranillo, Malvasia Bianca, Cabernet Sauvignon
us-sonoita.summary: Arizona's first AVA (1984), a grassland basin southeast of Tucson at about 1,500 m. Dr. Gordon Dutt of the University of Arizona planted test vineyards in the 1970s and founded Sonoita Vineyards in 1983. Red, iron-rich soils and monsoon rains in July and August; Callaghan Vineyards and Dos Cabezas made it known.

us-sonoma-coast.name: Sonoma Coast
us-sonoma-coast.summary:
A huge AVA (1987) of more than half a million acres that runs from the Mendocino line to San Pablo Bay and reaches well inland. It was drawn so broadly that it lumps cold coastal ridges with warm inland flats, and its creation is usually traced to Sonoma-Cutrer, whose vineyards needed a single AVA to qualify for 'estate bottled' labels. For decades the name promised more coolness than many wines delivered, which is why growers on the true coast pushed for Fort Ross-Seaview (2011) and West Sonoma Coast (2022).

At its best Sonoma Coast Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are lean, saline and intensely perfumed.

TTB drew Sonoma Coast in 1987 around a 'marine climate' line, but because it reached far inland to the edge of the Sonoma Valley and Russian River, it included warm sites as well as cold ones. That is why growers on the true coast pushed for Fort Ross-Seaview (2011) and West Sonoma Coast (2022). The best Sonoma Coast wines still come from ridgetops near the ocean and from the cool southern hills around Petaluma, where winds and fog keep sugars low and acidity high.
us-sonoma-coast.nerd_note: Sonoma Coast contains the Russian River Valley, Green Valley, Petaluma Gap, Fort Ross-Seaview and West Sonoma Coast AVAs.

us-sonoma-mountain.name: Sonoma Mountain
us-sonoma-mountain.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Zinfandel, Chardonnay
us-sonoma-mountain.summary: A mountain AVA (1985) on the western side of the Sonoma Valley, above Glen Ellen, including Jack London's Beauty Ranch. Vineyards above the fog get sun and a long season, and thin volcanic soils keep yields low. Cabernet Sauvignon is fine-grained and savoury; Patrick Campbell's Laurel Glen (from 1981) defined it.

us-sonoma-valley.name: Sonoma Valley
us-sonoma-valley.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Merlot, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Syrah
us-sonoma-valley.summary:
The 'Valley of the Moon' (1982), running from Carneros north to Santa Rosa between the Mayacamas and Sonoma Mountain. This is where Sonoma wine began: Mission San Francisco Solano (1823), General Vallejo's vineyards, Haraszthy's Buena Vista (1857) and Gundlach Bundschu's Rhinefarm (1858). Jack London ranched at Glen Ellen.

The south is cooled by San Pablo Bay; the north around Kenwood is warm, and its hillsides grow powerful Cabernet and Zinfandel. Old vineyards such as Old Hill Ranch (planted in the 1880s) carry Zinfandel field blends; Hanzell (planted 1953) is a Chardonnay and Pinot Noir landmark.

us-south-coast.name: South Coast
us-south-coast.grapes: Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Viognier, Zinfandel
us-south-coast.summary: Umbrella AVA (1985) of about 2.1 million acres covering the coastal portions of Orange, Riverside and San Diego counties, including Temecula Valley, Ramona Valley, San Pasqual Valley and San Luis Rey. Two further AVAs inside it were proposed by TTB: Rancho Guejito (2024) and Rancho Santa Fe (August 2026).

us-southeastern-new-england.name: Southeastern New England
us-southeastern-new-england.grapes: Chardonnay, Vidal, Riesling, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir
us-southeastern-new-england.summary: A coastal AVA (1983) of about 2 million acres across Connecticut, Rhode Island and Massachusetts, including Cape Cod and the islands. The ocean extends the season by a few weeks compared with inland New England. Sakonnet Vineyards (now Carolyn's Sakonnet) in Little Compton, Rhode Island, petitioned for it; Westport Rivers in Massachusetts makes fine sparkling wine.

us-southern-oregon.name: Southern Oregon
us-southern-oregon.grapes: Pinot Noir, Syrah, Tempranillo, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Viognier
us-southern-oregon.summary: Umbrella AVA (2004) joining the Umpqua and Rogue valleys, created so wines blended across them could carry a regional name. At approval it had about 120 vineyards, 3,000 acres and 17 wineries.

us-spring-mountain-district.name: Spring Mountain District
us-spring-mountain-district.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Riesling
us-spring-mountain-district.summary:
Mountain AVA (1993) on the Mayacamas slopes directly west of St. Helena, from about 120 m to almost 800 m. Steep, terraced vineyards on a mix of volcanic and sedimentary soils give Cabernet Sauvignon with firm tannin, bright acidity and a herbal, forest-floor note, and they hold some of Napa's most interesting whites: Stony Hill's taut, unoaked Chardonnay (first vintage 1952) and Smith-Madrone's dry Riesling.

The district has deep history (Tiburcio Parrott's Miravalle mansion of the 1880s later starred as the house in the TV soap Falcon Crest) and recent scars: the 2020 Glass Fire destroyed or damaged several estates here, including Newton and Cain.
us-spring-mountain-district.terroir: Volcanic and uplifted marine sedimentary soils, steep slopes, fog-free afternoons and cool mountain nights.
us-spring-mountain-district.nerd_note: Pride Mountain Vineyards straddles the Napa-Sonoma county line, so it keeps separate records for grapes grown on each side. Spring Mountain Vineyard's 1973 Chardonnay finished fourth among the whites at the 1976 Paris tasting.

us-squaw-valley-miramonte.name: Squaw Valley-Miramonte
us-squaw-valley-miramonte.summary: A foothill AVA (2015) of about 44,690 acres in eastern Fresno County, at 450 to 1,000 m on the western slope of the Sierra, much cooler than the San Joaquin Valley floor. Three wineries and a few vineyards at approval.

us-st-helena.name: St. Helena
us-st-helena.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Sauvignon Blanc, Zinfandel
us-st-helena.summary:
Mid-valley AVA (1995) around the town of St. Helena, where the valley floor is narrowest and the heat of the north meets the last of the bay's influence. It is the historic heart of Napa: Charles Krug founded the valley's first commercial winery here in 1861, Beringer followed in 1876, and Heitz, Spottswoode, Duckhorn and Corison all sit within a few kilometres.

Cabernet Sauvignon from St. Helena tends to be plush and ripe, with the warmth of the upper valley, while the benchland vineyards on the west side (Spottswoode, Corison's Kronos) give more perfume and finesse. Merlot and Sauvignon Blanc also do well.
us-st-helena.terroir: Alluvial fans from the Mayacamas on the west, heavier clay and volcanic soils toward the Vaca side; warm days with modest fog.
us-st-helena.nerd_note: Beringer made sacramental wine through Prohibition and claims to be Napa's oldest continuously operating winery; its 1884 Rhine House is a Victorian copy of the family home on the Rhine.

us-sta-rita-hills.name: Sta. Rita Hills
us-sta-rita-hills.summary:
The cold western end of the Santa Ynez Valley (2001, expanded 2016), where the Santa Rosa Road and Highway 246 corridors run between hills of sand, clay and diatomaceous earth straight toward the Pacific. It is one of the coolest places in California to grow red grapes, and its Pinot Noirs combine dark fruit with high acidity, herbs and a saline edge; Chardonnay is equally tense.

Richard Sanford and Michael Benedict planted the Sanford & Benedict vineyard in 1971, proving the area could ripen Pinot Noir. The AVA was approved as 'Santa Rita Hills' and shortened to 'Sta. Rita Hills' in 2005 after Chile's Viña Santa Rita objected to the use of its name.
us-sta-rita-hills.terroir: Marine sediments, sand, chert and diatomaceous earth; steady afternoon winds; many growing-season days under 25 degrees Celsius.
us-sta-rita-hills.nerd_note: The 2016 expansion drew 41 objections arguing that the added land sat on a different landmass, a rare public fight over a few hundred acres.

us-stags-leap-district.name: Stags Leap District
us-stags-leap-district.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Petit Verdot, Cabernet Franc, Sauvignon Blanc
us-stags-leap-district.summary:
A tiny AVA (1989) of about 1,200 ha below the rocky palisades of the Vaca Range on the Silverado Trail. The bare volcanic cliffs soak up and radiate heat, while afternoon wind from San Pablo Bay funnels through and cools the vines, a combination that gives Cabernet Sauvignon of ripe, silky texture over a firm core, the 'iron fist in a velvet glove' of local cliché.

This is where Warren Winiarski planted the S.L.V. vineyard in 1970, next to Nathan Fay's pioneering Cabernet. His 1973 S.L.V. Cabernet won the red flight at the Paris tasting of 1976. Stag's Leap Wine Cellars (S.L.V., FAY, Cask 23) has been wholly owned by Marchesi Antinori since 2023. Shafer's Hillside Select, Clos du Val (founded 1972) and Pine Ridge are also here.
us-stags-leap-district.terroir: Volcanic rock and gravelly loam fans at the foot of the palisades; heat reflected from bare rock, cooled by afternoon bay breezes.
us-stags-leap-district.nerd_note: The AVA name carries no apostrophe at all: Stag's Leap Wine Cellars and Stags' Leap Winery fought for years over the name, a settlement let each keep its own punctuation, and TTB sidestepped the issue.

us-suisun-valley.name: Suisun Valley
us-suisun-valley.grapes: Petite Sirah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel, Chardonnay
us-suisun-valley.summary: A valley (1982) just east of Napa across the Vaca Range near Fairfield, among the first AVAs approved in California. Afternoon winds from the Suisun Bay cool it, and it grows Petite Sirah, Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel. Wooden Valley and Ledgewood Creek are among its wineries.

us-swan-creek.name: Swan Creek
us-swan-creek.summary: A small sub-AVA (2008) of the Yadkin Valley in Wilkes, Yadkin and Iredell counties, with three wineries and 75 acres at approval; sandy-loam soils of the Brushy Mountains foothills.

us-tehachapi-mountains.name: Tehachapi Mountains
us-tehachapi-mountains.summary: A high mountain AVA (2020) of about 58,000 acres in Kern County, at roughly 1,000 to 1,500 m, between the San Joaquin Valley and the Mojave. Cool nights and big temperature swings; six small vineyards and one winery at approval.

us-temecula-valley.name: Temecula Valley
us-temecula-valley.grapes: Syrah, Tempranillo, Sangiovese, Viognier, Cabernet Sauvignon
us-temecula-valley.summary: Southern California's main wine district (1984), in Riverside County about 35 km from the Pacific. Cool air comes through the Rainbow Gap and Santa Margarita River gap each afternoon, and elevations of 300 to 450 m moderate the heat. Ely Callaway planted here in 1969; today there are dozens of wineries, mostly tourist-oriented, growing Rhône, Italian and Spanish varieties. Pierce's disease, spread by the glassy-winged sharpshooter, devastated vineyards around 1999 to 2000.

us-templeton-gap-district.name: Templeton Gap District
us-templeton-gap-district.grapes: Zinfandel, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir
us-templeton-gap-district.summary: The southwestern corner of Paso Robles (2014), where gaps in the Santa Lucia Range let ocean air and fog reach the vineyards. It is the coolest of the districts, with calcareous soils; Zinfandel has been grown here by Italian families since the early 20th century.

us-texas-davis-mountains.name: Texas Davis Mountains
us-texas-davis-mountains.summary: A high, remote AVA (1998) in the Davis Mountains of West Texas, around Fort Davis, with vineyards at about 1,500 m on volcanic soils, among the highest in the state.

us-texas-high-plains.name: Texas High Plains
us-texas-high-plains.grapes: Tempranillo, Mourvèdre, Tannat, Cabernet Sauvignon, Viognier, Roussanne, Sangiovese
us-texas-high-plains.summary: The engine of Texas wine (1993), about 8.9 million acres on the Llano Estacado around Lubbock, at 900 to 1,200 m. It grows the large majority of Texas wine grapes. Hot days, cool nights, wind and low humidity keep disease down, though hail and spring freeze are serious risks; soils are sandy loam over caliche. Tempranillo, Mourvèdre, Tannat, Viognier and Roussanne lead.

us-texas-hill-country.name: Texas Hill Country
us-texas-hill-country.grapes: Tempranillo, Mourvèdre, Sangiovese, Viognier, Blanc du Bois, Cabernet Sauvignon
us-texas-hill-country.summary: By area the largest AVA wholly within one state (1991), about 9.3 million acres (some 14,500 square miles) west of Austin and San Antonio, centred on Fredericksburg. It is the heart of Texas wine tourism, with more than 100 wineries, though only a small share of the state's vineyards; many wineries use High Plains grapes. Limestone and granite soils; hot, humid summers. Two new AVAs, Llano Uplift and Hickory Sands District, were proposed inside it in 2026.
contains: Fredericksburg in the Texas Hill Country

us-texoma.name: Texoma
us-texoma.grapes: Blanc du Bois, Black Spanish, Cabernet Sauvignon, Munson hybrids
us-texoma.summary: An AVA (2005) of about 3,350 square miles along the Red River on the Texas-Oklahoma border, around Lake Texoma and Denison, where T.V. Munson worked. Pierce's disease limits vinifera; Munson's hybrids and Blanc du Bois do better.

us-the-burn-of-columbia-valley.name: The Burn of Columbia Valley
us-the-burn-of-columbia-valley.summary: An AVA (2021) of about 16,870 acres on a plateau above the Columbia River in eastern Klickitat County. The name is the one local residents have long used for the plateau; TTB declined to protect 'The Burn' on its own because the term is used elsewhere.

us-the-hamptons-long-island.name: The Hamptons, Long Island
us-the-hamptons-long-island.summary: The southern prong (1985) of eastern Long Island, cooler and windier than the North Fork with heavier, loamy soils. Channing Daughters, Wölffer Estate and Duck Walk make Merlot, Chardonnay, sparkling wine and rosé for the summer crowd.

us-the-rocks-district-of-milton-freewate.name: The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater
us-the-rocks-district-of-milton-freewate.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Tempranillo
us-the-rocks-district-of-milton-freewate.summary:
The only AVA in the United States defined almost entirely by a single soil feature (2015). It sits on the Oregon side of the Walla Walla Valley, on the alluvial fan of the Walla Walla River, where the ground is a jumble of rounded basalt cobbles (Freewater cobbly loam) that store heat and radiate it at night. At approval it had about 250 acres of vines on 3,770 acres.

Christophe Baron, a Champenois, spotted the stones in 1996 and planted Cayuse; the Syrahs from The Rocks have a savoury, olive, smoked-meat and iron character often compared to the northern Rhône, sometimes called 'funk' by fans.
us-the-rocks-district-of-milton-freewate.nerd_note: The AVA was the first in the US whose petition rested almost wholly on soil; it is entirely within Oregon, yet nearly all the wineries that use it are across the state line in Walla Walla, Washington.

us-tip-of-the-mitt.name: Tip of the Mitt
us-tip-of-the-mitt.summary: A cold AVA (2016) of about 2,760 square miles (1.75 million acres) at the northern tip of Michigan's Lower Peninsula, between Lakes Michigan and Huron. Cold-hardy hybrids dominate; 41 vineyards (94 acres) and 8 wineries at approval.

us-tracy-hills.name: Tracy Hills
us-tracy-hills.summary: An AVA (2006) of about 39,200 acres in the foothills southwest of Tracy, in San Joaquin and Stanislaus counties, with about 1,005 acres of vines at approval; afternoon winds from the Altamont Pass cool the area.

us-trinity-lakes.name: Trinity Lakes
us-trinity-lakes.summary: A remote mountain AVA (2005) of about 96,000 acres around Lewiston and Trinity Lake in Trinity County, high in the Klamath Mountains. Vines are few and the climate is cool and continental.

us-tryon-foothills.name: Tryon Foothills
us-tryon-foothills.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Petit Verdot, Viognier, Chambourcin
us-tryon-foothills.summary: A new AVA (effective October 2025) of about 176 square miles in Polk County, North Carolina, around Tryon and Columbus, on the escarpment where the Blue Ridge drops to the Piedmont. Its key feature is a thermal belt: on calm nights, cold air sinks to the valley floors and warmer air settles on the mid-slopes, so frost is rarer there. The petition placed 95 percent of the area in Winkler Region V; at approval it had five vineyards (about 78 acres) and four wineries.

us-tualatin-hills.name: Tualatin Hills
us-tualatin-hills.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling, Pinot Gris
us-tualatin-hills.summary: The northwestern corner of the Willamette Valley (2020), about 144,000 acres in the hills west of Portland around Forest Grove, Gaston and Hillsboro. Laurelwood loess soils, higher rainfall and cooler temperatures than further south. At approval it had 33 vineyards and 21 wineries, including David Hill and Ernest Reuter's historic Forest Grove plantings.

us-ulupalakua.name: Ulupalakua
us-ulupalakua.grapes: Syrah, Malbec, Grenache, Chenin Blanc, Viognier
us-ulupalakua.summary: The smallest AVA in the United States (2021), about 70 acres on the leeward slopes of Haleakalā on Maui, at around 600 m, with about 16 acres of vines at approval. It is essentially MauiWine's estate on the historic Ulupalakua Ranch, where Emil Tedeschi planted grapes in 1974; volcanic soils and trade winds suit Syrah, Malbec and Chenin Blanc, and MauiWine also makes pineapple wine.

us-umpqua-valley.name: Umpqua Valley
us-umpqua-valley.grapes: Pinot Noir, Tempranillo, Syrah, Albariño, Riesling
us-umpqua-valley.summary: The 'hundred valleys of the Umpqua' (1984) around Roseburg, a tangle of small valleys where the Klamath Mountains, Cascades and Coast Range meet. It has the most varied geology in Oregon and a climate between the cool Willamette and the warm Rogue. Richard Sommer's HillCrest (1961) restarted Oregon wine here, and Abacela planted the Pacific Northwest's first Tempranillo in 1995.

us-upper-cumberland.name: Upper Cumberland
us-upper-cumberland.summary: A large AVA (2024) of about 2.19 million acres on the Highland Rim and Cumberland Plateau in Middle Tennessee, with 55 small vineyards (about 71 acres) and nine wineries at approval. The petition stressed limestone and sandstone geology, elevation, soils and climate.

us-upper-hiwassee-highlands.name: Upper Hiwassee Highlands
us-upper-hiwassee-highlands.summary: A mountain AVA (2014) of about 690 square miles in the Hiwassee River basin straddling Georgia and North Carolina. At approval 26 vineyards grew about 54 acres of hybrids, natives and vinifera, and five wineries were operating.

us-upper-hudson.name: Upper Hudson
us-upper-hudson.grapes: Marquette, Frontenac, La Crescent, Seyval Blanc
us-upper-hudson.summary: An AVA (2018) north of the Hudson River Region around Saratoga and Albany, defined by its colder climate, which favours cold-hardy hybrids like Marquette, Frontenac and La Crescent; about 1,500 square miles.

us-upper-lake-valley.name: Upper Lake Valley
us-upper-lake-valley.summary: A valley (2022) at the north end of Clear Lake around the town of Upper Lake, about 17,360 acres. The petition stressed hydrogeology: a shallow water table fed by streams from the Mendocino National Forest, plus soils and a climate that differ from the rest of Clear Lake. Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet Sauvignon dominate.

us-upper-mississippi-river-valley.name: Upper Mississippi River Valley
us-upper-mississippi-river-valley.grapes: Marquette, Frontenac, La Crescent, St. Croix, Edelweiss
us-upper-mississippi-river-valley.summary: The second-largest AVA by area (2009), about 19 million acres along the Mississippi in Illinois, Iowa, Minnesota and Wisconsin, including the unglaciated 'Driftless Area'. Cold winters limit growers to hybrids bred at the University of Minnesota and by Elmer Swenson, such as Marquette, Frontenac, La Crescent and Brianna.

us-van-duzer-corridor.name: Van Duzer Corridor
us-van-duzer-corridor.summary: A low gap through the Coast Range (2018) about 59,900 acres in size, through which cold Pacific air flows into the Willamette Valley every summer afternoon, dropping temperatures fast. The AVA covers the valley floor and foothills where that wind hits hardest; at approval it had 17 vineyards on about 1,000 acres. Pinot Noir from here has thick skins, dark colour and high acidity.
us-van-duzer-corridor.nerd_note: The wind is so reliable that growers call it the 'Van Duzer winds'; TTB clarified Eola-Amity Hills' boundary when it created this AVA.

us-verde-valley.name: Verde Valley
us-verde-valley.summary: A valley AVA (2021) of about 200 square miles along the Verde River in Yavapai County, near Cottonwood and Jerome, at roughly 1,000 to 1,500 m. Maynard James Keenan of Caduceus Cellars helped lead its rise. At approval it had 24 vineyards (about 125 acres) and 11 wineries.

us-virginia-peninsula.name: Virginia Peninsula
us-virginia-peninsula.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Petit Verdot
us-virginia-peninsula.summary: A coastal AVA (2021) of about 673,000 acres between the James and York rivers, including Williamsburg and Jamestown, where Acte 12 ordered colonists to plant vines in 1619. It was petitioned by The Williamsburg Winery; at approval it had five vineyards on about 112 acres.

us-virginias-eastern-shore.name: Virginia's Eastern Shore
us-virginias-eastern-shore.grapes: Chardonnay, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot
us-virginias-eastern-shore.summary: A coastal AVA (1990) on the Delmarva Peninsula between Chesapeake Bay and the Atlantic. Water on both sides moderates temperatures and extends the season; sandy soils. Chatham Vineyards on Church Creek is the leading winery.

us-wahluke-slope.name: Wahluke Slope
us-wahluke-slope.summary: A broad, south-facing alluvial fan (2006) of about 81,000 acres on the north bank of the Columbia, east of Mattawa, one of the warmest and driest places in Washington. Huge vineyards supply many wineries with ripe Merlot, Cabernet and Syrah.

us-walla-walla-valley.name: Walla Walla Valley
us-walla-walla-valley.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Cabernet Franc, Grenache
us-walla-walla-valley.summary:
A celebrated AVA (1984, realigned 2001) shared by Washington and Oregon, around the town of Walla Walla at the foot of the Blue Mountains. Rainfall rises sharply toward the mountains (from about 300 mm in the west to more than 500 mm near the foothills), so some vineyards can be dry-farmed. Soils are wind-blown loess over Missoula flood deposits, plus basalt cobbles in The Rocks District.

Leonetti (1977), Woodward Canyon (1981) and L'Ecole No 41 (1983) built the valley's name for Cabernet, Merlot and Syrah; it now has well over 100 wineries. TTB proposed a Mill Creek-Walla Walla Valley sub-AVA of about 4,900 acres in August 2026.

Walla Walla is Washington's wine town par excellence: a small, historic farming town with over 100 wineries and tasting rooms in a valley that also grows its famous sweet onions. The valley shares its AVA with Oregon, and the Oregon side's cobbled Rocks District gives the Syrahs that made the area famous among sommeliers. A severe freeze in January 2024 damaged many vines, and growers continue to experiment with burying canes and frost protection.

us-warren-hills.name: Warren Hills
us-warren-hills.summary: An AVA (1988) in the valleys of Warren County in northwestern New Jersey, where limestone valleys run between forested ridges of the Highlands. Cold winters favour hybrids such as Vidal and Chambourcin alongside cool-climate vinifera such as Chardonnay and Cabernet Franc.

us-west-elks.name: West Elks
us-west-elks.summary: One of the highest AVAs in the US (2001), along the North Fork of the Gunnison River around Paonia and Hotchkiss, at about 1,700 to 1,900 m. Cool and high, it grows Pinot Noir, Riesling and Gewürztraminer; Stone Cottage and Azura are among its small wineries.

us-west-sonoma-coast.name: West Sonoma Coast
us-west-sonoma-coast.summary:
Approved in 2022, West Sonoma Coast (about 141,800 acres) is the 'true' Sonoma Coast that growers had wanted since the 1990s: the band nearest the Pacific, from the Gualala River to the Petaluma Gap area, including the ridges around Annapolis, Fort Ross, Freestone and Occidental. TTB accepted that topography, geology and the marine climate set it apart from the inland parts of the old Sonoma Coast AVA.

Vineyards sit on steep ridges between redwood forest, often above the fog, in cold, windy conditions with long hang time. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are tense and aromatic, Syrah is peppery and lean.
us-west-sonoma-coast.terroir: Marine sediments of the Franciscan complex and sandstone; strong marine influence with fog in the hollows and sun on ridgetops.

us-western-connecticut-highlands.name: Western Connecticut Highlands
us-western-connecticut-highlands.grapes: Seyval Blanc, Vidal, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc
us-western-connecticut-highlands.summary: An upland AVA (1988) in western Connecticut's Litchfield Hills, with cold winters and a short season; Hopkins Vineyard and others grow hybrids and cool-climate vinifera.

us-white-bluffs.name: White Bluffs
us-white-bluffs.summary: An AVA (2021) of about 93,700 acres on a plateau east of the Columbia near Pasco, named for the pale cliffs of ancient lake sediments (the Ringold Formation) along the river. The plateau's flat top and south-facing slopes are cut by the Ringold and Koontz coulees.

us-wild-horse-valley.name: Wild Horse Valley
us-wild-horse-valley.summary: A small, cool upland valley (1988) on the ridge east of Napa city that straddles the Napa-Solano county line, with most of it in Solano County. At around 300 to 600 m and open to wind from the bay, it is one of the coolest corners of the Napa Valley AVA, suited to Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Plantings are tiny and the name rarely appears on labels.
us-wild-horse-valley.terroir: Volcanic soils on a windy upland; cool, marine-influenced climate.
us-wild-horse-valley.nerd_note: It is one of the few Napa sub-AVAs that lies mostly outside Napa County.

us-willamette-valley.name: Willamette Valley
us-willamette-valley.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc, Riesling, Gamay
us-willamette-valley.summary:
Oregon's flagship AVA (1983, expanded 2016) of about 3.4 million acres, with most of the state's wineries and vineyards. Cool, wet winters and dry summers, with a long, mild ripening period in September and October, give Pinot Noir of red-fruit perfume, silk and bright acidity. Chardonnay has become a second calling card since the 2010s, made in a leaner, reductive style.

The valley's story is one of outsiders proving experts wrong. In the 1960s UC Davis advised that Oregon was too cold and wet for vinifera; David Lett, Dick Erath, David Adelsheim and Dick Ponzi planted anyway, choosing hillsides above the frost-prone floor. Today vintages swing between cool, rainy years that give translucent, high-acid Pinot and warm years (2014, 2015, 2018, 2022) that give richer, darker wines. Burgundian investment (Drouhin from 1987, Louis Jadot's Résonance, Lafon's Lingua Franca partnership, Roserock) and Champagne interest in sparkling wine have made the Willamette the New World's closest analogue to the Côte d'Or in spirit, though its soils (volcanic, marine sediment, loess) are quite different.

us-willcox.name: Willcox
us-willcox.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Tempranillo, Malvasia Bianca, Viognier
us-willcox.summary: Arizona's main growing area (2016), about 526,000 acres in a high basin around a dry lake bed (Willcox Playa) at about 1,300 to 1,600 m. At approval it had 21 vineyards on about 454 acres and 18 wineries; it now grows the majority of Arizona's wine grapes, mostly Rhône and Spanish varieties.

us-willow-creek.name: Willow Creek
us-willow-creek.summary: A small AVA (1983) along the Trinity River in eastern Humboldt and western Trinity counties, where coastal fog meets inland heat. A handful of growers make Zinfandel and Pinot Noir.

us-winters-highlands.name: Winters Highlands
us-winters-highlands.summary: A small upland AVA (2023) of about 7,300 acres in the foothills west of Winters, straddling Yolo and Solano counties near the Napa line. The petition cited higher humidity and less rainfall than surrounding areas, plus distinctive soils; vineyards grow Bordeaux and Mediterranean varieties.

us-wisconsin-ledge.name: Wisconsin Ledge
us-wisconsin-ledge.grapes: Marquette, La Crescent, St. Pepin, Frontenac
us-wisconsin-ledge.summary: An AVA (2012) of about 3,800 square miles (2.4 million acres) in northeastern Wisconsin along the Niagara Escarpment, including the Door Peninsula. Lake Michigan and Green Bay moderate the climate; cold-hardy hybrids dominate.

us-yadkin-valley.name: Yadkin Valley
us-yadkin-valley.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Chardonnay, Viognier, Chambourcin
us-yadkin-valley.summary: North Carolina's first AVA (2002), about 1.4 million acres in the Piedmont along the Yadkin River northwest of Winston-Salem. Former tobacco farmers replanted with vinifera and hybrids; more than 40 wineries make Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Chardonnay and Viognier. Shelton Vineyards (1999) led the expansion.

us-yakima-valley.name: Yakima Valley
us-yakima-valley.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Chardonnay, Riesling
us-yakima-valley.summary: Washington's first AVA (1983), along the Yakima River from Union Gap to near the Tri-Cities. It is the historical centre of Washington grape growing: Concord for juice, then wine grapes from the 1960s. Today about a third of the state's wine grapes grow here. The west end is cooler, the east end warmer; famous vineyards include Red Willow (planted 1973, an early source of Syrah) and Boushey.

us-yamhill-carlton.name: Yamhill-Carlton
us-yamhill-carlton.summary: A horseshoe of low foothills (2004, boundary refined 2010) around the towns of Yamhill and Carlton, limited to elevations between 200 and 1,000 feet. Coarse-grained, ancient marine sediments (Willakenzie) drain quickly, and vines ripen early; the Pinot Noirs are dark-fruited and broad-shouldered. The AVA was approved as 'Yamhill-Carlton District' and later shortened.
us-yamhill-carlton.nerd_note: Ken Wright's Carlton winery helped turn the town into a tasting-room hub; Shea Vineyard is one of Oregon's most bottled single vineyards.

us-york-mountain.name: York Mountain
us-york-mountain.summary: A tiny, cool AVA (1983) in the Santa Lucia Range between Paso Robles and the coast, at about 450 m. Andrew York founded a winery here in 1882, one of the oldest in the county; marine air makes it far cooler than Paso Robles, which is why TTB kept it separate.
us-york-mountain.nerd_note: York Mountain sits outside the Paso Robles AVA even though it is almost surrounded by it.

us-yorkville-highlands.name: Yorkville Highlands
us-yorkville-highlands.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah
us-yorkville-highlands.summary: Rolling, rocky hills (1998) along Highway 128 between Cloverdale and the Anderson Valley, at about 300 to 760 m. Gravelly, low-fertility soils and a climate between the warm Alexander Valley and the cool Anderson Valley suit Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir and Bordeaux and Rhône reds.

us-yountville.name: Yountville
us-yountville.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Chardonnay
us-yountville.summary:
Named for George C. Yount, who planted the valley's first vines in the late 1830s, Yountville (1999) sits where the valley floor starts to feel the bay: cooler and windier than Oakville, with clay-rich and gravelly soils around a few low volcanic knolls. Cabernet here is firmer and more savoury, and Merlot does well.

Dominus Estate is the flagship: Christian Moueix of Pomerol leased and later bought the historic Napanook vineyard (once owned by Inglenook's John Daniel Jr.), made his first Dominus in 1983, and in 1997 built a winery by Herzog & de Meuron whose walls are wire cages filled with local basalt. Domaine Chandon, Moët & Chandon's California outpost (1973), is also here.
us-yountville.terroir: Mixed alluvial and clay soils with volcanic knolls; marine air from San Pablo Bay moderates afternoons.
us-yountville.nerd_note: Dominus's gabion walls let air and light filter through the stones, cooling the cellar without much air conditioning.

us-yucaipa-valley.name: Yucaipa Valley
us-yucaipa-valley.summary: A new AVA (2024) of 36,467 acres in San Bernardino County, in the foothills of the San Bernardino Mountains, with about 23 vineyards and two wineries at approval. Elevations of 600 to 1,500 m and cool canyon winds set it apart from the hot inland valleys.

sites.name: Chateau Montelena
sites.text: Alfred L. Tubbs, a San Francisco rope maker, built this stone château under Mount St. Helena in 1882. Revived in 1972 by Jim Barrett, with Mike Grgich as winemaker, it made the 1973 Chardonnay that beat four white Burgundies at the 1976 Paris tasting and became the subject of the film Bottle Shock.

sites.name: Stag's Leap Wine Cellars (S.L.V. and FAY)
sites.text: Warren Winiarski bought land next to Nathan Fay's Cabernet vineyard in 1970 and planted S.L.V.; its 1973 Cabernet, from three-year-old vines, won the red flight in Paris in 1976. The estate bought FAY in 1986. Cask 23 is a blend of the two. Antinori has owned it outright since 2023.

sites.name: To Kalon Vineyard
sites.text: Hamilton W. Crabb planted these western Oakville benchlands from 1868 and called them To Kalon, 'the highest beauty'. Robert Mondavi built his 1966 winery on its edge. Today the vineyard is split among Mondavi (Constellation), Beckstoffer, Opus One and the Detert and MacDonald families, and its Cabernets fetch some of the highest grape prices in the country.

sites.name: Robert Mondavi Winery
sites.text: Cliff May's mission-style arch on Highway 29 marks the first major winery built in Napa after Prohibition (1966). Mondavi pushed cold fermentation, French oak, varietal labels and the dry, oaked 'Fumé Blanc', and he opened his doors to visitors when tasting rooms were rare.

sites.name: Opus One
sites.text: The joint venture of Robert Mondavi and Baron Philippe de Rothschild of Château Mouton Rothschild, announced in 1980 with the 1979 vintage. The half-buried limestone winery opened in 1991 opposite the Mondavi winery, and the wine is a single Bordeaux-style blend sold, in part, through the Bordeaux négociant system.

sites.name: Inglenook
sites.text: Gustave Niebaum founded Inglenook around 1880 and built the ivy-covered château in 1887. Under his great-nephew John Daniel Jr. it made Cabernets such as the 1941 that are still counted among the greatest American wines. Francis Ford Coppola bought it in 1975 and restored the Inglenook name in 2011.

sites.name: Beaulieu Vineyard
sites.text: Georges de Latour founded Beaulieu in 1900 and kept it alive through Prohibition with sacramental wine for the Catholic Church. From 1938 André Tchelistcheff introduced cold fermentation, malolactic control and small French oak here, and the Georges de Latour Private Reserve (first vintage 1936) set the template for Napa Cabernet.

sites.name: Schramsberg Vineyards
sites.text: Jacob Schram, a German barber, planted here in 1862 and dug caves with Chinese labourers; Robert Louis Stevenson visited in 1880 and wrote of wine as 'bottled poetry'. Jack and Jamie Davies revived the estate in 1965 for traditional-method sparkling wine, and their Blanc de Blancs was poured at Nixon's 'Toast to Peace' in Beijing in 1972.

sites.name: Harlan Estate
sites.text: Bill Harlan planted terraced hillside vineyards in the western Oakville hills from 1984; the first vintage was 1990. With tiny production and near-perfect scores, Harlan became one of the defining 'cult Cabernets' of the 1990s.

sites.name: Screaming Eagle
sites.text: Jean Phillips bought a small vineyard on the eastern side of Oakville in 1986 and released her first Cabernet, the 1992, by mailing list. It became the archetype of the cult Napa wine. Stan Kroenke and Charles Banks bought the estate in 2006.

sites.name: Dominus Estate (Napanook)
sites.text: Christian Moueix of Château Pétrus made his first Dominus in 1983 from the Napanook vineyard, once owned by Inglenook's John Daniel Jr. The 1997 winery by Herzog & de Meuron is built of basalt-filled steel gabions.

sites.name: Diamond Creek Vineyards
sites.text: Al Brounstein planted 8 ha on Diamond Mountain in 1968 and from 1972 bottled Volcanic Hill, Red Rock Terrace and Gravelly Meadow separately, the first block-by-block Cabernets in Napa. The Henriot family's Maisons & Domaines bought the estate in 2020.

sites.name: Martha's Vineyard (Heitz)
sites.text: Tom and Martha May's vineyard on the western edge of Oakville gave Joe Heitz a single-vineyard Cabernet from 1966, one of the first in California. Its mint and eucalyptus note made it famous; the 1974 is a legend.

sites.name: Heitz Cellar
sites.text: Joe and Alice Heitz founded their winery in 1961 and made Martha's Vineyard Cabernet one of the first famous single-vineyard wines in America. The Heitz 1970 Martha's Vineyard topped one of the 1986 Paris rematch tastings.

sites.name: Mayacamas Vineyards
sites.text: John Henry Fisher built the stone winery high on Mt. Veeder in 1889. Under Bob and Elinor Travers (1968 to 2013) it made slow-ageing Cabernet; the 1971 was in the 1976 Paris tasting and tied for third in the 2006 rematch.

sites.name: Charles Krug Winery
sites.text: Founded in 1861 by Prussian immigrant Charles Krug, Napa's first commercial winery. Cesare Mondavi bought it in 1943; a family quarrel there in 1965 sent his son Robert off to build his own winery at Oakville.

sites.name: Beringer Rhine House
sites.text: Jacob and Frederick Beringer founded the winery in 1876 and dug tunnels into the hillside; Frederick's 1884 Rhine House copies the family home in Mainz. Beringer stayed open through Prohibition with sacramental wine.

sites.name: Trefethen (Eshcol winery)
sites.appellation: Oak Knoll District of Napa Valley
sites.text: The three-storey wooden Eshcol winery was built in 1886 for the Goodman brothers to a design by Hamden McIntyre. The Trefethens bought it in 1968; their 1976 Chardonnay was named best Chardonnay at the 1979 Gault-Millau tasting in Paris. The building leaned badly after the 2014 earthquake and was restored.

sites.name: Far Niente
sites.text: John Benson built Far Niente ('without a care') in 1885 with architect Hamden McIntyre. Abandoned after Prohibition, it was restored from 1979 by Gil Nickel and is known for Oakville Cabernet and Chardonnay.

sites.name: Domaine Carneros
sites.text: Champagne Taittinger's California sparkling house (1987), built as a copy of the 18th-century Château de la Marquetterie in Champagne and sitting on a knoll above Carneros vineyards.

sites.name: Buena Vista Winery
sites.text: Agoston Haraszthy bought this land in 1856 and from 1857 dug tunnels and built the first stone wine cellars in California. In 1861 he returned from Europe with more than 100,000 vine cuttings of over 350 varieties. The 1862 Press House still stands. Jean-Charles Boisset bought and restored the estate in 2011.

sites.name: Mission San Francisco Solano
sites.text: Founded on 4 July 1823, the last and northernmost of California's 21 Franciscan missions. Its vineyard of Mission grapes was the start of wine in Sonoma; after secularisation in the 1830s General Mariano Vallejo took over the vines.

sites.name: Gundlach Bundschu (Rhinefarm)
sites.text: Jacob Gundlach planted the Rhinefarm vineyard in 1858; Charles Bundschu joined later. The family survived the 1906 earthquake and Prohibition and still farms the land, making it one of California's oldest family-run wineries.

sites.name: Hanzell Vineyards
sites.text: James D. Zellerbach, a paper magnate and US ambassador to Italy, planted Chardonnay and Pinot Noir here in 1953 and built a small winery modelled on Clos de Vougeot. Hanzell is credited with introducing French oak barrels and temperature-controlled stainless steel to California winemaking. Its Pinot Noir vineyard is among the oldest in the state.

sites.name: Monte Rosso Vineyard
sites.text: A red-soiled vineyard high on the Mayacamas above the Sonoma Valley, planted in the 1880s by Emmanuel Goldstein and bought by Louis M. Martini in 1938. Its own-rooted Zinfandel and old Cabernet supply Martini and a string of small producers.

sites.name: Williams Selyem
sites.text: Burt Williams and Ed Selyem made their first Pinot Noir in 1981 in a garage, buying grapes from Rochioli and others along Westside Road. Their single-vineyard Pinots became the cult wines of the Russian River Valley; John Dyson bought the winery in 1998.

sites.name: Rochioli Vineyards
sites.text: The Rochioli family has farmed on Westside Road since the 1930s and planted Pinot Noir in the late 1960s. Its East Block, West Block and other parcels supplied the wines that built Williams Selyem's and Gary Farrell's reputations.

sites.name: Kistler Vineyards
sites.text: Steve Kistler and Mark Bixler made their first wines in 1979; from the Vine Hill Road winery in the Russian River Valley they produced dense, single-vineyard Chardonnays and Pinot Noirs that became benchmarks.

sites.name: Hirsch Vineyards
sites.text: David Hirsch planted vines on a remote ridge above the Pacific in 1980, astride the San Andreas fault. Fruit sold to Kistler, Littorai, Williams Selyem and others proved that the extreme coast could ripen Pinot Noir; the family now makes its own wines.

sites.name: Fort Ross
sites.text: The Russian-American Company's outpost on the Sonoma coast (1812 to 1841), where Russian settlers are said to have planted some of the first vines in northern California by 1817. Now a state historic park; the AVA above it borrows its name.

sites.name: Ridge Lytton Springs
sites.text: Ridge bought Lytton Springs in 1991, after making wine from its century-old Zinfandel, Petite Sirah and Carignan since 1972. The straw-bale winery and its field-blend Lytton Springs bottling are a lesson in how old California mixed plantings work.

sites.name: Korbel Champagne Cellars
sites.text: The Czech Korbel brothers cleared redwoods here for lumber and turned to wine; from 1882 they made bottle-fermented sparkling wine. Korbel still uses the term 'California Champagne', allowed for brands grandfathered under the 2006 US-EU wine agreement.

sites.name: Simi Winery
sites.text: Giuseppe and Pietro Simi from Tuscany founded the winery in 1876 and built the stone cellar at Healdsburg in 1890. Isabelle Simi ran it for decades and kept it going through Prohibition.

sites.name: Iron Horse Vineyards
sites.appellation: Green Valley of Russian River Valley
sites.text: Barry and Audrey Sterling bought this foggy Green Valley ranch in 1976. Its traditional-method sparkling wines were served at the Reagan-Gorbachev summits and have been poured at White House state dinners ever since.

sites.name: Fountaingrove Round Barn site
sites.text: Site of the Fountaingrove community founded by Thomas Lake Harris in 1875, where Kanaye Nagasawa, a samurai-born Japanese immigrant, made some of California's most admired wines before Prohibition. The 1899 Round Barn survived for more than a century until the Tubbs Fire destroyed it in October 2017.

sites.name: Roederer Estate
sites.text: Champagne Louis Roederer chose the cool Anderson Valley in 1982 after a long search for a California site. Its estate-grown sparkling wines, especially the vintage L'Ermitage, are among the best traditional-method wines in the United States.

sites.name: Navarro Vineyards
sites.text: Ted Bennett and Deborah Cahn started Navarro in 1974 and made it the reference for dry Alsace-style Gewürztraminer and Riesling in California, sold mostly by mailing list.

sites.name: Ridge Monte Bello
sites.class: Monte Bello Cabernet: 1st at the 2006 Judgment of Paris rematch
sites.text: Osea Perrone planted on this limestone ridge in the 1880s. Four engineers from the Stanford Research Institute bought the property in 1959 and made their first commercial wine in 1962. Paul Draper's Monte Bello Cabernet placed fifth among the reds at Paris in 1976 and won the rematches of 2006, establishing it as one of the longest-lived wines of the New World.

sites.name: Mount Eden Vineyards
sites.text: Martin Ray, a purist who fought for honest varietal labelling, planted this mountaintop above Saratoga in the 1940s. The estate, run by Jeffrey Patterson since 1981, makes long-lived Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Cabernet from 'Mount Eden' clones descended from old California selections.

sites.name: Calera (Mt. Harlan)
sites.text: Josh Jensen found limestone and an old lime kiln (calera in Spanish) high in the Gabilan Range and planted Pinot Noir from 1975. Calera's single-parcel Pinots from Mt. Harlan are among California's most Burgundian.

sites.name: Calera Winery (Cienega Road)
sites.text: Calera's gravity-flow winery, built in 1977 into the hillside of an old limestone rock-crushing plant on Cienega Road, below its Mt. Harlan vineyards. The terraced building lets grapes and wine move by gravity from level to level, a Burgundian approach Josh Jensen chose before it was fashionable in California.

sites.name: Chalone Vineyard
sites.text: Vines were first planted on this limestone bench below the Pinnacles around 1919; some Chenin Blanc from that era survives. Dick Graff's Chalone made some of California's first Burgundian Chardonnays; the 1974 placed third among the whites at Paris in 1976.

sites.name: Pisoni Vineyards
sites.text: Gary Pisoni planted vines high on the family's cattle ranch in the Santa Lucia Highlands from 1982, using cuttings of disputed Burgundian origin. Pisoni and Garys' Vineyard Pinot Noir made the Highlands famous.

sites.name: Wente Vineyards
sites.text: Carl H. Wente bought land in Livermore in 1883. In 1912 Ernest Wente is said to have obtained Chardonnay cuttings from the vine nursery at the University of Montpellier; selections from them, the 'Wente clone', became the source of most California Chardonnay. Wente claims the first varietally labelled Chardonnay in America (1936).

sites.name: Concannon Vineyard
sites.text: Irish immigrant James Concannon founded the winery in 1883 and kept it alive through Prohibition with sacramental wine. In 1961 Concannon released the first varietally labelled Petite Sirah in the United States.

sites.name: Bien Nacido Vineyard
sites.text: The Miller family planted Bien Nacido ('well born') on old Spanish land-grant benches above the Santa Maria River from 1973. Its blocks are leased to and named by dozens of wineries; Au Bon Climat and Qupé built their shared winery on the property.

sites.name: Sanford & Benedict Vineyard
sites.text: Richard Sanford and Michael Benedict planted Pinot Noir and Chardonnay on Santa Rosa Road in 1971, the first vineyard in what became the Sta. Rita Hills. Its own-rooted 1971 blocks still produce, now owned by the Terlato family.

sites.name: Tablas Creek Vineyard
sites.text: Founded in 1989 by the Perrin family of Château de Beaucastel and importer Robert Haas, who chose the limestone hills of west Paso Robles. Their imported Rhône clones, quarantined and propagated in their own nursery, went on to supply hundreds of American wineries.

sites.name: Mission San Antonio de Padua
sites.text: Founded in 1771, the third California mission. Its restored grist mill and mission-era water system recall the irrigated gardens and vineyards that supplied wine for mass.

sites.name: Old Palmtag-Almaden winery, Cienega Valley
sites.text: William Palmtag planted here in the 1850s. The old winery building sits right on the San Andreas fault, whose slow creep (about 1 cm a year) has visibly split the structure, a favourite stop for geologists.

sites.name: Mission San Gabriel Arcángel (Trinity Vine)
sites.text: Founded in 1771, San Gabriel became the 'mother vineyard' of southern California, supplying Mission grape cuttings and wine. A vine in the mission garden, known as the Trinity vine, is traditionally said to be descended from the original planting and is often called the oldest living Mission vine in California.

sites.name: Mission San Diego de Alcalá
sites.text: Founded by Junípero Serra in July 1769, the first of California's 21 missions. Tradition credits it with the first planting of the Mission grape in what is now California; some historians favour San Juan Capistrano or San Gabriel for the first vintage.

sites.name: Guasti (Italian Vineyard Company)
sites.text: Secondo Guasti founded the Italian Vineyard Company here in 1900 and built a company town with a church and school. At its peak the vineyard covered about 5,000 acres and was promoted as the largest in the world. The old winery buildings survive next to Ontario airport.

sites.name: Galleano Winery
sites.text: Founded in 1927 by Domenico Galleano, a family winery that still farms and buys old, dry-farmed Zinfandel and Mission vines in the Cucamonga Valley, a living remnant of what was once the largest wine district in California.

sites.name: Bechthold Vineyard
sites.text: Joseph Spenker planted this Cinsault in 1886 on Lodi's sandy soils, and the own-rooted, head-trained vines are among the oldest Cinsault in the world. His descendants, the Bechthold family, still own it; Michael David farms it and it supplies producers from Turley to Bedrock.

sites.name: Sobon Estate (D'Agostini winery, 1856)
sites.text: Adam Uhlinger founded a winery here in 1856, later the D'Agostini Winery and one of the oldest in California. Sobon Estate now runs it, with a museum of Gold Rush-era winemaking in the old stone cellar.

sites.name: The Eyrie Vineyards (original vineyard)
sites.text: David and Diana Lett planted Oregon's first Willamette Valley Pinot Noir here in 1965 to 1966 against the advice of UC Davis. The 1975 South Block Reserve stunned French judges at the 1979 Gault-Millau tasting and in Drouhin's 1980 rematch. Eyrie also made the first Pinot Gris in the United States.

sites.name: The Eyrie Vineyards winery
sites.text: The Letts' winery in a converted turkey-processing plant in McMinnville, where Jason Lett now makes wine from his parents' old, own-rooted Dundee Hills vines. The family still releases older vintages from its library, showing how long Willamette Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris can age.

sites.name: Domaine Drouhin Oregon
sites.text: Robert Drouhin of Beaune, impressed by Eyrie's showing in 1979 and 1980, bought land in the Dundee Hills in 1987, made a first vintage in 1988 and built this multi-level gravity-flow winery in 1989, the first major Burgundian investment in Oregon. Véronique Drouhin-Boss makes the wines.

sites.name: Sokol Blosser
sites.text: Bill Sokol Blosser and Susan Sokol Blosser planted in the Dundee Hills in 1971; in 2002 their winery was the first in the US to earn LEED certification for a green building.

sites.name: HillCrest Vineyard
sites.text: Richard Sommer, a UC Davis student, planted Riesling and other varieties near Roseburg in 1961 and founded what is regarded as Oregon's oldest continuously operating estate winery; he also planted the state's first post-Prohibition Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Abacela
sites.text: Earl and Hilda Jones searched the West for a climate like Spain's Ribera del Duero and planted Tempranillo here in 1995, Oregon's first. They also pioneered Albariño in the Pacific Northwest.

sites.name: Cayuse Vineyards (The Rocks)
sites.text: Christophe Baron noticed the cobblestone fields south of Walla Walla in 1996 and planted the Cailloux vineyard in 1997, farmed biodynamically. Cayuse's Syrahs and Grenaches (Bionic Frog, God Only Knows) became cult wines.

sites.name: Ciel du Cheval Vineyard
sites.text: Planted in 1975 by Jim Holmes and John Williams (who also founded Kiona), one of the first vineyards on Red Mountain. Its Cabernet, Merlot and Syrah supply a who's who of Washington wineries.

sites.name: Champoux Vineyard
sites.text: Planted in 1972 as part of Mercer Ranch and farmed by Paul Champoux from 1989. Quilceda Creek's Champoux Cabernets helped put Washington among the world's great Cabernet regions.

sites.name: Leonetti Cellar
sites.text: Gary Figgins founded Leonetti in 1977 on land his Italian grandfather farmed; its 1978 Cabernet appeared on the cover of a national wine magazine and made Walla Walla famous.

sites.name: Quilceda Creek
sites.text: Alex Golitzin, nephew of André Tchelistcheff, founded Quilceda Creek in Snohomish west of the Cascades in 1979 and trucked grapes from eastern Washington. Its 2002 Cabernet was the first Washington wine to receive 100 points from The Wine Advocate.

sites.name: Chateau Ste. Michelle
sites.text: Washington's largest and best-known winery, whose roots go back to Prohibition-era companies; the château at Woodinville near Seattle opened in 1976. Its Eroica Riesling partnership with Ernst Loosen (from 1999) helped make Washington a Riesling powerhouse.

sites.name: Red Willow Vineyard
sites.text: Mike Sauer planted Red Willow in 1973 on the western edge of the Yakima Valley and, working with David Lake MW of Columbia Winery, planted some of Washington's first Syrah in the mid-1980s. A small stone chapel on the hilltop is a landmark.

sites.name: Ste. Chapelle
sites.text: Founded in 1975 by the Symms family and named for the Gothic chapel in Paris that inspired its original building, Ste. Chapelle led the revival of Idaho wine and remains its largest producer.

sites.name: Dr. Konstantin Frank Winery
sites.text: On the west side of Keuka Lake, Dr. Konstantin Frank, a Ukrainian-born viticulturist who had grown vinifera in the Russian cold, planted Riesling and other European vines in the late 1950s and released his first vintage in 1962. His success showed that the eastern US could grow vinifera, and his estate is still family-owned.

sites.name: Hermann J. Wiemer Vineyard
sites.text: Hermann Wiemer, from a Mosel winemaking family, planted on the west side of Seneca Lake in 1973 and ran a grafting nursery that supplied vinifera vines across the East. His dry Rieslings set the Finger Lakes standard; Fred Merwarth and Oskar Bynke now run the estate.

sites.name: Brotherhood Winery
sites.text: Founded by Jean Jacques, a French Huguenot shoemaker, who made his first commercial vintage in 1839; it survived Prohibition by making sacramental wine and is commonly called the oldest continuously operating winery in the United States. Its underground cellars date from the 1880s and 1890s.

sites.name: Pleasant Valley Wine Company
sites.text: Founded in 1860 near Hammondsport as one of the first bonded wineries in the United States; its 'Great Western' sparkling wine won a medal at the 1867 Paris Exposition. The stone cellars are on the National Register of Historic Places.

sites.name: Castello di Borghese (former Hargrave Vineyard)
sites.text: Alex and Louisa Hargrave planted Long Island's first commercial vinifera vineyard here at Cutchogue in 1973, starting an industry on old potato fields. Marco and Ann Marie Borghese bought it in 1999.

sites.name: Benmarl Winery
sites.text: Hilltop vineyard above the Hudson at Marlboro, said to have been planted in the 1700s and later worked by Andrew Caywood, who bred grapes here in the 19th century; illustrator Mark Miller revived it in 1957 and it holds New York Farm Winery licence No. 1.

sites.name: Thomas Jefferson's Monticello
sites.text: Jefferson planted European vines in the gardens below his house from 1770 and for decades tried to grow wine grapes, without success; he was also America's most ardent buyer of Bordeaux and Burgundy. The restored vineyard on the south terrace grows varieties he planted.

sites.name: Barboursville Vineyards
sites.text: The Zonin family from Veneto founded Barboursville in 1976 on the estate of Governor James Barbour, whose 1814 mansion, designed by Jefferson, burned in 1884 and stands as a ruin. Gabriele Rausse planted vinifera here when experts said it was impossible; Octagon, its Bordeaux blend, is a Virginia classic.

sites.name: Jamestown (Acte 12, 1619)
sites.text: At the first General Assembly of the Virginia colony in 1619, legislators passed Acte 12, requiring every householder to plant and maintain ten grapevines. French vignerons were later recruited, but disease defeated the vinifera.

sites.name: The Mother Vine (Roanoke Island)
sites.text: A giant Scuppernong vine at Manteo on Roanoke Island, reputed to be about 400 years old and possibly planted by Croatan people or the Roanoke colonists of the 1580s; often called the oldest cultivated grapevine in the United States. It is privately owned.

sites.name: Renault Winery
sites.text: Louis Nicholas Renault, sent by Champagne houses to find an American site for sparkling wine, founded this winery at Egg Harbor City in 1864. It survived Prohibition by selling 'Renault Wine Tonic' in pharmacies and is one of the oldest continuously operating wineries in the US.

sites.name: Biltmore Estate Winery
sites.text: The Vanderbilt family's estate at Asheville opened a winery in the old dairy barn in 1985; it is often described as the most visited winery in the United States, though much of its fruit comes from California and Washington.

sites.name: Stone Hill Winery
sites.text: Founded in 1847 by German immigrant Michael Poeschel above Hermann; by the 1880s it was billed as the second-largest winery in the US, with wines winning at world fairs. During Prohibition its arched cellars were used to grow mushrooms; the Held family revived it in 1965.

sites.name: Mount Pleasant Estates
sites.text: Founded in 1859 by Friedrich Münch, a German pastor and writer, in Augusta, the town that became America's first AVA in 1980. Its 19th-century cellars survive.

sites.name: Hermann Jaeger's Neosho vineyards
sites.text: Swiss-born Hermann Jaeger settled near Neosho in 1865 and bred more than 100 grape varieties from native species. Working with George Husmann, he shipped about 17 boxcars of phylloxera-resistant cuttings to France, and in 1893 France made him a Chevalier of the Légion d'honneur. He disappeared in 1895.

sites.name: T.V. Munson Memorial Vineyard
sites.text: At Denison, Thomas Volney Munson studied native Texas grapes and bred hundreds of varieties. His rootstock recommendations helped France replant after phylloxera, earning him the Mérite Agricole in 1888; Cognac is Denison's sister city. Grayson College maintains this vineyard of his varieties.

sites.name: Val Verde Winery
sites.text: Frank Qualia, an Italian immigrant, founded Val Verde at Del Rio in 1883; it is the oldest continuously operating winery in Texas and survived Prohibition selling table grapes.

sites.name: Llano Estacado Winery
sites.text: Founded near Lubbock in 1976 by Texas Tech professors and others, it led the modern Texas wine revival and is one of the state's largest wineries.

sites.name: Eden Park (Longworth's Garden of Eden vineyard)
sites.text: Nicholas Longworth's hillside vineyard, which he called the Garden of Eden, grew the Catawba for his sparkling wine, America's first famous wine in the 1840s and 1850s. The land became Cincinnati's Eden Park.

sites.name: Lonz Winery (Golden Eagle), Middle Bass Island
sites.text: Golden Eagle Winery on Middle Bass Island was billed as America's largest winery in the 1870s; the castle-like Lonz building of 1942 stands over its old cellars and is now a state park.

sites.name: Chateau Grand Traverse
sites.text: Edward O'Keefe planted Michigan's first commercial vinifera vineyard here on the Old Mission Peninsula in 1974, when most local growers relied on hybrids and cherries. Riesling, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir on the lake-moderated slopes proved that northern Michigan could make fine wine, and the family still runs the estate.

sites.name: Wollersheim Winery (Haraszthy site)
sites.text: Agoston Haraszthy planted vines on this hillside above the Wisconsin River in the 1840s before he left for California; Peter Kehl dug the stone cellars in 1858. The Wollersheim family has run it since 1972.

sites.name: Senecú mission area (first vines in the US, c. 1629)
sites.text: Around 1629 Franciscan friars García de San Francisco and Antonio de Arteaga planted Mission grapes at the Piro pueblo mission of San Antonio de Senecú south of Socorro, to make sacramental wine: the first wine grapes in what became the United States. The exact site is lost.

sites.name: Gruet Winery
sites.text: The Gruet family, Champagne growers from Bethon, planted vineyards near Truth or Consequences in southern New Mexico in 1984 at about 1,300 m and makes traditional-method sparkling wine in Albuquerque. Gruet Brut and Blanc de Noirs became some of the best-value American sparklers.

sites.name: Sonoita Vineyards
sites.text: Dr. Gordon Dutt, a University of Arizona soil scientist, ran test plots that led to Arizona's first AVA (1984) and founded this winery at Elgin in 1983.

sites.name: MauiWine (Ulupalakua Ranch)
sites.text: Emil Tedeschi and rancher Pardee Erdman founded Tedeschi Vineyards on the slopes of Haleakalā in 1974; the tasting room is the 19th-century King's Cottage, built for King Kalākaua's visits, a short drive below the estate vineyards that make up America's smallest AVA.

sites.name: Palisade wine country
sites.text: Orchards and vineyards on the Colorado River below the Book Cliffs, where warm air and canyon breezes protect fruit from frost. Most of Colorado's wine grapes grow within a few kilometres of this town.
